en: (B1) (1 Topic: Since Dharma has its root in the Word [of the Veda], that which lacks the Word as its basis should be disregarded. Jaimini 1.3.1.

When there is doubt as to whether the Smṛtis composed by Manu and others—which are accepted by the learned members of the three higher castes—possess authority regarding dharma and adharma or not, they lack authority because there is no means of ascertaining that they have a foundation in the Veda.
(B2) Now begins the third quarter of the first chapter.
(The connection of the *Smṛti* quarter with the two preceding quarters, as well as the determination of the seeds for the commencement of the *Smṛti* quarter prior to the *Nāmadheya* quarter:

Following the declaration of the inquiry into the nature of *dharma* and *adharma* by the opening aphorism of the treatise, "Now, therefore, the inquiry into *dharma*" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*), [the following is stated].

Since the inquiry into the mere means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that [Dharma] has already been undertaken, in the first chapter— aimed at defining the means of valid cognition as a whole— the validity of *codanā* (Vedic injunction), which is the primary among those means, was established first in the first quarter (*pāda*). Then, in the second quarter, the validity of the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and mantras, which appear as subordinate parts of that [injunction], was established through their syntactic unity with the injunction (*vidhyekavākyatā*), because they are more closely related [to the injunction] than names (*nāmadheya*).

Since names are established as being rooted in explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), mantras, and so forth, and since the investigation into the authority of *smṛti* and other sources follows immediately after the proof of the authority of *arthavāda* and mantras, this forthcoming inquiry into the authority of *smṛti* and the like is introduced through the logical connection of "opportunity" (*avasara-saṅgati*). Therefore, it is not irrelevant to the chapter (*adhyāya*), for nowhere is it observed that *smṛti* and the like are rooted in names.

Furthermore, since a name lacks the status of being an independent constituent sentence of the Veda— unlike injunctions, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), or mantras— within the context of the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*),
and since its authority is already established by the very proof of the authority of the *codanā*,
its treatment at the beginning is not irrelevant.
For this very reason, at the beginning of the section, the Commentator stated: "In this way, the authority of the entire Veda has been declared.

This is because the restriction that "injunction alone is the means of valid knowledge" can be understood as emphasizing its primacy; just as the rule regarding clarified butter (*ājya*) for the acts of spreading and sprinkling excludes other substances, and the rule regarding rice (*vrīhi*) for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) excludes other grains, so too does this restriction exclude other independent means of knowledge of the same class. Furthermore, since explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and mantras serve such a purpose [of exclusion], they are included within the scope of the Veda’s authority.

There is no contradiction, just as in the case of [the Veda's] authority; the meaning is that he begins the investigation into the authority of Smṛti and so forth, having kept in mind the point that the authority of Smṛti and the rest is established precisely by their being rooted in the Vedic injunction (codanā)—thus: "By the learned... (śiṣṭa).

Since the lack of authority is ascertained precisely because of its being of human origin, the phrase beginning with "by the learned" (*śiṣṭa*) was stated in order to dispel the doubt: "How could there be even a possibility of its authority?"
(The division of the Purāṇas included among the fields of knowledge, and the mention of their names:
Here, the term "of the Smṛtis" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for right conduct (*sadācāra*) and other sources of Dharma apart from the Vedas.
And these are: "The Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, the Dharmaśāstras, along with the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*)."
Yājñavalkya has stated that "the Vedas are the fourteen sources of knowledge and of dharma.

Among these, the Purāṇas— composed by the venerable Bādarāyaṇa, which set forth the accounts of primary creation, secondary creation, the Manvantaras, and the genealogical histories— are the Brāhma, Pādma, Śaiva, Bhāgavata, Nāradīya, Mārkaṇḍeya, Āgneya, and Bhaviṣya.
The Brahmakaivarta, Laiṅga, Vārāha, Brahmāṇḍa, Vāyu-purāṇa, Skānda, Vāmana, Kaurma, Mātsya, and Gāruḍa— these are the eighteen [major Purāṇas] in their respective order.
Furthermore, the eighteen Upapurāṇas are also included within the category of Purāṇas themselves.
Nyāya is the science composed by Gautama consisting of five chapters, and that composed by Kaṇāda consisting of ten chapters.

(An Analysis of the Meaning of the Term *Mīmāṃsā*): *Mīmāṃsā* refers to the twelve-chapter work composed by Jaimini beginning with “Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma,” as well as the four-chapter *Saṃkarṣaṇakāṇḍa*, which together constitute Karma-mīmāṃsā; and the four-chapter work composed by Vyāsa beginning with “Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman,” which constitutes Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā.
(The subject matter of the Dharmaśāstras and the names of their authors:

The Dharmaśāstra, however, is that which was composed by the authors of the respective Smṛtis as a systematic exposition of the specific duties of the social classes (varṇas) and stages of life (āśramas).

And these—Manu, Atri, Viṣṇu, Aṅgiras, Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Yama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Kātyāyana, Bṛhaspati, Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Dakṣa, Gautama, Śātātapa, Vasiṣṭha, and others—are the promulgators of the Dharmaśāstras as stated by Yājñavalkya;
likewise: "Of those [promulgators], moreover, Aṅgiras, Vyāsa, Gautama, Atri, Uśanas, and Yama..."
Vasiṣṭha, Dakṣa, Saṃvarta, Śātātapa, Parāśara, Viṣṇu, Āpastamba, Hārīta, Śaṅkha, Kātyāyana, Guru, Pracetas,
Nārada the Yogi, as well as Bodhāyana and Manu.
Sumantu, Kāśyapa, Babhru, Paiṭhīnasi, Vyāghra,
Satyavrata, Bharadvāja, Gārgya, Kārṣṇyājini, Jābāli, Jamadagni, and Yaugākṣi, who was born from Brahmā.
Thus, thirty-six sages are traditionally remembered as the promulgators of Dharma;
these, as stated by Paiṭhīnasi, are to be known [as such].
Furthermore, the Mahābhārata, Rāmāyaṇa, Sāṃkhya, Pātañjala, Pāśupata, Vaiṣṇava, and other systems are included within the category of Dharmaśāstra itself.
The Sāṃkhya treatise consisting of six chapters was composed by the Blessed One Kapila; likewise, the Pātañjala consisting of four quarters was composed by Patañjali;
and the Pāśupata consisting of five chapters was composed by the Blessed One Paśupati.
The Śaiva mantra-śāstra is included within the Pāśupata itself;
likewise, the Vaiṣṇava [mantra-śāstra] was composed by Nārada and others,
and the Pāñcarātra is included right here within this Vaiṣṇava mantra-śāstra.
However, many maintain that the Vāmāgama and other such works are entirely outside the scope of the scriptures.
Thus, this quartet beginning with the Purāṇas is conventionally designated as the "Upāṅgas" (subsidiary limbs) of the Vedas.
For here there is no basis in perception and the like, because those [means of knowledge] do not apply to dharma and adharma,
and because the Veda is not perceived as being recited through direct perception.

Alternatively, if [the Veda] were perceived [directly], the formulation of its memory (smṛti) would be useless; nor can it be postulated that the Veda is an impermanent object of inference, because the Vedas—as recited in direct perception—are maintained by the followers of the Vedic tradition through the preservation of their respective branches (śākhās), even while discarding minor portions as enumerated.
Nor is the Veda a root based on an impermanent inference.

Since memory, although pervaded by the general [condition] of having a basis, lacks the specific pervasion of being based on the Veda, inference is untenable; furthermore, if one were to assume that even the *Manusmṛti* is merely inferable, it would result in a "blind tradition" (*andhaparamparā*).

Therefore, since it is impossible for it to have the existent as its basis, it follows that it lacks authority because its basis is error and the like—this being the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). (B2)

(Definition of the Vedāṅgas) The auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) are six: phonetics (*śikṣā*), ritual manuals (*kalpa*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), prosody (*chandas*), etymology (*nirukta*), and astronomy (*jyotiṣ*).
Among these, that which is common to all the Vedas is the *Śikṣā* composed by Pāṇini, consisting of five sections beginning with "Now I shall expound the Śikṣā."
Furthermore, there are the Śikṣās, composed under the name *Prātiśākhya* by other sages in various forms according to each Vedic branch (*śākhā*).

The Kalpas were composed by sages such as Bodhāyana and Āpastamba for the sake of knowing the specific sequences of Vedic performance through the synthesis of the subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) belonging to different branches.
The Sūtras composed by sages such as Baijavāpi, Āśvalāyana, and Grāhyāyaṇa are included within these very categories.
As it has been said in the Vārttika: "Those by whom the application [of words] is understood as having an established form with respect to actions..."
“It is said that the sūtras have the purpose of explaining the characteristics.”
The grammar consisting of eight chapters, composed by the venerable Pāṇini through the grace of Maheśvara, is the "Māheśvara" [grammar].
Grammars such as the Kaumāra and others are not limbs of the Veda;
for they are devoted solely to the grammatical derivation of worldly words.
The Nirukta was composed by the venerable Yāska in thirteen chapters, beginning with the words "The collection has been handed down" (samāmnāyaḥ samāmnātaḥ) and so forth;
the work consisting of five chapters known as the Nighaṇṭu, as well as other lexicons composed by Yāska, are all included herein.
And the Jyotiṣa was composed by the venerable Āditya and by Garga and others.
The Vedic prosody (chandas), however, was composed by the venerable Piṅgala in the form of the Aṣṭādhyāyī.
(An exposition on how all branches of knowledge fall within the scope of the *Smṛti* section:
Thus, together with these ten, there are the four Vedas known as the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and Atharvaveda; these constitute the fourteen foundations of Dharma (*dharmasthāna*).
These same fourteen, when combined with the Upavedas known as Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, Gāndharvaveda, and Arthaśāstra, become eighteen.

Although it will be stated that conduct (*ācāra*) and self-satisfaction (*ātmatuṣṭi*), like the Vedas, possess authority regarding *dharma*, nevertheless, because these do not have the nature of verbal scripture (*aśabdarūpa*), this enumeration refers to those works whose nature is verbal, such as the Purāṇas and others; thus there is no contradiction. Since the authority of the Vedas has already been established previously, [the remaining sources] are those distinct from them, excluding those matters perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

The sense is that all those things which, because their purpose is unseen (adṛṣṭa), are accepted as established bases of Dharma (dharmasthāna) and whose status as valid means of knowledge is to be proven on the basis of being rooted in the Veda— these are all the examples here.
(An examination of the lack of authority [of Smṛti], because its source is required and that source—perception and so forth—is impossible):

Now, since the Smṛtis are of human origin—as evidenced by the firm recollection of their authors—they must necessarily have been composed by their authors after they had ascertained, by some means of valid cognition, the relationship of means and end between the Aṣṭakā rites and heaven; for this very reason, the designation "Smṛti" (Recollection) is also justified.
And since the determination of the relationship between the probandum and the probans is not possible through perception and other means, he says: "For it is not here... etc.

Furthermore, if one assumes that [the authority] is rooted in verbal testimony (śabdamūlatva), since that [testimony] is a product, its validity cannot be ascertained; thus, it is impossible for it to be the root. Therefore, it must be stated that the Vedic word itself is the root.
Yet, even that is untenable because it is not perceived; thus he says: "And of the Veda... (vedasya ca).

(Regarding the doubt that the root scripture has been lost and its refutation: Now, even though it is not perceived by people like us, it was perceived by Manu and others through direct recitation; and while it may have now been lost due to human negligence, or may be recited by some in another region, or may even be recited by us, because it is found within the context of other [works], we do not recognize it as being based upon a Smṛti.
Since it is known that conceptual construction (kalpanā) is possible according to the circumstances, how can there be a certainty regarding the non-existence of eternal words?
To this, he says: "Even when there is perception... (upalambhe 'pi ca).
He refutes the claim that its scriptural basis has been lost by saying: "Nowadays... (idānīm).
For those students who do not abandon even a fraction of what they have learned, it is impossible to abandon numerous Vedic statements that serve as the foundation for many Smṛtis.
"The seers know the Ṛgveda to be composed of twenty-one paths;
the Sāmaveda has a thousand paths, and the Yajurveda exceeds one hundred."
They say that the fifteenfold path is called the Navādhvātharvaṇa.

Thus, because the disciple of the true guru has enumerated the various Vedic branches (*śākhā*), and because it is possible for all of them to be studied in one region even if they are not studied in another, the assumption of their total disappearance is not tenable.

Furthermore, the assumption that these [Smṛtis] are rooted in Vedic texts (*śruti*) currently being studied in other regions is also untenable; for if those very texts could have been taught by Manu and others, the composition of the Smṛtis would result in futility.
The meaning is this: "path" (*adhvan*), "divine course" (*devagati*), and "branch" (*śākhā*) are synonymous terms.
(Refutation of the view that the Veda is always inferable):

Regarding this, what is stated by the Guru—“It is not only for us that the Śrutis are to be inferred solely through a logical mark (*liṅga*); rather, they are also to be inferred by Manu and others through other Smṛtis.”
The same applies to what follows that as well;
however, since it has not been seen by anyone, [the opponent suggests] that its basis is the eternally inferred Śruti.
He refutes that too with the words "nor even... (nāpi).

The meaning is as follows: there is a disparity because, although other human-authored Smṛtis are generally pervaded by some underlying source of authority (*mūlapramāṇa*), they cannot be followed as they lack exclusive reliance on Śruti; for if one were to admit that they have some minor basis, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and result in a "blind tradition" (*andhaparaṃparā*).

However, since indicators such as *liṅga* are non-human (*apauruṣeya*), they cannot have another source, and thus there is no contradiction in their being the inferential basis (*kalpaka*) for Śruti. This is the point of difference.

(B1) Since the learned have, up to the present day, accepted through an unbroken tradition both the Aṣṭakā rites and the eating of *kalañja* as being respectively dharma and adharma— just as they have accepted the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices— and since Manu and others, being members of the three higher castes, could have had access to the Vedas,
it is logical that [the Smṛtis] are indeed rooted in those [Vedas].
But it does not have its root in error and the like;
for there would be the fault of unnecessary complexity (gaurava) in postulating such causes as well as their ignorance from time immemorial.
Furthermore, the Śruti itself, as directly perceived, is its very root.
Nor is the composition of the Smṛtis purposeless;

for the composition of the Smṛtis is purposeful because it serves to synthesize other Vedic branches, to extract the meaning from explanatory passages (arthavādas), and to state matters established by logic.
Therefore, it is established that the Smṛtis function as a means of valid knowledge regarding dharma and adharma solely by bringing to mind their source in the Śruti. // 1 //
Thus ends the first section concerning Smṛti.
(B2) (The conclusion regarding non-authoritativeness due to its roots being error and so forth:
By this [same reasoning], presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) based on what is perceived (*dṛṣṭa*) is also to be rejected, as there is no impelling factor (*ākṣepaka*).

Since it is also possible that [the practice] is rooted in error, deception, and so forth—and since the performance of such conduct likewise presupposes knowledge—when one seeks to know the instrument of knowledge for those who performed it previously, it is impossible for it to be rooted in a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*); rather, its root must be error and the like. With this in mind, he concludes the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding its lack of authority with the words: "Therefore... (*ataśca*).
(Proposition regarding the authority of Smṛti, preceded by the determination that in the Siddhānta-sūtra, the term "inference" refers exclusively to presumptive testimony [arthāpatti]:
it is logical that [Smṛti] is rooted in that very [Veda].)

The meaning is that it is proper to postulate that these [Smṛtis] are rooted in Śruti based on the presumption (*arthāpatti*) of a perceptible fact—that their acceptance by learned *śiṣṭas* who possess steadfast wives and belong to the three higher castes would otherwise be inexplicable.
As for the statement:
"Or rather, because the agents are the same, the Smṛti should be authoritative as an inference" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.3.2).

Thus, by the natural force of the word "inference" (*anumāna*) occurring in the Sūtra, and by accepting the inference of Vedic words, the authority of the Smṛtis of Manu and others regarding Dharma is established through the following inference: "The Smṛtis are authoritative with respect to Dharma because they enjoin matters that are practiced by those who perform the injunctions of the Veda, just like the Veda itself";

and [the authority] of Smṛti and custom (*ācāra*) is established through the inference: "Smṛti and custom have the Veda as their source because they were composed by Vedic agents, or because they possess the nature of Dharma and the nature of Smṛti, just like our own memory of the Agnihotra."
And some establish that [the work] is rooted in the Vedas;
and the author of the Prakāśa likewise accepts it as such.
Therefore, it is incorrect [to claim] that there is deviation in the practices of mindfulness that follow after those aims and desires.
For this very reason, it has been refuted; the detailed demonstration of this should be seen in that very same place, the Kaustubha.
Therefore, the statement of inference found in the Sūtra-bhāṣya is in fact nothing but presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).
Consequently, the intended meaning is that this alone serves as the means of valid cognition for establishing that [the Smṛti] is rooted in Śruti.
(Establishing that [the Smṛti] is rooted in a Śruti text recited directly, preceded by the demonstration of the sign of non-perception:
Once its being rooted in Śruti is established, that Śruti was determined by Manu and others precisely through direct recitation.

As for our own non-perception [of it], this is due to the absence of study of those [texts] read in other branches, because—by virtue of the word *svādhyāya* in the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vākya*)—only the study of one’s own branch is required, as will be demonstrated in the section concerning other branches (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*).

Even if [the Veda] were mastered by means other than formal study (*adhyayana*), this is not untenable precisely because those Vedic recensions (*śākhā*) studied by other persons in various regions cannot be heard even by persons possessed of negligence, laziness, and so forth, due to their inability to travel to those respective regions; and furthermore, regarding even those scriptural passages (*śruti*) studied in a single recension that fall within the context of a ritual (*kratuprakaraṇa*), there is the sublation of the property of the rite (*taddharma*) in favor of the property of the person (*puruṣadharma*).

Regarding those [rules] pertaining to human conduct (*puruṣadharma*) which, by subverting their status as human conduct, are established as ritual properties (*kratudharma*) through injunctions inferred from mantras, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and so forth—it is observed that they are beyond the capacity of contemporary persons to determine.

However, since Manu and others, being omniscient, were able to ascertain them through direct recitation (*pratyakṣapāṭha*), it is with the intention that the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) itself is the source, as it was directly recited, that he says: "And the Śruti."
Moreover, the *mantra*s and *arthavāda*s that are clearly recited in the Vedas themselves are seen to be the very source of those various *smṛti*s;
for example, the mantra "yāṃ janāḥ" [is the source] of the *Aṣṭakā-smṛti*.
Likewise, there is the *arthavāda*: "When the king of men has arrived... [which serves as the source] for this [practice regarding] the pregnant cow (*vehata*).
The statement "He bit him with his teeth" is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), based on the *smṛti* rule: "A great bull or a great goat [should be offered].
The same applies to the other [explanatory passages].

Likewise, for practices such as following after one's teacher, the root source is the explanatory passage found in the section on the fire-altar construction (*cayana-prakaraṇa*): "Therefore, the inferior follows behind the superior."
The meaning is that this should be inferred in other cases as well.
(An exposition on the purposefulness of the composition of the Smṛtis):
Anticipating the objection that the composition of the Smṛtis would be useless if those [objects] were already established by Śruti and perception, he refutes it with the words "And not... (na ca).
"By way of an introductory statement of commendation."

The point is that since people of the present day are unable to perform the synthesis of the injunction alone by abandoning the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) whose nature is not that of an injunction, the composition of those [scriptures] is purposeful for the sake of their knowledge.
(Conclusion following the description of the figurative nature of the conventional usage of the authority of Smṛti:
Now, an objection is raised: since Smṛtis and established practices are exhausted by their function as indicators of Śruti, how can they generate valid knowledge regarding dharma and adharma?
For, since dharma and adharma are cognizable solely through the Veda, it is impossible for them to be cognized by those [Smṛtis and practices].
To this he says: "Therefore" (ataḥ).
And thus, the conventional usage of its validity is figurative, just as in the case of inferential marks (*liṅga*) and so forth.
The intention is that the promise to define the means of valid cognition for dharma and adharma in the first sūtra applies to both the primary and the figurative senses alike.

As for the fact that the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) stated that the authority of the Smṛtis concerning the preparation of food and so forth rests on their having a visible purpose in the form of assisting others, and likewise that the authority of practices such as following the teacher rests on their having a visible purpose in the form of pleasing the teacher—

this should be understood as already refuted in the Vārttika itself. Furthermore, regarding those aforementioned sources of Dharma, whatever among them has a visible purpose is rooted solely in perception and other such means of knowledge.
In this regard, the specific distinction between visible and invisible purposes should be consulted in the original treatise;
it is not stated here for fear of prolixity.
Thus ends the first section concerning Smṛti.
(B1) (Section 2 / Adhikaraṇa 2:
"But in case of contradiction, [the Smṛti] should be disregarded, for there is no inference [of a Vedic basis] when [such a basis] does not exist.
(Jaimini Sūtra 1.3.3) Even for those Smṛtis that contradict Śruti—such as "The Audumbarī post must be entirely covered"—validity exists because they are equally rooted in Śruti.
The [proposition] that "one should not chant the udgītha while touching the Audumbarī post" is untenable because it contradicts direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*).

For even when there are contradictions— such as those seen frequently between scriptural injunctions regarding the taking up or not taking up of vessels which have mutually contradictory meanings— there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) to their validity,
since the contradiction can be resolved in exactly the same way by means of option (*vikalpa*).
For in this case, the expectation for a basis of the Smṛti is not satisfied by the direct Vedic text (pratyakṣa-śruti),
such that— by the destruction of its imagined basis— the Smṛti would be sublated by the contradictory direct Vedic text, as is the case with an inferential mark (liṅga).
Nor is there here an absolute contradiction between the two objects, as there is between coldness and heat.

In this context, there would be a sublation (*bādha*) characterized by the removal of the object of knowledge (*prameyāpahāra*), as in the case where the inference of coldness is sublated by the direct perception of heat.

However, this is not the case here, because both [alternatives] are possible through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). To this, the author of the *Bhāṣya* established the following conclusion: in every inference...

Because the desire to know the object of inference (*anumeya-jijñāsā*) is a necessary cause [for inference], and because the *audumbarī* post has already been determined by direct Vedic scripture (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) through the injunction regarding its touch—thereby being characterized as not being wrapped—it follows that there is an absence of such a desire to know; consequently, the inference of a scriptural text concerning the wrapping of the *audumbarī* is impossible.
Likewise, even in cases where there is no contradiction with direct scripture, if greed or similar motives are observed, [the inference of scripture does not arise].

Just as in the case of "the Adhvaryu takes up the cloth used for the Vaiśarjana oblation" and so forth, even there there is no assumption of a Vedic text (*śruti*), because it is appropriate for an already established cause (*klṛptahetu*) alone to serve as the basis [for the Smṛti].

(B2) [The demonstration of the connection by way of exception with the preceding section: By means of the word *tu* ("but") in the Siddhānta-sūtra—"But in case of contradiction, it would be independent, for there is inference only when [the Smṛti] does not exist"—it serves as that which is to be set aside.

In order to demonstrate the investigation of the topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) by means of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) indicated in that sūtra, he states the illustrative example: "Even those [means] which are contrary to Śruti..."

By the word "also" (api), there is an indication of an exceptional connection (*āpavādikī saṅgati*) which serves to dispel the following objection: "If the authority of the Smṛtis of Manu and others is based on their being rooted in Śruti—because the acceptance of them by the learned members of the three higher castes would otherwise be untenable—then let these [Smṛtis] that are contradictory also possess authority for the same reason."
(An explanation of how the phrase "and so forth" includes the two Smṛtis beginning with "forty-eight years," etc.

By the phrase "and so forth," just as the Smṛti regarding the total wrapping of the *audumbarī* post—which contradicts the direct Vedic injunction that "one should chant the *udgītha* after touching the *audumbarī*"—is cited as an example, so too is the Smṛti stating "one should observe Vedic celibacy for forty-eight years," which contradicts the Śruti: "One who has fathered a son and whose hair is black should establish the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*)."

Likewise, the example of the Smṛti rule, "One whose king has been purchased [for sacrifice] has food fit to be eaten," which contradicts the Śruti rule—"When the Agniṣomīya sacrifice is concluded, one should eat at the house of the sacrificer"—is also included as an illustration; for this Smṛti provides the required limit for the prohibition, "One should not eat the food of one who has been initiated."
In the *sadas* pavilion, a piece of wood from an *udumbara* tree is planted upright, reaching up to the height of the sacrificer;
this is the meaning of the term *audumbarī*. [The phrase] "optionally" (*vikalpena*) refers to this.

(An examination of the alternative [view] regarding the distinction between the application of touching and enveloping: Since coldness and heat cannot coexist in fire, and since their contradiction— consisting in their being co-present with the absolute mutual absence of one another— is established by perception, it is impossible for coldness to be inferred [in fire], as it would be sublated by perception.
The meaning is as follows: sublation (*bādha*), characterized by the removal of the object of cognition (*prameya*), is appropriate [in cases where contradiction occurs];

however, in this case, since it is possible for "touching" and "being covered" to be optionally introduced through different applications while coexisting in the same locus (*samānādhikaraṇa*) as mutual absolute non-existence (*parasparātyantābhāva*), their status as valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) is justified.
[This applies] "in all cases."

The meaning is that even when the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs immediately after seeing smoke and so forth, inference does not arise in the absence of a desire to know (*jijñāsā*); therefore, it is only in the case of indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*), or specifically in inference and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), that this [desire to know] functions as a cause. (The phrase "the offering belonging to the *vaisarjana-homa*" indicates the purpose of seeking another subject matter.
Furthermore, [this is so] because of the observation of a reason (*hetudarśanāt*) here. (Jaimini Sūtra 1.3.4)
This is the sūtra immediately following the previous one.
In that regard, if it is impossible for [the Smṛti] to be rooted in direct Vedic revelation (pratyakṣa-śruti), then,
when the Smṛti requires a basis, it is more reasonable to postulate that its root is error (bhrānti) and the like.

In that regard, from the recollection of the *veṣṭana* (the binding), there arises greed for clothing through the giving to the *udgātṛ*; from the recollection of the forty-eight years of *brahmacarya*, there is the concealment of one's impotence; and from the recollection of the purchase of the *rājā* (Soma) and the slaughter, there is merely hunger.

Since this observed cause is possible, the Commentator— having once explained it as supplementary to the preceding [section] with the intent of demonstrating other reasons such as "being of human origin" (pauruṣeyatva)— then explained it as pertaining to a different topical section (adhikaraṇa) by way of an alternative position. In that case, since the lack of authority was already established in the previous instance by the primary reason of contradiction with direct Vedic revelation (pratyakṣa-śruti), he was dissatisfied with merely stating the observed causes such as greed as secondary (anvācaya) reasons, as there would be no purpose in mentioning them.
A second explanation has been provided;
he now demonstrates that this alone is correct according to that [author's] view, beginning with the words "tathā" (thus).

"Regarding the *vaisarjana-homīya* (the substance for the concluding oblation): when the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice has commenced, [the priest] addresses the sacrificer, his wife, sons, and brothers with a fresh garment for the purpose of carrying forth Agni and Soma. (Note: The term *vaisarjanahomīya* refers to the substance used for the concluding oblation; by the word "etcetera," the inclusion of the *yūpahasti-vākya* is intended.)

Having covered [the ladle] with a cloth and tied the *sruc* to the end of the cloth, one offers oblations; thus, four *vaisarjana* (concluding) offerings are prescribed for the *śālāmukhīya*, *āgnīdhra*, and *āhavanīya* fires using clarified butter taken in four portions (*caturgṛhīta*).
The meaning is that this cloth belongs to those *vaisarjana* offerings.
By the phrase "and so forth" (*ādipadena*), there is an inclusion of another Smṛti text stating that "they perform the gift of the *yūpahastinaḥ*.

Based on the etymology "that by which the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is grasped (*hasti*) or wrapped (*veṣṭyate*)," the meaning of the term *yūpahasti* is a cloth for the purpose of wrapping the sacrificial post.
And that [cloth] is prescribed as seventeen cloths for wrapping the post, as it is handed down in the Vājapeya ritual.

(Refutation of the two aforementioned topical sections according to the view of the Vārttikakāra, as accepted by the Bhāṣyakṛt): Thus have the two topical sections been explained according to the opinion of the Bhāṣyakṛt;
that has been refuted by the Vārttikakāra.

To explain: when there is a contradiction with direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), the absence of a foundational scripture (*mūla-bhūta-śruti*) for the Smṛtis is due either to a lack of evidence or to the presence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*).

It cannot be the former, because the means of establishing the existence of a Vedic basis—such as being composed by great sages (*maharṣi*) and being accepted by the learned members of the three higher castes (*śiṣṭa-traivarṇika*)—are no different here than they are in the case of other Smṛtis.

Nor can it be the latter, because the subverting factor consisting in the observation of a contradictory Śruti is inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*), since such contradictions are frequently observed even among Śruti texts themselves, such as those concerning *vrīhi* and *yava* grains.

Even though the Vedic texts contained within various scattered branches are not perceived by people such as ourselves, there is no sublation consisting of non-perception on the part of Manu and others, because they are of greater stature.

Therefore, since the perception of another is equal to one's own perception, it is possible for the Vedic texts seen by them to serve as the source [of the Smṛti]; thus, the total lack of authority asserted by the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) is not established.
But the author of the Vārttika [states]: "The desire to know (*jijñāsā*) is not a constituent factor of inference, because inference arises even when there is no desire to know fire and so forth;
or, even if it were a cause, [inference would still occur] because the *śruti* which is the object of inference is itself what is desired to be known."

Alternatively, if one were to admit that [the Smṛti] is rooted in greed and other such motives in the absence of contradiction with direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), then the same consequence would apply to the *Smṛti* rules concerning the Aṣṭakā and so forth.

Therefore, even when there is a contradiction with direct Vedic revelation, it is logical for the Smṛti to possess authority because its basis in the Veda can be inferred through the specific fact of its acceptance by the learned members of the three twice-born classes (*śiṣṭa-trairvarṇika*).
However, until the Vedic text is ascertained, the act of wrapping [the sacrificial post] should not be performed.

Since it is observed that even in the case of the Smṛtis, there are instances where they are rooted in injunctions inferred from explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and the like, it is possible that the present case is also rooted in such [an inference]. Furthermore, since such an inference may be fallacious when it contradicts a directly perceived Vedic text (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), the Sūtra intends to convey the view that as long as the Vedic text remains unascertained, there is invalidity characterized by non-performance. Thus he says: (B2) [The investigation of the directly perceived Vedic text which is the root of the Smṛti regarding the wearing of the sacred thread].
Furthermore, in his own work, the *Chāndogyānupada*, Jaimini states: "The cloth is indeed the *viṣṭuti*; the cloth is prosperity (*śrī*); the *sāman* is prosperity.
This refers to the *kuśa* grass stalks of the *audumbarī* wood, each a span in length, which are used for counting the *stotrīyā* verses.
These are designated by the term *viṣṭuti* because they manifest the specific modes found in the *viṣṭuti* designations, such as "he [chants] with one, he with three, he with one," and so forth.

He wrapped [the post] for the sake of stabilization; thus, by the passage in the *Audumbarī-prakaraṇa* stating, "The followers of the Śāṭyāyana branch show two garments on both sides at the upper part," he demonstrated that this is indeed based on a direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*). In this same way, even regarding the Smṛti rule concerning forty-eight years of studentship, [the text says]: "Forty-eight years..."

Furthermore, since the direct Vedic revelation itself—namely, the passage from the Atharvaveda cited by Rāṇaka which reads "He indeed [should practice] Vedic celibacy" (sa vai vedabrahmacaryam)—is the root authority, the examples [adduced by others] are also inappropriate.
(The statement "forty-eight" is a reference to direct Vedic revelation which is the root of Smṛti); and how there is no contradiction here, that should be seen in the Ākara and in the Kaustubha.
Therefore, the first section is not tenable.
(An exposition of that author's view, preceded by an introduction to the Vārttikakāra’s opinion):

The second section (*adhikaraṇa*) is also untenable; for if one were to assume that even those [practices] which are not contradictory [to the Vedas] are rooted in greed, then the same consequence would apply to the Smṛtis concerning giving and so forth.
Indeed, the authority of custom (*ācāra*) will not be established by this section—namely, "Or rather, when no motive is perceived"—merely on the grounds that a visible basis is impossible.

If it were possible for that [lack of authority] to be established here by means of a reason based on the possibility of an observed basis (dṛṣṭamūlatva) distinct from that [performance with a religious motive], then it would be so;
however, it is established solely by virtue of being performed with the understanding that it pertains to Dharma (*dharmabuddhyā*).

The reason for the alternative inclusion (*anvācaya*) was merely presented as the impossibility of an observed basis. With this refutation of the two-fold section made by the Teacher in mind, the author of the Vārttika shows it as a different opinion, stating: "But the author of the Vārttika... and so forth.
And the wrapping is also to be performed.

In this context, since it has already been stated that the Smṛti rules regarding the binding of the sacrificial post (*veṣṭana*) and so forth are rooted in specific Vedic texts (*śruti*) that have been directly recited, it is untenable to claim that they should not be practiced until those Vedic texts are ascertained. Therefore, the word *veṣṭana* must be explained through a non-abandoning indication (*ajahatsvārtha-lakṣaṇā*) as referring to Smṛtis whose basis is unperceived (*adṛṣṭa-mūla*).

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Nyāyasudhā*: "The illustrative commentary (*udāharaṇa-bhāṣya*) as well must be understood as referring to Smṛtis that exist in a state where their basis is unperceived."
(An exposition on establishing that the definition of invalidity—consisting in not being based on the Veda, being uncertain, and not being practiced—is rooted in the Sūtras:

Now, one might object: since Smṛtis whose basis is unperceived cannot be considered absolutely sublated because they lack a foundation in deception, and since it is impossible for them to be equal to other Smṛtis that are entirely different [in status] due to the uncertainty regarding their literal scriptural source, if one were to somehow grant them validity...
Since there is a contradiction with the sūtra stating that "in case of conflict, [the Veda] is not to be relied upon," which establishes a lack of authority, he says: "And therefore... (ataśca).

Even though the foundational scripture (*mūlabhūta-śruti*) may be perceived by others, it lacks perception for oneself; whereas one's own perception, however, depends upon the investigation of its source and is therefore weak. Consequently, when there is a conflict between these two, that scriptural cognition which is independent must be accepted as the authority. For, in the absence of a scriptural meaning, an inference based on an inferred scripture is to be accepted. Thus, the meaning of the Sūtra is that the word "authority" (*pramāṇa*), which is carried over from the preceding Sūtra, refers here specifically to the authority characterized by ritual performance (*anuṣṭhāna*). This is the sense.
(Variations in the reading and interpretation of the sūtra beginning with *virodhe tu*):

In this sūtra, there is a variation in the reading based on whether the letter *y* is absent or present, as in *anapekṣam* and *anapekṣyam*. When it includes the letter *y*, the meaning is "that which has nothing else to depend upon."
But that which is devoid of those [characteristics] has indeed already been explained.
(Herein is the agreement between the established conclusion of the *Vārttika* not accepted [by others] and the verses of the *Vārttika* itself:

As it was stated by the Teachers: "As long as one action is perceived in the Śruti and another in the Smṛti, when there is a conflict between the two, the performance of that which is based on the Śruti is desired."
"And for this very reason, no distinction is shown between Śruti and Smṛti;
there is neither absolute sublation nor absolute equality. Thus [it is said].
But when the Vedic text that serves as the basis for a conflicting Smṛti is directly perceived by oneself,
then the meaning established is that both [texts] should be respected either through option (*vikalpa*) or through a restrictive application (*vyavasthā*).

(The manner of applying the Sūtra *hetudarśanācca* according to the Vārtika school: As for the Sūtra *hetudarśanācca*, it refers to cases where there is a conflict between two contemporary Smṛtis whose roots lie in conduct that is based on Smṛti contradicted by direct Śruti— such as, for example, the eating of food offered to Jagannātha when it has been defiled by the touch of those who are untouchable (*asparśya*), and so forth— in which case another possible root [for the Smṛti] may exist.
It should be explained as being for the purpose of demonstrating disregard; this is the general direction.

(An exposition of another version by the author of the Vārttika: Having thus explained that, [it is said: "Because it is employed everywhere and because of the proximity of the scriptural injunction" (Jaimini 1.3.14).
Thus, the matter has already been covered by the *Adhikaraṇa* (the section on the authority of the Kalpasūtras).

For in that context, since the words of the Kalpasūtras—which serve as a summary of the meaning of the *Pratyakṣasūtra*—are not to be respected when they contradict Śruti, it follows all the more that Smṛtis are not to be respected; yet, being dissatisfied with this, the Teacher composed another interpretation (*varṇaka*), which he now connects [with the following]: "Or rather... (*yadvā*).
(An examination of how the description of the lack of authority of the Smṛtis of the Śākyas and others is not redundant with other topical sections):

Since the reason of "commonality of authorship" (*kartṛ-sāmānya*) mentioned in the *siddhānta-sūtra* of the preceding section (*apivā kartṛsāmānyāt*) is intended to indicate the primary reason consisting in the firm acceptance by the learned members of the three higher castes (*śiṣṭa-traivarṇika*), authority was previously asserted on that basis;
therefore, it is stated here that where that [acceptance] is absent, there is a lack of authority. Thus, its connection as a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) is established elsewhere.

Although it was stated in the *Pratyakṣasūtra* that [the Kalpasūtras] lack authority because they are based on perception and other means of knowledge, and although it was stated in the section on the Kalpasūtras (*Kalpasūtrādhikaraṇa*) that they lack independent authority, the author begins the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) after first indicating the subject matter, with the intention of demonstrating that the matter has not already been settled— since the suspicion of authority based on being rooted in the Veda had not been refuted elsewhere— and of showing the connection to the chapter through the examination of fallacious means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*).
"Of the Śākyas and others."

(B1) Or rather, since even the Śākyas and others are well-known to be Kṣatriyas, it is possible that they had access to the Vedas; therefore, the Smṛtis composed by them must also be rooted in the Veda. If the Veda were their source, it must have been lost by now. This being the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*), we reply: because the acceptance of these [Smṛtis] as dharma by the learned members of the three higher castes—which was the primary reason for the previous section—is absent, and on the contrary, they are remembered precisely as being non-authoritative, [these Smṛtis lack authority], according to those who maintain the non-authority of the Veda.
And because its authority is accepted [by others], it is impossible to postulate that it is rooted in the Veda; therefore, it lacks authority—this is the meaning of the Sūtra. // 2 // 6 //
Thus ends the second section on contradiction.
(B2) [The Utility of Describing the Smṛtis of the Śākyas and Others as Invalid]:
Nor is the statement that these [Smṛtis] are fallacious without utility.
For if their lack of authority were not stated with disregard for them, [they would indeed be authoritative].
Thinking that it is simply impossible, others might develop a distorted view; and due to the influence of the Kali age, as well as the arguments regarding beauty and ease,
they may fall into the delusion that the slaughter of animals prescribed for sacrifice should be abandoned.
Since, according to the method stated in the Vārttika— “Without refuting all of those, the purity of Dharma cannot be attained”— it is necessary to address them; therefore,
although there is no purpose in refuting the Śākyas and others because they do not themselves accept the authority of their own texts on the grounds that they are rooted in the Veda;

Nevertheless, the sense is that this undertaking is appropriate as a means of demonstrating the fallacious nature [of the opponent's position] by refuting the misconception held by the Vaidikas that [the Smṛtis] are rooted in the Veda.

(An examination of the term *śākya* as characterizing the founders of the Pāśupata, Pāñcarātra, and other systems: Here, the word "Śākya" and others refers to those [systems] which are not accepted by the knowers of the Triple Veda (*trayī*), which possess the shadow of a cloak of dharma mixed with various [heterodox elements], which are intent on the purposes of winning over the world, gaining profit, fame, and honor, and which consist primarily of arguments based on perception, inference, analogy, and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) regarding visible beauty and the like that are contrary to and disconnected from the Triple Veda.
These are rooted in the fundamental [scriptures] and consist of the treatises on dharma and adharma established by the adherents of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, and Pāśupata;
as well as those more external ones which are rooted in the mixed practices of Mleccha conduct and dietary habits—this is the characterization of their authors.
(Regarding the doubt concerning the authority of the Smṛtis of Śākya and others, similar to those of Manu and others:

Having observed that [the Buddhist tradition] is based on non-violence, truth, self-restraint, charity, compassion, and so forth—which are in agreement with the Śruti and Smṛti—one might conclude that even practices such as the worship of Caityas, which fall within that system, are properly considered *dharma*.
With this intention, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) presents the reason: "because of the well-known status of [the Buddha] as a Kṣatriya."

By the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "of the Smṛtis also," it is indicated that the authority of the Smṛtis composed by Manu and others—who, being members of the three higher castes, are presumed to have had contact with the Veda—derives from their being rooted in the Veda;
thus, the expression "likewise of these" suggests an illustrative comparison.
Therefore, just like that [previous case], the root-inference (mūlānumāna) would be contradicted by non-perception (anupalabdhi).
This has already been refuted and made known under the view that [the Smṛti] is rooted in direct Vedic revelation (pratyakṣa-śruti).

Now, intending to show that under the view that it is rooted in a "defiled branch" (malina-śākhā), there is not even a suspicion of contradiction, he presents that position with the words: "tanmūla" (rooted in that).
And thus, whatever has become well-known, having been respected by some for however long a time, even if it contradicts the extant branches of direct perception, its root lies in lost branches.
Therefore, in this view, the fault—that "whatever pleases someone, that he may take as authoritative"—does not arise; such is the intended meaning.
(Establishing the invalidity of the Smṛtis of the Śākyas and others:
"Because of their being based on those [Smṛtis]."

The meaning is that Manu and others have recorded these texts as being non-authoritative, stating: "Whatever Smṛtis are outside the Veda, and whatever false views there may be—all of them are fruitless after death, for they are declared to culminate in darkness. Thus, by such statements, their lack of authority has been remembered.
(The demonstration that the invalidity of the Smṛtis of the Śākyas and others is established in the Sūtras.
Regarding the meaning of the Sūtra:
The meaning is that this is the sense of the two sūtras.

Regarding the contradiction consisting of hatred toward the Vedas, such a work as this, which is outside the Trayī (the three Vedas), is to be disregarded and is not authoritative. Alternatively—the first meaning of the sūtra is as follows: since Śākya is well-known to be a Kṣatriya, and because [the scriptures] prohibit him from being a teacher or a recipient [of gifts], and since he is a practitioner of those [teachings], his word is to be disregarded when it contradicts one's own dharma (svadharma). This is the meaning of the initial sūtra.
(An examination of the difference [between Manu and Śākya] by refuting the doubt regarding their equality:

Nor does this imply that it is impossible for Manu to be an expounder because he is a Kṣatriya; for his authority as such is authorized by the Vedic scripture: "Whatever Manu said was indeed medicine."

Furthermore, because the Śākyas and others employ only numerous fallacious reasons (*asaddhetu*) regarding their own doctrines and fail to present even a single valid reason (*saddhetu*), their works are to be disregarded.

As for Manu and others, however, there is an absence of formal logical arguments; or even if some exist, since they primarily declare that the Veda alone is the supreme means for the ultimate good of the twice-born—as in the passage, "The Veda alone is the highest source of spiritual welfare for the twice-born"—they are not at fault, as those passages are merely explanatory statements (*arthavāda*) according to the principle of the section on reasons (*hetvadhikaraṇanyāya*).

For this very reason, because the Śākyas and others rely on reasoning (*hetukatva*), their status as those with whom one should not converse is stated in such passages as, "One should not honor even with mere words those who are rationalists (*haituka*) or those who act like herons (*bakavr̥tti*). This is the meaning of the second sūtra.

Furthermore, the phrase "because the assumption of being rooted in the Veda is untenable" should be understood as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of "seeing [fallacious] reasons" (*hetudarśana*) as well.
(Description of the lack of authority of the Pāñcarātra and other systems:
As for the acceptance of the Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, and so forth by learned members of the three higher castes, that is not based upon them [the Vedas].
However, [the *Nṛsiṃhatāpanīya* and *Rāmatāpanīya Upaniṣads*] are rooted solely in the *Śrutis* and the *Saṃhitās* of Agastya and others.
For this very reason, those [Tantras] which expound the Vāmāgama—being unaccepted by the learned members of the three higher castes (*śiṣṭas*)—lack authority.

As for whatever therein accords with other [orthodox] Āgamas, such as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and so forth, that is intended merely to inspire devotion toward the acceptance of the Vāmāgama, like the [teachings of] the Śākyas; thus, even their practice does not have that [accordance] as its root.
However, even for those cultured predecessors, that [tradition] is rooted solely in an incorrect scripture; thus there is no fault, and therefore it is invalid in every respect—so say many.
(An exposition of the established doctrine that even the Pāñcarātra and other systems possess authority insofar as they are not in conflict with Śruti, being rooted in Śruti.

In the *Kaustubha*, the venerable teacher has stated that authority belongs to those portions [of the Pāñcarātra] which are rooted in direct Śruti and are accepted by the learned among the three twice-born castes (*varṇas*).
For this very reason, it is said: "Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, the Vedas, and likewise Pāśupata..."

Although the authority [of these paths] was stated by the Mahābhārata passage, "These are authoritative for oneself; they should not be refuted by arguments," Mādhava has shown that this is qualified by the specific eligibility [of the practitioner], as concluded by the statement in the fourth chapter of the *Muktikhaṇḍa*: "Whatever part of the paths is not contradicted by the Veda, that part is said to be authoritative for certain qualified persons."
And how, this being the case, the validity of the means of knowledge belonging to the Śākyas and others—which are not contradictory [to our own]—will be refuted later on.
(An application of the description of authority found in the *Smṛtyadhikaraṇa* as being intended for specific qualified persons:

As for the demonstration in the *Smṛtyadhikaraṇa* of the utility of the Sāṃkhya and other external texts, that is intended to state the reasoning that establishes detachment (*vairāgya*) and so forth, which are useful for the knowledge that serves as a means to *dharma* and *mokṣa*; it is not intended to provide instruction on *dharma* and so forth. Thus, there is no contradiction.

This being the case, although the authority of the Vāmāgama—which is rooted in direct Vedic revelation such as the Tāpanīya Upaniṣad, yet contradicts direct Vedic revelation—is difficult to deny; nevertheless, it is said: "The Pañcarātra, the Bhāgavata, and the Tantra known as Vaikhānasa were spoken by the Lord of Kamalā for the sake of those who have fallen away from the Vedas."

Likewise: "For the twice-born who have utterly strayed from the Vedic path, the Pāñcarātra and other paths become beneficial in the course of time. And similarly: "Due to the curse of Gautama and others, or due to great sin, men [fall away]."

Based on such statements from the Purāṇas as, "Those who have gone outside the Veda, those born of mixed castes, women, and Śūdras— all these are entitled [to practice] at the beginning of the Tantras, each according to their respective status," its authority is indeed accepted as being directed toward specific qualified persons, and not regarding those qualified for the Vedic path.
Therefore, since they are not accepted by the learned members of the three higher castes, enough with this elaboration.
Thus ends the second section concerning contradictions.
(B1) (Section 3: If it is argued that "there is no contradiction when there is no conflict with the learned," [we reply:
No, because the scripture has a fixed extent. (Jaimini Sūtra 1.3.5)

When there is a conflict between Smārta practices such as sipping water (ācamana) and Śrauta requirements regarding order, time, and quantity, the Śrauta rules—due to their scriptural origin—possess greater authority; consequently, the Smṛtis concerning those matters lack authority.

For instance, if one were to perform the Smārta sipping of water prescribed by the rule "one should sip water after sneezing" in the midst of preparing the altar according to the Vedic injunction "having prepared the Veda [grass mat], one prepares the altar," it would be impossible to carry out the sequence established by that Śruti.
(B2) (The determination of the connection through two ways by means of the section on contradiction:

Thus, in the preceding section, according to the view of the Bhāṣyakāra, it was established that those Smṛtis—whether concerning the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) or the ritual goal (*kratvartha*)—are invalid in their very nature because they contradict Śruti; and according to the view of the Vārtikakāra, it was established that they are invalid in the sense of being non-implementation (*ananuṣṭhāna*).

Now, since it is clear, this section may be connected as a "cleansing of the stomach" (*koṣṭha-śodhanikā*) by investigating where there is indeed a contradiction with direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) and where there is not— just as in the sections concerning relative strength (*balābala-adhikaraṇa*), the *ahīna* sacrifices, and so forth; or else, it may be connected as an "exceptional case" (*āpavādikī*) by establishing an exception to the rule that even when there is a contradiction with Śruti, the Smṛti possesses authority due to its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because its subject matter is a real entity (*padārtha*).

Likewise, disregarding even the fact that the Sūtra indicates the commencement of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) due to a lack of purpose, [the author], while demonstrating the subject matter, states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "Also of those belonging to the Smṛti..."

The meaning is that these refer to those things prescribed by Smṛti, such as "it must be performed by one who has sipped water," "it must be performed while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder," and "it must be performed with the right hand.

Since the final Smṛti rule states that it "must be performed with conduct using the right hand," this injunction of the right hand—which was not previously established—should be understood as being like the injunction "red turbans" (*lohitoṣṇīṣāḥ*) [in the Vedic context].

(Refutation of the doubt that the subject matter [of this section] is already contained within the *Śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*; the demonstration that this is so by means of the term "Smṛti") At the conclusion of the *Śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*, the Sūtra states: “Or rather, due to the connection with sequence, the distinctness of injunctions remains restricted to a single [branch], because of the contradiction regarding sequence, time, and measure. Having raised the objection that there is no inclusion of ritual elements from other branches due to such contradictions, [the author] addresses those contradictory [elements]: ...of the contradictory ones...

The statement that the sequence and other factors of ritual elements will be shown to be sublated by the sūtra, "But because of the lack of connection [with the primary injunction], there is unity of action; because of that connection, there would be the cognition of all actions as being enjoined," does not render this point redundant.

For in that case, since both [the primary injunction and the sequence] are based on direct scriptural authority (*śruti*), there is no inherent coexistence between them; thus, it is logical that the ritual elements themselves should sublate the sequence.

However, in this context, the phrase "of the Smṛtis" is stated to resolve the objection that sublation might occur here due to the weakness of their authority; it serves as an indication for raising such a doubt.
This is an elliptical reference (upalakṣaṇa) to those [Smṛti rules] established by custom (ācāra).

Since the strength of the object of cognition (prameya-bala) itself is presented there to determine the relative strength or weakness of the means of cognition (pramāṇa-bala), the sense is that its purpose is not already covered by this [previous] argument.
(Justification for the contradiction of the sequence by means of sipping water and so forth) Regarding the word "in case of contradiction" (*virodhe*).

Although there is no contradiction in the occurrence of *ācamana* (sipping water) during the middle of a performance— even when it is performed at the beginning of every ritual application because *ācamana* caused by eating and so forth serves a human purpose (*puruṣārtha*)—

nevertheless, when *ācamana* caused by hunger and so forth, which serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), occurs between two ritual acts (*padārtha*), that [interruption] certainly takes place. For this very reason, even if there is no injunction for *ācamana* when a cause such as hunger arises during the performance of a single, extensive ritual act, [the interruption still occurs].

However, there is indeed a contradiction regarding the touching of the right ear as prescribed by the Smṛti: "But while engaged in ritual action, one should not sip water for purification after sneezing, spitting, putting on a garment, or shedding tears; rather, one should touch the right ear. Therefore, that [Smṛti rule] serves as a counter-example.

Similarly, regarding the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), because of its connection with the word "always" in the Smṛti—"One should always remain wearing the sacred thread"—it is established as being for the sake of the person's spiritual welfare alone.

Even though [the sacred thread] is enjoined by the latter half of the verse, "And whatever one does without the *upavīta*, that is as if not done," as an auxiliary to all obligatory rites (*kartavyakarman*), there is no contradiction in its essential nature; nevertheless, such a contradiction certainly exists when one who has let it slip down readjusts it, or when one who has lost it puts it on again.
This same principle applies to the binding of the topknot (*śikhābandhana*); thus, these serve as examples.

Thus, even in the case of the statement regarding the right hand, although there is no conflict with the practice of using the right hand for eating and so forth—which is prescribed for the sake of human ends (puruṣārtha)—there is indeed a conflict with that which is for the sake of the sacrifice (kratvartha).

This is because if the performance were carried out with both hands, the swiftness of execution (prayoga-prāśubhāva), which is synonymous with non-delay, would be obstructed if one were to perform it with only a single hand.
Therefore, the point is that it is appropriate for all these cases to serve as examples, as a conflict arises in each instance.

(B1) Furthermore, because the items prescribed by the Smṛti are numerous, it is impossible to accommodate both the time such as the forenoon and the extent determined by the injunction of performance.

Nor is it the case that, despite being based on Śruti, sequence and so forth are weaker than the acts of sipping water (*ācamana*) and the like—which are themselves items—simply because they are properties of those items;

for since the cognition of an object of knowledge (*prameya*) is preceded by its means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the relative strength or weakness of the objects of knowledge depends upon the relative strength or weakness of the means of knowledge first apprehended. This being the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa): (B2) [The Siddhāntin replies:]...
(The meaning of the terms *vedakaraṇa* and *vedikaraṇa-pada*):
In order to demonstrate the contradiction with scripture that establishes the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), the word "by those based on scripture" (*śrautaiḥ*) was stated.
He demonstrates that very contradiction as follows: "For not... (*na hi*).
"Having made this altar," so it is said.
The *veda* is a handful of *darbha* grass used as a means for sweeping. Its preparation (*karaṇa*) refers to the ritual refinements such as tying its ends together and trimming it.
The *vedi* is the ground dug four finger-breadths deep between the *gārhapatya* and *āhavanīya* fires.

The meaning of the terms *vedakaraṇa* and *vedikaraṇa* is the preparation of the altar-ground (*vedi*), namely, the sweeping, the sprinkling, and other such consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*) performed by means of the Veda.
(Justification for the lack of contradiction regarding the secondary order, since acts such as sipping water are not included within the injunction of the ritual procedure:
"It is taught by the Śruti."

And this is an illustration of the sequence alone, which is understood through the six means of proof known as direct statement (*śruti*), meaning (*artha*), textual order (*pāṭha*), position (*sthāna*), primary function (*mukhya*), and application (*pravṛtti*);
for even the sequence based on meaning and so forth is to be enjoined by the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vidhi*).

Since the injunction of performance is designated as such merely by assuming a syntactic unity with the injunctions for the subsidiaries of the principal act that is directly heard in the scripture, there is no contradiction with its being prescribed by direct scriptural audition.

And thus, since there is no evidence for a fixed order between the Vedic [elements] and the Smṛti-based acts such as sipping water (ācamana) occasioned by hunger and so forth— just as there is none between different *homas*— and because the sequence is determined only for those elements that are Vedic, and because the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*) prescribes only those constituent parts whose order is already fixed,
there can be no application of the injunction of performance to acts like sipping water which fall outside of that [Vedic set]. This is the meaning.

(An examination of the contradiction arising from the performance of *ācamana* [sipping water] in the middle [of a rite], such as the loss of the promptness required for the morning ritual application.
"The morning and so forth," etc.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādipadena*), the evening and morning times for the subsidiary rites (*aṅga*) of the *agnihotra* are also included.

Just as the forenoon time is prescribed by the Vedic text, "The forenoon indeed belongs to the gods," so too, through the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vidhi*), which prescribes the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) qualified by the performance of the subsidiaries, there arises an implication of simultaneous execution; yet, because absolute simultaneity is impossible, [the subsidiaries]— [...are to be performed sequentially. (Note: The sentence is incomplete in the source text.)
Time is understood as characterized by the mutual proximity of the primary and subsidiary elements, as well as by the rapidity of their performance;
the meaning is that between these two [characteristics], there would certainly be a contradiction in the performance of the items prescribed by the Smṛti.
(Also the determination of the understanding of the application-injunction regarding measure:
"And that which is understood from the application-injunction."

When a deficiency arises due to doubt—such as wondering whether some element has been forgotten or whether everything has been performed correctly—the absence of *śraddhā* occurs; for *śraddhā* consists in the certainty that the result will inevitably arise, as understood from the scriptural statement: "Whatever one performs with *śraddhā*, that alone becomes more powerful.
This certainty produces a superior fruit. Thus, there is a lack of such *śraddhā*.

Because, even when all Vedic ritual acts have been performed, the fruit may not arise due to fate, and because the doubt as to whether an act has been performed or omitted must necessarily be removed for the attainment of the complete fruit— and since that doubt cannot be dispelled without reflecting on the completion of the number of items to be performed— it is stated that "it is understood" with the intention that the *prayogavacana* (the injunction of performance) implies, by the force of the context, the determination of the total number of items to be accumulated, which are enjoined by the direct statement (*śruti*) and other means.

The meaning is as follows: because there is a lapse in the performance of the items remembered later—which were not included in the initial determination of the ritual measure—due to the execution of those items arranged at the outset;

and because, owing to the failure to ascertain what was done and what was left undone, one remains subject to the suspicion of deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) and lacks the mental clarity (*pāṭava*) resulting from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of having performed the rite correctly;
consequently, due to the weakness of the *apūrva*, there arises the contingency of obtaining a diminished fruit.
As it has been stated in the Vārttika: "All that possesses excellence is understood from the injunction along with its explanatory passages (arthavāda);
by the very necessity of [avoiding] deficiency, it necessarily sublates a contradictory Smṛti."

(Resolution of the objection regarding the conflict with the *aṅgaguṇavirodha* maxim raised in the prima facie argument: As for the point that— in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*)— according to the twelfth-lunar-day principle (*dvādaśika-nyāya*), "In case of a conflict between a subordinate quality and [the primary], [the former prevails] because it is for the sake of that," the subsidiary rites such as the *iṣṭi* must conform to the time of the principal Soma sacrifice, thereby subverting the time of the lunar day (*parvan*) enjoined by the text "He who [performs] the *iṣṭi*," so too here...

It is said that when there is a conflict, it is proper for the sequence and so forth of the subsidiary parts to be set aside in accordance with the principal acts of sipping water (ācamana) and the like, which are primary by virtue of being constituent elements;
having restated this, he refutes it with the words "And not... (na ca).
"Perceived for the first time."

The meaning is that once the relative strength or weakness of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) has been first understood, and it has been determined—on the basis of that *pramāṇa*—that sequence and the like are stronger than acts such as ritual rinsing (*ācamana*), then, because the requirement for further cognition has been satisfied (*nirākāṅkṣatvāt*), the subsequently understood relative strength or weakness of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) need not be taken into account.

(This concludes the final position [siddhānta] that acts such as ritual rinsing prescribed in the Smṛtis do not conflict with sequence, time, and so forth; it also establishes how this conclusion is grounded in the Sūtra.)

And here, regarding the concluding sūtra (*siddhāntasūtra*)— "Or rather, when the cause [of conflict] is not perceived, those [texts] employed [in ritual] should be understood [as authoritative]"— the author of the Vārttika, despite the existence of contradiction, demonstrates once again that there is no contradiction by bringing the sūtra down as it was recited to its full extent, for the purpose of establishing the authority of the *ācamana* (ritual rinsing) and other such acts based on the relative strength or weakness residing in the objects of knowledge (*prameya*).
To this end, he appends the portion "because no contradiction is seen among them" (*teṣv adarśanād virodhasya*) and proceeds with the intent of demonstrating the absence of contradiction.
This has been introduced by means of a connected second limit (*avadhi*).

In that context, although there is a contradiction, because the relative strength or weakness of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) is the cause of predominance, it must be established according to the maxim "let the wicked man be satisfied.
Therefore, since the absence of contradiction is the primary reason due to its primacy, the meaning of the Sūtra is first presented with the intent of demonstrating that very point.
Having thus connected [the previous discussion], he states the established conclusion (siddhānta): "Regarding the categories (padārtha)," and so forth.

Since the extent of the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) for the *kratvapūrva* (the transcendental result of the sacrifice) is not definitively known, there is no lack of expectancy (*nairākāṅkṣya*) through the scriptural subsidiaries alone; therefore, just as in the absence of contradiction, one accepts the subsidiaries—

whether obtained through direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth up to name (*samākhyā*)— along with those established by isolated injunctions (*anārabhyavāda*), disregarding considerations of relative strength, so too are those obtained through Smṛti and custom (*ācāra*) accepted.

This is because the *prayoga-vidhi*—which consists of the performance itself—is operative for the sake of the subsequent execution of all the means (*sādhana*) that assist in the performance; and thus, at the very moment the procedure is made known by it, the sequence, time, and so forth, which are required for the ritual items (*padārtha*), are integrated as delimiters of the performance. This is because, as will be explained in the eleventh book (*adhyāya*), the integration of time and other factors with the *prayoga-vidhi* occurs precisely as delimiters in a manner that does not contradict the performance of the ritual items as established by whatever means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) they may have been obtained through, and this applies equally to both the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the primary acts (*pradhāna*).
Nor is there an absence of a regulating factor for the sequence of Smṛti-based rites alongside Vedic ones;

for, just as in the case of the oblation for breaking [the vessel], their presence arises precisely from the coincidence of the occasion, and thus the sequence is established by position (*sthāna*) itself.

This is because it is impossible for position—which relies on the constituent elements (*padārtha*)—to be sublated even by a stronger scriptural sequence (*śruti-krama*), since that would entail the sublation of the constituent elements themselves.

(B1) Since subsequent elements such as sequence depend upon the attainment of the constituent items (padārtha), they must be postulated only insofar as they do not contradict the items as understood through the available means of knowledge; therefore, they cannot contradict those items.
However, since size (parimāṇa) is not the subject matter of any scriptural injunction, it lacks the status of being "Vedic" (śrauta).
Furthermore, even if there were a contradiction, rites such as sipping water (ācamana) possess greater authority precisely because they are constituent items.

For there is no contradiction among means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in their own nature, but rather it is based on a contradiction between their objects of cognition (*prameya*). Thus, at the very moment a contradiction between the objects of cognition is perceived, the meaning of the scripture is determined by the relative strength or weakness residing therein; consequently, the strength or weakness of the means of cognition themselves has no further restrictive power. Therefore, that Smṛti is indeed a means of valid cognition. Or alternatively, having raised the objection: "Let that which is not contradicted by the Vedas—such as the teachings on giving and so forth found in the texts of the Śākyas and others—be considered a means of valid cognition," [the author responds:]
“One should study one’s own recitation”;
“The entire Veda is the root of Dharma, as well as the tradition and conduct of those who know it”;
“The Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, the Dharmaśāstras, along with the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas)...”

"Vedas are the fourteen seats of knowledge and of dharma. According to such statements, since dharma is cognized only through those things whose scope is fixed by authoritative means of knowledge, anything cognized by other means lacks the capacity to be a means for attaining the fruit [of dharma]; therefore, those [other means] lack authority. // 3 //
Thus ends the third section, *Śiṣṭākopādhikaraṇa*. (The performance of certain Smārta items at the end.
Here, it should be noted as follows: where the injunction for a Smārta item is specifically predicated upon a particular location, its sequence is determined by that very mention of the location.
However, when there is a conflict with the sequence prescribed by Śruti, the latter prevails, and the performance of the ritual items occurs at the end.

But where in Smṛti there is an injunction for a ritual item as a constituent part of the sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*) without specifying a particular location, then because of the rule that "accessory elements (*āgantūnām*) are inserted at the end," their performance must indeed take place at the end— this is to be understood.

In this case, however, since their sequence is determined by the very place [of the ritual action] as assisted by the *smṛti* rule stating "it must be performed after sipping water," there is no contradiction.

As for the measure (*parimāṇa*), however, because there is no direct injunction for it in the scripture, even if it is somehow implied according to the previously mentioned method, it is required at the very time of performance—just like sequence and time—and thus functions solely as an auxiliary to the items being employed; consequently, after its application, [the requirement for] incidental offerings such as the *bhedana-homa* expiation and so forth [arises].

The meaning is that there is no contradiction, because just as by the determination of inherence (samavāya), so too by the determination of ritual elements such as the Smṛti-prescribed sipping of water (ācamana) and so forth, the injunction of performance (prayogavacana) encompasses [the rite] precisely through the delimitation of all its constituent elements, which would otherwise have to be postulated.
