(An examination of the authority of the Smṛti on sipping water [ācamana], based on its reliance upon the more powerful matter consisting of the act of sipping itself, even while accepting a contradiction between the two procedures for sipping):
Now, following the maxim "let the wicked man be satisfied," he establishes its authority even by accepting the contradiction, stating: "Even if there is a contradiction."
He establishes that very point: "For [it is said] 'of the means of valid cognition'... etc.

Since there is no contradiction between the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by way of their own nature—just as there is none between a horse and a buffalo—their opposition is perceived only through their capacity to establish contradictory objects of cognition (*prameya*).
Thus, even when the nature of the means of valid cognition is first examined, that [opposition] is not perceived without an examination of the nature of the objects of cognition.

Consequently, after examining their natures, when the contradiction is reflected upon, one determines the relative strength of the *ācamana* (ritual sipping of water) and so forth based on the strength or weakness of the objects of cognition in the form of the subject (*dharmin*) and its property (*dharma*), provided that no opposing factor has yet arisen.
In that case, the favoring of one [cognition] over the other in a sequential manner is not possible.

Or, even if—following the consideration of the contradiction between the objects of cognition (*prameya*) at the moment immediately subsequent to it—the contradiction between the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) themselves were to arise at the time when their relative strength and weakness (*balābala*) are presented, because they both establish contradictory objects;

nevertheless, since no contradiction has yet arisen at the moment immediately following the presentation of the strength and weakness of the objects of cognition, once a definitive determination (*nirṇaya*) has been reached:

At the time of that determination, there is no presentation of the relative strength or weakness residing in the means of knowledge; therefore, for the other [means], which has not yet reached the stage of determination and arises later—just like *śruti*, *liṅga*, and so forth—it possesses weakness.
Furthermore, there is no absolute sublation of the Vedic injunction (śruti), because it retains its purpose when the occasion for performing the ritual rinsing (ācamana) does not arise.

Moreover, since acts such as rinsing are accepted as being for the sake of the Vedic injunction and as auxiliary elements (aṅga) of the subsequent ritual act, they cannot serve as an intervention between that act and the preparation of the altar (vedikaraṇa); thus, the conclusion is that [the injunction] is not set aside. This is the intended meaning.
As it is said in the Vārttika: "Purity, the sacrificial thread, and so forth do not constitute independent ritual acts;
for everything is for the sake of the subsidiary and the primary rites, and therefore they do not cause an interruption."

Therefore, because acts such as sipping water (ācamana) are weak and thus do not sublate it through direct Vedic statement (śruti), he concludes its authoritative status: "Thus, it is indeed a means of valid knowledge."
(Regarding the Vārtikakāra’s refutation of the Bhāṣyakāra’s view that this constitutes a separate *adhikaraṇa*, and his indication of the view of Nyāyasudhākāra, who differs from it:

Here, the Vārtikakāra [argues] that because the contradiction is evident according to the previously stated method, a prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is untenable; for this very reason, even a prima facie position based on the strength of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is untenable while assuming the contradiction. [This is so] regarding the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), as in: "He wears it across the left shoulder; this is indeed the mark of a god."

By the statement found in the section on the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, "he performs that," since it is prescribed by direct scriptural audition (*śruti*) through extension (*atideśa*) even in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), this [act]— even if its purpose is the arrangement of the garment— is likewise prescribed by direct scriptural audition for the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) as well, via the *Kāṭhaka* statement, "One should study while wearing the sacrificial thread over the left shoulder" (*yajñopavītī*).
Furthermore, by other scriptural texts, the rinsing of the mouth, the right hand, and so forth are also directly perceived [as prescribed].

Since the injunction [in question] is of the nature of *smṛti* (tradition), it is untenable as an example [for the present topic], and because it is improper to cite it as such, the author of the *Bhāṣya* has refuted his own arrangement of a separate *adhikaraṇa*. Furthermore, since it is inappropriate to explain it as a separate *adhikaraṇa*, the first two *sūtras* are subordinate to the preceding section, being intended to resolve the objection regarding the lack of authority of the texts of the Śākyas and others— which was established in the *Virodha-adhikaraṇa*— whereas the third *sūtra* is intended to resolve the objection regarding the authority of custom (*ācāra*), which was established in the *Smṛti-adhikaraṇa*.
It has been stated that this must be explained as being a mere supplement to that;
keeping that in mind, he states another interpretation with the words "or else."

Just as the Vārttikakāra’s statement regarding the Vedic (śrauta) nature of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and other items here is merely an argument by way of corroboration (*abhyuccaya-yukti*), so it should be understood from the *Nyāyasudhā* and the *Kaustubha*;
however, for fear of prolixity, it is not elaborated upon here.
(The authority of giving and so forth as established by the Śākyas and others): "Giving and so forth."
The term "and so forth" includes [the qualities of] the monastery, the seat, detachment, meditation, the truths, self-restraint, generosity, compassion, non-violence, and others.
(An exposition on how even prohibitive and other such sentences culminate in dharma: "The Veda is entirely... and so forth.
Although it is not possible for the entire Veda to be the source of Dharma—
since sentences such as those concerning the Śyena sacrifice and prohibitive injunctions cannot logically have Dharma as their basis—
nevertheless, even those sentences that do not inform one of Dharma serve to produce Dharma by means of fulfilling the recitation of the Vedas, the Brahma-yajña, and other such rites.

There is no fault, because [the Vedic passage] serves as the provider of the occasion (*nimitta*) required by the injunction for expiation (*prāyaścitta-vidhi*), since it functions as an agent (*kāraka*); furthermore, there is the possibility of its indirect utility for the knowledge of Dharma, just like the passage concerning the "learned man" (*vidvad-vākya*).
Thus, [the text] says: "In memory and conduct... (*smṛti-śīle*).
"By such statements as 'śīla is conduct' and so forth."

By the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), there is an inclusion of the following: "Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, and Gāndharvaveda—these three; and Arthaśāstra as the fourth; for these are indeed the eighteen branches of knowledge."
(The lack of authority regarding gifts and other acts prescribed by the Śākyas and others):
"Lack of authority" means...

Therefore, although the meaning of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and so forth is accepted by the learned (*śiṣṭa*), it is also justified as being rooted in the Veda; since the Śākyas and others have not been granted authority over that subject by the learned, their words regarding it are not authoritative because they are not accepted by the learned. Thus, what is known from them and practiced does not become a means to the highest good (*śreyas*), and consequently, those words concerning that subject lack authority—this is the meaning.

As it is stated in the Vārttika: "Likewise, at the time of administering penance and so forth, if someone were to utter their own statement or a verse or aphorism composed by another poet, and then offer a penance consistent with Manu and others, no one would accept that for the sake of dharma.
For only those whose authority to speak has been authorized by the Veda [are accepted]."

"Regarding those eternal beings who are the subjects [of scripture] and who, throughout the transitions of Manvantaras and Yugas, compose compendiums of Dharma— their words are authoritative, and not those of others; this is the settled conclusion."
Thus [it is said].

Likewise: "In the Purāṇas, which describe the causes for the corruption of dharma, it is recorded that in the Kali age there will be the Śākyas and others; who then would be fit to listen to their words?
Therefore, even the teaching on non-violence and other virtues, though rooted in truth, is unfit for consumption and not to be trusted, like milk poured into a dog's leather bag.
Thus ends the third section, concerning the non-contradiction of what is established by the learned.
(B1) (Section 4:
Or rather, even when the cause is not perceived, those [words] employed [in scripture] should be understood as authoritative.
When there is doubt as to whether the authority of uncodified customs such as the spring festival (*vasantotsava*) and others exists or not— given that if these were rooted in the Veda,

they would have been codified by Manu and others just like the *aṣṭakā* rites; and even though there is a general codification for those who know them through such [Vedic] injunctions as "the tradition and conduct of those who know it" (*smṛtiśīle ca tadvidām*), yet because they are not specifically codified, it is certain that no Vedic revelation (*śruti*) for them is observed— the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that they lack authority.

Because they are performed by those learned in the Vedas with the conviction that they are dharma, they possess Vedic status just like the Smṛtis. As for the lack of specific scriptural basis, there is no fault, as it is due to a fear of prolixity.
However, the observation of transgressions and acts of violence is not Vedic, because they are not performed with the conviction that they constitute dharma.
Nor does this imply that everything is non-Vedic;
therefore, traditional practices (ācāra) are also authoritative regarding dharma and adharma. // 4 //
Thus ends the fourth section, concerning the authority of conduct. (B2) (Introduction of another interpretation:
Alternatively—here, either it is contrary to the Sūtra, or...

"Because [the Veda] has the same extent as the scripture" (Jaimini 1.3.6)—intending that this previously established siddhānta-sūtra serves here as the *pūrvapakṣa*, he states the sūtra's *pūrvapakṣa* after first indicating its subject matter: "Of those not [verbally] connected... (*anibaddhānām*).
(The prima facie argument against the authority of custom and self-satisfaction):

Since established customs (*nibaddhācāra*) possess authority precisely as *smṛti* (tradition), and since the reasons for the objection to be stated later are impossible in their case, the phrase "of those not established" (*anibaddhānām*) is used to indicate that they are not the subject of the example.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in "the spring festival etc.," there is the inclusion of all various regional customs, as well as the object of a vow (*saṃkalpa*) not contrary to *śruti* and *smṛti*, such as "I shall not drink water except during meals."
And there is the inclusion of "the satisfaction of the self of the learned" and so forth. Thus [it is said].

By the word "etcetera" (*ādipadena*), there is an inclusion of such passages as: "Revelation (*śruti*), tradition (*smṛti*), the conduct of the virtuous (*sadācāra*), that which is pleasing to oneself, and desire born of right resolve—this is remembered as the root of Dharma";
"whatever conduct exists in whatever region"; and "the conduct of the righteous (*sādhūnām*)," and so forth.
"Because of certainty."

And this is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the fact that because practices consisting of actions (*kriyārūpa-ācāra*) are not verbal in nature (*aśabdarūpatva*), it is impossible for them to convey what is beneficial to man (*puruṣahitabodhakatva*).
Thus, he concludes the objection against the authority established in the *Smṛtyadhikaraṇa* with the words: "lack of authority" (*aprāmāṇya*).
(The doctrine establishing the authority of conduct as being bound to performance through the cognition that it is dharma):

As for the establishment of the authority [of practices] based on geographical distinction, as seen in the statements of Āpastamba and others: “Those for whom [practices] have been handed down through tradition and were performed by their ancestors—they alone are not censured for those customs, and not other people”; and “One person is not censured for what another does, because of the authority of the region.”
Since it is improper to restrict a powerful *smṛti* in accordance with a weak and contested practice, and because Bodhāyana, after presenting the opinion of Āpastamba, stated,
"Gautama says this is false," and "because of conflict with the *smṛti* of the learned," [the author] concludes that Āpastamba’s statement was intended merely to express censure;
thus, he summarizes the established conclusion with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).

In this context, the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*, in the section on the relative strength (*balābala*) of authorities, has stated that the practice of marrying a maternal uncle’s daughter (*mātulakanyā*) or a father’s sister’s daughter (*paitṛṣvasreyī*) is not a valid example [of a practice contradicting scripture], because it is supported by direct Vedic indications (*liṅga*) such as: "The parents [conceived] the embryo; the two lords [are] this; who is the lord? Tvaṣṭṛ, Savitṛ, the omniform one. Thus, due to its being grounded in direct Vedic revelation, the practice of such marriages possesses greater authority even than Smṛti. This also implies a refutation of the *Smṛticandrikā* and other works which hold otherwise.
In accordance with that, the authors of the *Smṛticandrikā* and others also accept this very view; their refutation, preceded by a detailed demonstration, is to be found in the *Kaustubha*.

[The determination that words such as *trivṛt*, *carya*, and *aśvavāla*, whose specific meanings are disputed between common usage (*loka*) and the Veda, fall within the scope of the aforementioned section:
The author of the Vārttika states a second alternative interpretation, beginning with "Or rather" (*evaṃ vā*).

Regarding the word *trivṛt* as recited in the passage “the *bahiṣpavamāna* is *trivṛt*,” in common worldly usage the meaning of the word *trivṛt*— derived from the etymology “that which is woven by three”— is understood to be triplicity, as seen in expressions such as “a threefold rope” (*trivṛdrajjūḥ*) or “a threefold knot” (*trivṛdgranthiḥ*).

However, in the Veda, because of the sequence of three triplets beginning with “Sing unto him, O men” (*upāsmai gāyatā naraḥ*), and because of another scriptural statement, “They praise with nine” (*navabhiḥ stuvanti*), its meaning here is a group of nine *stotrīyā* verses.

Likewise, while in common worldly usage the word *caru* denotes a cooking vessel (*sthālī*), in the Veda it refers to the sacrificial oblation itself; for instance, having prescribed, "The *prāyaṇīya* [offering] is the sun, a *caru* in milk," the text continues: "Having filled this *caru* with clarified butter, he performs four *ājyabhāga* offerings; having sacrificed to Pathyā Svasti, he sacrifices to Agni and Soma; having sacrificed to Agni and Soma, he sacrifices to Savitṛ; and [he sacrifices] to Aditi with the boiled rice (*odana*)."

In the sentence concerning the sequence [of cooking], because it refers to boiled rice (*odana*) as an established fact (*siddhavat*), it has the boiled rice as its primary object. Even there, by virtue of common usage among ritualists (*yājñika*), it refers specifically to a type of boiled rice that is cooked internally without being drained.
Similarly, regarding the word *aśvavāla*, in common worldly usage, its meaning is the horse's hair through the connection with its parts.

In the supplementary passage to the statement, "The *aśvavāla* grass is the sacrificial strew (*prastara*)," the meaning is the substance in the form of *kāśa* grass, because it is heard [in scripture] that: "Indeed, the sacrifice, having become a horse, departed from the gods; it entered the waters; it was seized by its tail; having released the hairs, it entered [the earth]; those hairs attained the state of *kāśa* grass."
Thus he provides an example of the object of misconception: "trivṛt."

By the phrase "and so forth," it is indicated that in the expression *aikṣavī vidhṛtī*, the word *aikṣavī*—by virtue of its etymological connection understood in common worldly usage—refers to parts of sugarcane;
however, by means of the supplementary portion of the text (*vākyaśeṣa*) inferred from the writing of the Vārttika, it refers to *kāśa* grass roots in the Veda.
Similarly, the word *stoma*, as in *brāhmaṇastoma*, is a term for a collective group in common worldly usage.

By the well-known usage among ritualists (*yājñika*) that "stoma" denotes the measure of praise, and by grammar— supported by the rule for the suffix *ḍa* applied to "stoma" in the sense of "fifteenfold" and so on— as evidenced by the grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in expressions such as "the threefold stoma" and "the fifteenfold stoma," it is established that these terms refer to the number of praises produced by the number of verses (*stotrīyā*). Thus, both of these points of contention are subsumed under this [definition].

(B1) Or rather: in cases such as the words *trivṛt*, *caru*, and *aśvavāla*, where there is a conflict between the meaning derived from common usage (*loka*) and the supplementary explanatory passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), it might initially be argued that since there is no evidence for the Veda having greater authority than common usage regarding the relationship between words and their meanings, the two possess equal force.

However, this is not so; because a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) between an injunction (*vidhi*) and its praise (*stuti*) is untenable unless they refer to the same subject matter, it must be admitted that the injunction derives its power [to convey meaning] precisely from the supplementary explanatory passage.

Therefore, since the meaning is already understood through worldly means of valid cognition (*laukikapramāṇa*), one does not postulate a primary denotative power (*śakti*) for fear of over-extension; rather, comprehension occurs solely through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and so forth.

For this very reason, it will be stated later that even in cases where there is no supplementary scriptural passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), the meaning of words such as *trivṛt* must be understood according to its Vedic usage alone.
Consequently, the primary denotation of the word *trivṛt* is the ninefold arrangement of verses within a hymn (*stotra*), and not the state of being threefold (*tattraiguṇyam*).
The word *caru* refers to boiled rice (*odana*), not to the cooking pot;
the word *aśvavāla* refers to *kāśa* grass, not to horse-hair.
Furthermore, the supplementary explanations (*vākyaśeṣa*) are to be found in the *Kaustubha*. // 7 //
Thus ends the third section.
(B2) [The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the optionality of worldly versus Vedic usage, based on their lack of equal strength:

Now, one might object: since worldly usage has no bearing upon *dharma*, Vedic usage alone must be more authoritative. To this, we reply: "This is not so; for regarding the meanings of words, the Veda is not superior."

He provides the resolution according to the method stated in the Vārttika: "For that [Vedic statement] exceeds the world [of experience] regarding the meaning of its sentence, whose cause is the unseen (adṛṣṭa)," by saying "therein."
"Equality of strength."

Nor should it be argued that—since the assumption of a single power in one case allows for usage in another case by virtue of similarity to that [first], it is not proper to assume multiple powers—for two reasons: first, because the two meanings are so utterly distinct that no similarity exists between them; and second, because there is an absence of any decisive criterion (vinigamanā) [to favor one over the other].
Therefore, since both meanings are understood to be denotable by the force of two means of knowledge that cannot be established otherwise, there is an option (*vikalpa*) due to their equal strength.

Thus, regarding the statement "The *bahiṣpavamāna* [laud] is threefold" (*trivṛd bahiṣpavamānam*), in the view that adopts the worldly meaning, one verse (*ṛk*) is to be tripled, making a triplet (*tṛca*); the mention of another triplet [of verses] in the scripture should be understood as being for the sake of an alternative option.
Thus, by the word *caru*, there is an injunction for the vessel-content itself— which is inedible— just like the *kṛṣṇala* berry;
whereas milk serves as the substratum through an unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) means,
and the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is merely a restatement of an alternative possibility.
The intended meaning is that this should be inferred in other cases as well.
(An exposition of the position that worldly renown is stronger than Vedic renown:
The phrase "equal strength" is also an indication of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that worldly renown is stronger.

For instance: in the case of a conflict, worldly renown attains its own existence independently of anything else, as in: "The sacred thread (*upavīta*) of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of cotton, wound upwards, and triple-stranded."

In the statement of Manu, "with a single threefold knot," although the number nine exists among the nine threads that constitute the rope, it is observed that the purpose is to enjoin a threefold structure (*traiguṇya*) for the rope that constitutes the sacred thread (*upavīta*). Furthermore, since there is Vedic usage in the form "the girdle (*raśanā*) becomes threefold" (*trivṛd*), which establishes a well-known convention among ritualists (*yājñika*) regarding the meaning of threefoldness, the word *trivṛt* is supported by both Manu’s and Vedic usage. Consequently, because it is free from contradiction, the Vedic usage—being established through its co-referentiality with other words whose meanings are well-known in common worldly usage—[prevails].
Because it is remote, it is weaker in comparison [to the direct statement], and thus only its own meaning is grasped.

As for the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*), since they serve merely to provide encouragement, they can be justified even through figurative interpretation—as in the case of "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*). Therefore, they do not necessarily have as their primary purpose the establishment of a relationship between a name and the thing named; and since there is no lack of purpose (*ānarthakya*) here, they cannot be set aside on the grounds of being obstructed by such lack of purpose.
Since it is the grasping of that [primary] meaning, there is no optionality (*vikalpa*) even by virtue of grasping two meanings.
And thus, on the view of equality, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) would have the status of a partial restatement (*pākṣikānuvāda*) due to optionality;

whereas on the view of predominance, because the worldly well-known meaning itself is taken up in the injunction, it is established that the words *odana* and so forth occurring in the explanatory passage must be understood as indicating (*lakṣaka*) the cooking vessel and so on through their connection with the rice.

(Regarding the two positions—that worldly and Vedic consensus are of equal strength or of unequal strength—there is no dispute in cases involving injunctions accompanied by explanatory passages (*arthavāda*); therefore, the intention lies in the words constituting the *arthavāda* that lack such an injunction.

The authors of the *Prakāśa*, however, maintain that in both positions, because the purport of the injunction regarding the subject at hand is understood through the *arthavāda* concerning the boiled rice (*odana*) itself—just as in the established conclusion—one may [employ] "either a secondary (*gauṇa*) or an indicative (*lākṣaṇika*) sense, or even by means of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*)."

"Since this Veda relies upon the meaning, who indeed would oppose it?"—according to this principle stated in the *Vārttika*, there would be no difference in practice because one would necessarily have to accept only the boiled rice (*odana*).

Nevertheless, they say that where there is no explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), as in the case of "the *saurya* oblation of *caru*," this [distinction] serves a purpose. That is not correct; for rather than resorting to a secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the word *caru* to conform to the explanatory passage within the injunction, it is more reasonable to assume a figurative indication of the cooking vessel (*sthālī*) within the explanatory passage itself. Thus, the understanding arises through such figurative indication.

(Resolution of the meaning of the term *trivṛt*): Herein lies the distinction: since the words *trivṛt* and so forth have their power determined to refer to a group of nine *stotrīyā* verses by virtue of the sequence of three triplets (*tṛca*), that very meaning must be accepted wherever there is a connection with a *stotra*.

Otherwise, in the case of the *bahiṣpavamāna*, since a group of nine *stotrīyās* would already be established through the injunction of three triplets, the employment of the word *trivṛt* in the statement "the *bahiṣpavamāna* is *trivṛt*" would result in redundancy.

Therefore, just as in the case of the *stotrīya*-navaka, even when there is a threefold repetition (*traiguṇya*), its purposefulness is fulfilled precisely by being denoted by the term "threefold" (*trivṛt*); thus, where there is no sequential mention of three triplets—as in "The *Agniṣṭut* *agniṣṭoma* is threefold" (*trivṛd agniṣṭud agniṣṭomaḥ*)—there is an injunction of that very [term] through its established conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*), which sets aside the etymological derivation (*yoga*). However, where that conventional meaning is not sublated, [the etymological sense applies].

For example, in passages such as "the sacrificial post is threefold" (*trivṛd yūpaḥ*), even though the threefold nature well-known in common worldly usage is grasped there, there is no indication (lakṣaṇā) because no connection can be established with the worldly sense of "threefold. Therefore, since the word is capable of denoting merely a group of nine *stotrīyā* verses, even if it were to denote that mere group of nine here, it would result in the fault of indication; and since the comprehension of the meaning is possible through the application of the well-established etymological parts, there is no evidence for a figurative (lākṣaṇika) meaning. Thus, only the primary (śakya) meaning is to be accepted, and even regarding a meaning established in common usage, there is only direct denotative power (*śakti*); hence, there is indeed polysemy.

For this very reason, the view that the term is conventionally restricted (*rūḍhi*) to the group of nine verses occurring within the *stotrīyās* of the *bahiṣpavamāna*—based on the sequential mention of three triplets (*tṛca*) specifically in the *bahiṣpavamāna* itself—is also refuted; because if that were the case, the mention of the "ninefold" (*trivṛt*) would remain useless as it was before.
Indeed, in that scenario, it would not be possible to enjoin a group of nine for all the *stotras* in the *agniṣṭut* sacrifice.
Because, as in the case of the expression "the sacrificial post is threefold" (*trivṛd yūpaḥ*), this would result in a figurative meaning;

because it would follow that only the denoted meaning consisting of the triad of qualities (*traiguṇya*) is grasped; because the nine-fold set of *stotrīyā* verses is already obtained there by extension (*atideśa*) alone, rendering the injunction redundant; and because the futility of the word *trivṛt* in that context cannot be avoided—therefore, there is a primary power (*śakti*) in the word for both the nine-fold set of *stotrīyā* verses and for the triad of qualities.

Likewise, in the case of the statement regarding the *mānava* [text] as well, it refers precisely to the threefold nature well-known in common worldly usage, just like the nine-fold set of *stotrīyā* verses.
(Regarding the resolution of the contradiction with the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* in the case where the word *trivṛt* denotes a group of nine *stotrīyā* verses:
Nor does the denotation of a group of nine *stotrīyā* verses contradict the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*;

for that [sūtra] is the domain of the principle of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* only in cases where, once a capacity for the mere qualifier has been postulated, the cognition of the qualified follows by way of its necessary concomitance (*avinābhāva*).

Furthermore, since there is no absence of inseparable concomitance with the son, there is no contradiction in accepting that these words— such as "daughter-in-law" and so forth— denote a qualified entity (the wife of the son), just as they denote the wife qualified by the son in other cases.

(Resolution of the meaning of the word *caru*): Since the word *caru* is accepted as having a conventional (*rūḍhi*) meaning in the sense of "boiled rice" (*odana*)— in accordance with the force of the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*) and the requirement of a common referent—
and since there is only figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the vessel commonly known in the world due to an invariable connection, there is no polysemy.

Therefore, when the capacity [of a term] has been determined here, even in cases where there is no supplementary scriptural statement (*vākyaśeṣa*)—such as in "the *saurya* oblation of *caru*" and so forth—there is no evidence for adopting a figurative meaning; thus, only the boiled rice (*odana*) itself is understood. Although ritual experts do not accept that what is cooked in a pan (*kapāla*) or a cauldron (*kaṭāha*) is *caru*, and since the term is used only for rice situated in a pot (*sthālī*), it would be more appropriate—according to the principle of the section on generic form (*ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*)—to take it as denoting the pot alone. Nevertheless, [the primary meaning remains the rice].
Therefore, because of the exclusive connection, it would follow that the word "śyena" denotes the rice-gruel alone;

nevertheless, since it is established that one must adopt a figurative meaning in accordance with the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), and since it is determined that the word "śyena"—which is compared by means of the simile of the hawk—refers primarily to the sacrifice, it is established that the sacrifice is denoted even through a figurative function (*gauṇī vṛtti*). Consequently, due to the strength of that [figurative application], [the rule] "the rest is the same as the śyena" applies.

Just as in the case of [the word] *tyādi* and so forth, it is proper to understand that very same thing [is denoted] in *sauryam* and so forth as well. Furthermore, even for ritualists (*yājñika*s), if the word *caru* were based solely on the specific mode of cooking in relation to boiled rice (*odana*), then— even though the pot is implied because that [cooking] is impossible without a pot— since it is not admitted that the word denotes the rice situated in the pot, the pot's status as the denotable object does not arise, as it falls outside the scope of the principle established in the *Akṛtyadhikaraṇa*.

Although a definitive conclusion can indeed be reached through the technical usage of experts in sacrifice (*yājñika-prasiddhi*), which overrides common worldly usage (*loka-prasiddhi*) regarding the word *caru*, such that it need not be understood as depending solely on the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*); nevertheless, since even occasional technical usage can be explained as figurative (*lākṣaṇika*), it is improper to override its more extensive prevalence.

Therefore, one must accept that the supplementary statement itself is the basis for the technical usage of experts; thus, by the maxim "it is determined by that very cause," the supplementary statement serves as the deciding factor—this is how it should be understood.

(Resolution of the Meaning of the Word *Aśvavāla*) In the same way, regarding the two words *aśva* and *vāla*, by virtue of their etymological derivation (*avayavayoga*), the meanings of the constituent parts—namely "horse" and "hair"—are established through direct denotative power (*śakti*) alone.

This is because the Veda describes the transformation of horses themselves into the form of *kāśa* grass; and because the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikāra*) share common characteristics such as length and so forth.

Although a figurative application (*gauṇa-prayoga*) is possible on the basis of similarity, nevertheless—in the absence of a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) in every case—it is proper to accept [the primary sense] according to the method previously stated, just as in the case of the word *śyena*.

In reality, however, if one were to admit a figurative meaning for the word *aśvavāla*, there would arise the consequence that the secondary sense depends upon coordination with another word (*padāntara-sāmānādhikaraṇya*), which would result in a loss of syntactic capacity (*asāmarthya*); consequently, the formation of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) *āśvavāla* would be impossible.
There is no figurative sense (gauṇatva) at all;

rather, because the well-known meaning of the parts is set aside by the stronger conventional usage established in the Veda—as in the case of the word *aśvakarṇa*—and because a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) is understood here, even though the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*) alone is grasped, the capacity [of the word] is determined through the connection of its parts as well; thus, there is indeed polysemy (*nānārthatva*).

By this, the following [objection] is refuted: "Let the word *kāśa* in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) itself signify the meaning of hair-like sprouts (*vāla*) in the form of *kāśa*-grass; there is no need for the postulation of another possible meaning.
For that would result in a lack of syntactic connection (incoherence) with the statement: "Those hairs attained the state of *kāśa*."
(Resolution of the meaning of the word *stoma*):
Thus, by means of Vedic co-referentiality and other criteria, it should be understood that the word *stoma* denotes the number of hymns (*stuti*) determined by the number of *stotrīyā* verses;
or else, according to the method stated by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*, it should be understood as denoting merely the collection of *stotrīyā* verses themselves.

However, whether [the word] refers to the conventionally established aggregate by means of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) or by primary denotation (śakti), such is the general direction [of the argument].
It will be explained.
The word "in the tenth" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
The intention is that there is no tautology because this [passage] serves merely to state the purpose of the present section (*adhikaraṇa*).
The passage beginning with "And the supplementary statements" (*vākyaśeṣāśca*) has already been explained.

As for the argument that this [topic] is already covered by the rule "in cases of doubt, by the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) and so forth," that is not so; because although that [rule] functions as a determiner regarding a doubtful meaning prior to its connection with the remainder of the sentence, here, since there is no state of being doubtful due to the certainty of the opposite meaning prior to that connection, it does not function as a determiner.
Thus ends the fourth section: [The Authority of Words Well-Known in the Scriptures].
"But that which is enjoined should be accepted, because it is not contradicted by a means of valid cognition.
(Jaimini Sūtra 1.3.10) But that which is enjoined...
In cases where words such as *pika*, *nema*, and *tāmarasa* do not have a well-known specific meaning among the Aryas,
but among the Mlecchas, however, *pika* means "cuckoo" and *nema* means "half."
A "sata" is a large-leaved wooden vessel with a hundred holes, circular in shape; it is commonly known as a "tāmarasa," that is, a lotus.
In this context, one should take the meaning as it is already established by common usage, rather than imagining it through etymological analysis or grammatical derivation.
Nor does the unreliability of the usage among the Mlecchas follow from observing a corruption of word and meaning therein;
for words such as *pika* and others are seen even in the Veda, and thus they are not corrupted.
Consequently, when there is a requirement for their denotation, the usage of those [Mlecchas] is also accepted as a means of comprehension, since it is already established.

Therefore, although the usage established by the *nigama* and other Vedic sources is stronger by virtue of being well-known within that tradition, it is weaker because it is merely inferable (*kalpya*).
Conversely, although the usage established among the *mlecchas* is weaker by virtue of being established among them, it is stronger because it is already established (*kḷpta*);
for it has been established that the strength or weakness of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) prevails over the strength or weakness of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, no specific prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) has been stated here. // 8 //
Thus concludes the section on *pikanema*.
(B2) [In the determination of the meaning of words such as *pikanema*, the investigation of the grounds for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) begins:
Although in this context the Bhāṣya appears to concern itself with an analysis of the relative strength of the linguistic conventions of Āryans and Mlecchas;

Nevertheless, considering that the authority of the usage of Mlecchas has not been established anywhere previously, such [usage] is improper; therefore, only an inquiry into its validity or invalidity is undertaken here.

As for the inquiry into relative strength (*balābala*), it is already established by the very logic of the relative strength of means of knowledge as expounded in the *Śiṣṭākopādhikaraṇa*; it is merely shown here as a result by way of incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*). This is the intention indicated by the *Vārttika*, namely, that in case of conflict, the usage of Mlecchas is weak.

Even in the absence of contradiction, since that very [usage] is accepted as the authority, and since the usage well-known in the scriptures through the medium of etymological works (*nirukta*) and the like is accepted in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*),

the author— without demonstrating the *apavāda* connection (which is obvious) and without showing the lack of logical justification for the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) which accepts the usage established in the scriptures— states the final conclusion after first indicating the subject matter, beginning with the words "yatreti."

By the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), there is an inclusion of words such as *kloma* and others denoting specific parts of an animal, the word *patrorṇa* denoting washed silk (*dhautakauśeya*), and the word *vārabāṇa* denoting a tunic (*kañcuka*).
(Regarding the determination of the meaning of words such as *pika*, the establishment of their authority after first refuting the weakness of the usage of barbarians (*mleccha*) in its own right:
It was stated that the usage of barbarians is not accepted [as authoritative] because it has been proven to lack authority in the case of *kāśa* and other such words.

Even though the specific meaning established among the Āryas may lack existence in its own right, since it can be established through etymological analysis (*nirukta*) and other means by being rooted in that [usage], the speakers possess greater strength regarding that meaning in its own form.
Regarding the relative strength [of authorities]:

by stating "therein, of that which is well-known in that [tradition]," he demonstrates certainty while removing the cause of doubt—namely, that in the case of what is well-known among Mlecchas, there is weakness on the part of the speaker and intrinsic weakness in the form itself.
And thus, the meaning is that the authority for determining the denotation [of words] rests solely upon the usage of the Mlecchas;
this refers to words such as *pika* and the like.

Even if one lacks the capacity to dispel doubts regarding corruption in other words, in the case of Vedic injunctions such as "one should sacrifice a *pika*," "one desiring cattle should offer a *caru* oblation to Soma and Pūṣan with unground grains," and so forth— the *pika* and other such words being employed therein— there is a certainty that the nominal stem alone is free from corruption, despite the usage of non-Sanskrit (*mleccha*) speakers who do not apply case-endings. Furthermore, since these words are employed in the eternal Veda, it is necessary to postulate that they denote eternal objects, such as species (*jāti*), and the like.

Since a secondary (gauṇa) usage is impossible when the primary meaning is not established elsewhere— such as in the case of the *kokila* bird— and since there is no similarity with words like *kokila* that have the same meaning as the primary term,
it follows that, as in the case of words such as *gāvī*,

even a confusion regarding the expressive power (*śakti*) based on those [words] is impossible. Consequently, because the meaning is determined to be uncorrupted, the assumption of denotative capacity (*vācakatva*) for the usage of Mlecchas, though beginningless, is also precluded.

For regarding matters of unseen results (*adṛṣṭārtha*), there is nothing contradictory in the fact that others possess greater authority in determining the meaning than Manu and others do in knowing the form of words from the Śākyas and so forth; on the contrary, [their knowledge] is indeed a means for understanding the required word-meanings—this is the sense.
Furthermore, even assuming a contradiction, he demonstrates their weakness due to the established authority of the scriptures, stating: "Therefore... (*ata eva*).
Because it has been established.

This is not correct— because in that case, it was stated that [the Smṛti] is weak merely in terms of the strength or weakness residing in another means of knowledge related to it, with respect to the strength or weakness of its own nature (*svarūpa*), and not in terms of the strength or weakness of its substratum (*āśraya*);
for it has been established that its weakness consists solely in the strength or weakness residing in something else related to it, with respect to the strength or weakness of its own nature.
Furthermore, just as other things related to that [object] are valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), so too is the substratum (*āśraya*); thus there is no fault.
And this has been stated according to the view of the Bhāṣyakāra;
for according to the view of the Vārtikakāra, the sūtras are interpreted differently by refuting the section on "Non-contradiction with the Learned" (*śiṣṭākopādhikaraṇa*).

Because the relative strength or weakness of the objects of knowledge was not previously determined there, it is precisely here that the strength or weakness of the objects of knowledge must be investigated in relation to the strength or weakness residing in their respective substrates.
(An exposition according to the Vārtika school that this very section establishes the superiority of the usage of Mlecchas regarding specific objects):

Therefore, since according to the Vārtika school both the investigation into the validity or invalidity of Mleccha usage and the investigation into its relative strength or weakness must be conducted right here, this section— by virtue of being a prerequisite (*upajīvya*)—
should be understood in substance before the section concerning the *pīlu* tree and others.

And thus, in this view, there arises a need for a reason why the relative strength or weakness of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) has not been established here as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Nevertheless, it should be understood that its non-mention here is because, since the non-authoritativeness of Mleccha usage has already been stated in the case of contradiction, a reason for its authoritativeness in the absence of contradiction—which would serve as a *pūrvapakṣa*—is impossible by implication; and furthermore, the Author of the Sūtras himself did not state it independently either. Therefore, its non-mention here is for those very reasons.
Thus ends the fifth section concerning the authority of the conventions of the Mlecchas.
(B1) If it is argued that this is a treatise on practice (*prayogaśāstra*).
Whether all the *Smṛtis*, the *Kalpasūtras*, the six *Aṅgas*, or the works of Śākya and others possess the status of *Veda* or are equal to the *Veda*,
it is not so; for there would be no weight [in their authority] if they were rooted in *Śruti* and the like,
and because it would be logically untenable for them to be the subject of the injunction for the eternal *Brahmayajña*.

Regarding the six-limbed [auxiliaries], their status as Veda is established by the traditional authority (*smṛti*) stating, "Some say they are six-limbed. However, since names such as *Buddha*, *Baudhāyana*, and *Māśaka*—like those of the *Kaṭhas* and others—are also logically explained as being based on the act of promulgation (*pravacana*), it might be argued that these [texts] possess the status of Veda or are equal to the Veda.

This being the position reached, we reply: because there is a firm recollection of their authors, it is impossible for them to be based on promulgation like the *Kaṭhas* and others; therefore, they do not have the status of Veda, nor are they equal to the Veda.
Since such texts exist in every Manvantara, it is logical that they fall within the scope of the injunction for the daily Brahma-yajña.
The mention of "one" [text] is intended as a presentation of the opinion of others, namely, "some say there are six auxiliary limbs.
Therefore, according to the principle established in the *Smṛti-adhikaraṇa*, these works are indeed rooted in the Veda.
However, because that [authoritativeness] is impossible in the case of the texts of the Śākyas and others, they possess only the status of a semblance (*ābhāsatva*).

(B2) In order to avoid the redundancy of the body of the section (*adhikaraṇaśarīra*) belonging to the author of the subsequent commentary (*parabhāṣyakārīya*) concerning the authority of the *Kalpasūtras* with the section on *Smṛti*, the author of the Bhāṣya here— following the opinion of the Vārttikakāra and in accordance with the Sūtras— has cited the *Kalpasūtras* and conducted an inquiry into their authority and lack of authority by treating them as being for the purpose of intrinsic authority (*svataḥ prāmāṇya*).

That [position] is not tenable; for in the *Smṛtyadhikaraṇa*, it was established that all branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) other than the Vedas possess authority by virtue of being rooted in the Veda, and thus [the opponent's view] contradicts that.

Therefore, since the final conclusion (*siddhānta*)—through two sūtras stating the rules of accentuation and the supplementary passages (*vākyaśeṣa*)—demonstrates their distinction from the Veda, it is understood that their intrinsic authority (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) is rejected. Consequently, having accepted independent authority in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), one objects to the authority established in the *Smṛtyadhikaraṇa* on the grounds of its being based on the Veda.

Having set forth the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and then refuted it here within the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), thereby stabilizing what was established in the *Smṛtyadhikaraṇa*, [the author] intends the term "Kalpa-sūtra" found in the Bhāṣya as an elliptical indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).

This is because, in the explanation of the words "valid authority" (*pramāṇa*) and "non-valid authority" (*apramāṇa*) in the Bhāṣya as meaning "independence" (*svātantrya*) and "lack of independence" (*asvātantrya*), the grounds for the objection apply universally without distinction;
thus, the objection and its resolution are equally possible regarding Smṛtis and other such texts as well.
Since certain barbarian practices (*mlecchācāra*) are beginningless and thus equal to the practices of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), their authority is established as independent;

and here too, because their authority is justified either by being the Veda itself or by being equal to the Veda, it is not logical that they have the Veda as their source, nor is it logical that they lack authority due to contradiction with the Veda. Thus, by relying on the authority established in the immediately preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*), this [section] introduces two subsequent sections concerning contradictions with Smṛti; therefore, it is an "introductory" (*ākṣepikī*) discussion.
Without explicitly showing the connection because it is self-evident, he presents the examples with the words: "of all the Smṛtis."

(The determination of the definitions and other characteristics of the *Kalpas* and *Sūtras*, based on their inclusion within the scope of the *Smṛti-adhikaraṇa* and their connection to the scope of the subsequent *Adhikaraṇa* which addresses that objection:
Not only are the *smṛtis* of Manu and others the sole examples in the *Smṛti-adhikaraṇa*,
such that this objection would apply only to that limited scope.
Moreover, since all works other than the Vedas are cited as examples, he says "or of the Kalpasūtras" in order to indicate that this objection applies to their subject matter as well.
The analysis of the compound is "Kalpas and Sūtras.

By the etymology "those which prescribe the performance (*prayoga*) are Kalpas," the term refers to texts composed by Bodhāyana, Vārāha, Māśaka, and others, which set forth established ritual procedures.

By the etymology "those which indicate (*sūcayanti*) [the meaning] are Sūtras," they refer to those works characterized by their own technical conventions and designations, such as "the taking of a quarter-verse is called *ṛc*" and "this is called the *tīrtha*."

The distinction is that the works composed by Āśvalāyana, Baijavāpa, Kātyāyana, and others are treatises that set forth the characteristics (lakṣaṇa) which indicate specific ritual applications (prayoga). As it is stated in the Vārttika: "Those [works] by which the established application of rituals is followed are called Kalpas; they declare their sūtras to be for the purpose of providing definitions."
Elsewhere it is also said: "The wise say that *sūtras* are those which are concise, indicative of their meaning, consisting of few syllables and words, and containing the essence of everything."
(An exposition on how the texts of the Śākyas and others fall within the scope of the Kalpasūtras. Regarding the term "Śākyas and others":
Although it was not established in the *Smṛtyadhikaraṇa* that the texts of the Śākyas and others possess authority— such that they could be said to be the subject of this objection—

nevertheless, since the author of the Vārttika demonstrated in the *Virodhādhikaraṇa* their lack of authority due to the impossibility of their being rooted in the Veda, the reason established here as the basis for the objection [remains valid].

The sense is that even if independence is challenged by a lack of authority, and even if it is of no use for the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), its status as an object of inquiry is nonetheless justified.
In all these instances, the word "or" (vā) does not indicate an alternative position; rather, indicating a lack of insistence, it serves only to show that all [the cases mentioned] are examples.

(Regarding the prima facie argument for the authority of the Kalpasūtras on the grounds of their being either Vedas or equal to the Vedas due to parsimony: For this very reason, it is stated in the Vārttika, "In this way, these four are also branches of knowledge," [and] because of the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*).
As for the word "gauravāt" (due to complexity/weightiness), [it refers to the opposite case].

Just as in the *Smṛti-adhikaraṇa*, where the assumption of a basis in the Veda is adopted because it is simpler than the assumption of a basis in error and so forth, so too, since their authority must necessarily be affirmed due to their acceptance by the most steadfast and learned members of the three twice-born classes, it is more appropriate to adopt the assumption of their being authorless (*apauruṣeya*), as this is simpler than the assumption of a Vedic basis; thus, they are equal in their authorlessness.
The compendia of Manu and others,
as well as the Vedas, [are authoritative] because they are the root of Dharma.
The phrase "according to rule" refers to their status as Veda by means of inference. However, if it were argued that they are not Vedas—

either because they lack the seal of the Veda (*vedamudrā*) or because they lack the established renown among those expert in the Veda, and are thus like poetry— then this would be refuted by a counter-inference (*satpratipakṣa*).
The meaning is that, at that time, it possesses equality with the Vedas.

Furthermore, since the *smṛtis* of Manu and others are based on the contents of the Veda which have mostly become obscured, they may possess some degree of purposefulness; however, because the *kalpasūtras* clearly set forth the contents of the Veda as perceived by all people, their composition would otherwise result in futility. Consequently, their authority must be established on the basis of their being the Veda itself.
It is logical that these [Smṛtis] possess the status of Veda by virtue of being authorless (apauruṣeya), just like other Vedic branches (śākhā).
For it is impossible for humans to compose these [Smṛtis], which state matters concerning the meaning of Vedic sentences that are perceptible to all people.

The point is that if they were so composed, they would fulfill their purpose merely by presenting injunctions; consequently, they could not function as a source of valid knowledge regarding Dharma, and thus their status as Smṛti—which is rooted in Dharma—would be untenable.

(The determination of the authority of the Smṛtis as being the subject matter of the rules for the beginningless Brahma-yajña, and the determination of the authority of the texts of Śākya and others, by virtue of their generating the cognition of dharma and adharma through their own inherent validity.
[This is indicated by the phrase: "The eternal Brahma-yajña."

Beginning with the statement, “Day by day one should study the Veda,” and continuing with, “Whatever Ṛg-verses one studies, whatever Yajus-formulas, whatever Brāhmaṇas, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and Kalpas,” this refers to the eternal and beginninglessly established injunction for the Brahma-yajña;
for that [injunction] would not be tenable if the Kalpas were of recent origin—this is the meaning.
Although the texts of the Śākyas and others do not fall within the scope of the injunction for the daily Vedic recitation (*brahmayajña*),

nevertheless, because the knowledge of dharma and adharma derived from the texts of the Śākyas and others is self-evident (*svasaṃvedya*), and because that self-validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) has been established in the *Tarkapāda*, there is no impairment of their authority even in the absence of the excellence consisting in being spoken by a reliable person (*āptoktatva*).

And it is not the case that—although the Mīmāṃsakas do not accept [intrinsic] validity, the Śākyas do accept extrinsic validity (parataḥprāmāṇya)—how could validity be established in the absence of the excellence characterized by being spoken by a reliable person (āptoktatva)?

For the Śākya has stated that the permanence of dharmas exists whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, because he has described the permanence of dharmas as either a permanence of continuity (pravāhanityatva) or an immutably fixed permanence (kūṭasthanityatva).

In this regard, since the eternity of [the Veda] is untenable without the eternity of the scripture that establishes it, and since the authority of eternal scriptures cannot be maintained if they were not self-evident, and even if self-evidence is accepted, it would result in the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets; thus, even if this were the case, if one were to accept that [the Veda] was composed by its own author,
then the comprehension of its authority would be sublated by the defects of the author.
However, the acceptance of that [position] is not tenable because it is cumbersome.
And thus, although the status of being Veda or being equal to the Veda is far from established once its basis in the Veda has been refuted,
nevertheless, the Śākya thief is attempting to enter the village of the authority of his own scripture through another door, namely by means of perception and so forth as its foundation.

"Rather than entering [the path] while being warded off by the Mīmāṃsakas— who hold the staff of logic characterized by the inability to perceive supersensuous objects and by being outside the Vedic path— it is better not to enter at all; but now, he wishes to enter openly by way of the great highway of authorlessness (apauruṣeyatva), which is approved by the Mīmāṃsakas"— according to this method stated in the *Vārttika*, it is indeed possible [for the opponent] to raise an objection regarding lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) independently.
The meaning is that it possesses validity (*prāmāṇya*).
(The manner of determining the Vedic status of the auxiliary sciences):
Regarding the Vedic status of the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), he states the reason quite clearly with the words "But as for the auxiliary sciences... (*aṅgānāṃ tu*).
The meaning is that its status as Veda is perfectly clear from the Gautama-smṛti, which states: "The Mantra and Brāhmaṇa together constitute the single Veda, along with its six auxiliary limbs.

He refutes the objection regarding the inconsistency of names such as *Baudhāyana* and *Bauddha* if [the text] were not of human origin, by showing their consistency through the analogy of names like *Kāṭhaka*: "Because it was composed by Buddha... and so forth.
The meaning is that it is precisely because of such designations that people have the misconception that these [texts] are of human origin.
(Establishing the human authorship of the Smṛtis and other texts through the recollection of a firm author:

Just as the non-perception of the perceptible establishes the absence of that which is perceptible, here, the non-recollection of what ought to be recollected—which would establish the absence of an author—is absent;
therefore, it is untenable to claim they lack an author like the Vedas. Even if they are of human origin, their authority is established merely on the grounds of parsimony.)

Since that [status] would also result for the statements of Kālidāsa and others, and because it lacks intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) as it merely supports the authority [of the Veda], one might think that its status as the Veda or its equality to the Veda is not established by its being authorless (*apauruṣeya*). With this in mind, he states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*): "Firmly... etc.

Therefore, since the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Veda has been established through reasoning based on the cause of not remembering its author—supported by factors such as accents, syntactic fragments, and seals—even if one were to accept that names like *Kāṭhaka* are based on recitation (*pravacana*) in accordance with those [reasons], it is not proper to interpret those specific names as being based on recitation here. This is because there is an absence of any evidence proving an author, and on the contrary, there exists evidence establishing the very absence of an author. Thus, they cannot be led to mean "recitation."

Even this being the case, if the traditional recollection of the *dharmatva* (dharma-nature) of the three higher castes were not possible without its being authorless (*apauruṣeya*), then that [authorlessness] might indeed be postulated; however, since it is more appropriately accounted for by its having the Veda as its source, he concludes with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

(B1) Regarding the purpose of the Kalpasūtras and similar texts— whether they possess the status of Veda or are equal to it— in cases where there is a contradiction with direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), there is an option (*vikalpa*). Furthermore, even in cases where there is no contradiction with direct Vedic revelation, if a statement is made preceded by the presentation of a fallacious argument (*nyāyābhāsa*),
its performance follows from the fact that it is indeed a [scriptural] statement.

The presentation of reasoning (nyāya), however, is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) according to the principle of the locus of the reason (hetvadhikaraṇa). But in the established conclusion (siddhānta), when there is a conflict with direct Vedic revelation (pratyakṣa-śruti) or a conflict with sound reasoning (sannyāya), there is non-authoritativeness characterized by non-performance as long as the foundational Vedic text (mūla-śruti) is not observed. However, once the Vedic text is observed, there is an option (vikalpa).

However, where there is a statement of Smṛti that is devoid of the presentation of reasoning and contrary to the principles of Mīmāṃsā, since it is possible for it to be rooted in Śruti, the reasoning itself must be regarded as fallacious in the face of the contradiction with the statement; therefore, its specific meaning alone is to be performed. In this regard, all the examples and the refutations of the examples stated in the original source are to be found in our work, the Kaustubha. // 9 //
(B2) [The refutation of the claim that it is subject to the injunction for the daily *brahmayajña* and thus possesses a status equal to the Veda, etc.
He refutes the objection regarding the impossibility of its being the subject of the injunction for the daily *brahmayajña* with the words: "nitya... (the daily...).
Just as the contradiction regarding eternal conjunction is avoided by taking the genus *vrīhitva* (rice-ness) as the basis,

so too— in all treatises— even if one does not admit a genus such as "being a composition" (*vākyatva*) or "being imagined" (*kalpyatva*), it is possible for certain works of this kind to exist at all times, based on the adjunct (*upādhi*) of being the "imaginer of the meaning of the Veda" in accordance with the meaning of the root *kḷp*.
The meaning is that there is no fault, because the non-contradiction of eternal connection is established through the eternity of the stream (*pravāha*).

As for the traditional recollection (*smaraṇa*) that the auxiliary texts (*aṅga*) are Veda—that is based on a false foundation; for the status of a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is understood from the mention of "one" [Veda] alone, whereas the status of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is understood from the absence of the mention of "one" in the statement, "The name 'Veda' applies to both Mantra and Brāhmaṇa. Thus he says: [it is] rootless.
"But because of the mention of 'one-pointedness'..."

(Justification for the purposefulness of composing the Kalpasūtras) As for the objection that the composition [of the Kalpasūtras] would be useless, that refers [only] to the eleven potsherds and so forth found in various Śākhās when combined, as well as the mantras for the consecration of the sacrificial offerings (*prayāja*) and so forth.

It is incorrect [to claim that the *arthavāda* serves] for the sake of knowing such matters as sublation (*bādha*), extension (*upasaṃhāra*), exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*), the definition of terms (*padārtha-lakṣaṇā*), and novelty (*apūrvatā*) dependent upon sentences from other recensional branches (*śākhāntara*).

For although extension may be understood in certain specific examples by those learned in Mīmāṃsā who study only their own recensional branch, it cannot be understood in all examples; thus, the *arthavāda* must be accepted as avoiding the distraction of memory regarding those respective meanings.

Furthermore, since it is impossible to perform the ritual practice at the present time, the purposefulness of the *praṇayana* (the ritual act of leading forth) is established; thus, [the objection] must be refuted.

In the case at hand, because there is no difference in the students—as there is in the case of different Vedic branches (*śākhā*)—and because the students are identical, the futility of other injunctions would apply to your own position as well. Consequently, due to the repetition [of the rite], it would result in the extreme burden of treating it as a separate action (*karmāntara*).

For me, however, even though it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of a matter already enjoined by a direct injunction (*pratyakṣavidhi*), its presentation through the *Kalpa* texts and so forth for the sake of facilitating performance is meaningful.

Nor should it be argued: "In this way, the recitation of five or six Kalpasūtras in each individual Śākhā would be useless, since the required information is established by one alone. This is because, in the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*), due to the inclusion of the word "one's own" (*sva*), there is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) for the study of a single Śākhā that has been handed down through tradition. Just as [the injunction] states: "Whether much or little is proclaimed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra, whatever extent has been declared for him... [so too applies here].

Since it is stated, "When that much of the meaning of the scripture has been performed, everything has been performed," even in the rule regarding the secondary alternative (anukalpa) for the inclusion of all auxiliary parts found in the section on different recensions (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*), the mention of its own term implies the restrictive rule of studying a single *Gṛhya-sūtra* inherited through tradition, which includes the *Kalpa-sūtras* and other texts indicated by the term *gṛhya*. Consequently,

since the study of multiple *Kalpa-sūtras* and the like does not arise [as an option], the purposefulness of the injunction is established through the employment of multiple [mantras] for the ritual installation (*upasthāpana*).

For in the subsequent section (*uttarādhikaraṇa*), not even the restriction regarding the acceptance (*parigraha*) of the *Kalpasūtras* and so forth will be refuted; rather, only the restriction regarding their meaning (*tadartha*) will be.

Therefore, the sense is that since the *Āśvalāyana-sūtra*, *Kātyāyana-sūtra*, and others are to be studied only by those belonging to their respective *caraṇas* (Vedic schools), there is no redundancy due to such a restriction on acceptance.
As for what was said—that they cannot be generators of valid knowledge regarding Dharma—[that too is addressed].

In those cases where their foundational Vedic revelation (*śruti*) is not directly perceived, although they lack the capacity to produce valid knowledge of *dharma*— just like ordinary worldly sentences— they can nonetheless serve as the cause for the production of valid knowledge of *dharma* by means of presenting the foundational revelation; thus, their authority is merely figurative (*bhākta*), as has already been established and refuted in the *Smṛti-adhikaraṇa*.

Even where the Veda, which is the root source, is directly perceived, the ascertainment of its intended meaning (tātparya) depends upon the Kalpasūtras and other such works; therefore, since these works generate valid knowledge regarding the object that constitutes the intended meaning, their validity is established—this should be understood from the Kaustubha.

(Establishing the invalidity of the Śākya and other texts): Even though the authority of the Kalpas and other such works has thus been established on the basis of their being rooted in the Veda, [the author] dispels the misconception that might arise regarding the authority of the Śākya and other texts by the same previous reasoning—namely, "But as for the texts of the Śākyas and others... [he says].
Because that is impossible.
The meaning is that since those who deny the authority of the Vedas cannot accept its authority, it is impossible for [the Kalpasūtras] to be rooted in the Veda.
Regarding the purpose of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the section on the Kalpasūtras (*kalpasūtrādhikaraṇa*), one might ask:

"If, according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the authority of the Kalpas and so forth is accepted on the grounds of their being rooted in the Veda, what is the purpose of this inquiry? In response to this expectation, he says: "The purpose."
"Where there is perception," etc.

The meaning is as follows: just as, according to the view of the author of the *Bhāṣya*, there is a contradiction between the scriptural injunction (*śruti*) "Having touched the *audumbarī* [post], he should sing the *udgītha*" and the rule concerning its wrapping;
or just as there is a contradiction therein with the statements of the *Kalpasūtras*, such as "He carries fire around the sacrificial cake" (*puroḍāśaṃ paryagnikaroti*).

Regarding the phrase "whereas" (*yatravā*): it refers to the statement by Āśvalāyana found in the fifth chapter, "In other cases, there is the mention of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) regarding that."
"Indeed, at this time the animal is hollow when they extract the omentum; therefore, the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) made of rice is for the purpose of covering that [hollow].

From this explanatory passage (arthavāda), it is understood that the purpose of the Agniṣomīya animal-cake is to cover the cavity. Furthermore, although that [cake] is extended by rule (atideśa) to the Savanīya offerings, its non-performance is established by the statement: "The Savanīya cakes are offered at each pressing because of the rice-nature [of the material], which prevents hollowness."

The meaning is that, since the performance of that function is accomplished by the Savanīya offerings themselves— which have the form of closing the gaps as understood from the explanatory passages (arthavāda)— those words were set forth after first presenting a fallacious argument.
(Kalpasūtra, Adhikaraṇa-siddhānta, and Prayojana: And [it is invalid] when it contradicts sound reasoning.

In the twelfth chapter, in the section beginning with the sūtra, “The animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) should not exist because its purpose is to cover the gaps, as other [cakes] serve that same purpose,” the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is reached that— following the previously mentioned reasoning— the animal-cake is not to be performed at all, or else it may be performed optionally based on the indicative mark (liṅga) stating, “With the cake at the midday pressing. However, this is refuted by the fact that the explanation regarding the covering of gaps is merely an explanatory passage (arthavāda), as established in the tenth chapter.
Since it has been established that [the rite] is for the purpose of consecrating the deity, the final conclusion (siddhānta) is that it must indeed be performed as an obligatory duty;
this is the Mīmāṃsā principle (nyāya).
The meaning is that there is a contradiction with that [principle].
And it is contrary to the principles of Mīmāṃsā.

Just as in the ninth [chapter], in the *agniṣṭut* sacrifice, the non-modification (*anūha*) of the words beginning with *harivat* found in the *subrahmaṇyā* formula was established by means of logic, there is the statement of the author of the *Chandoga-sūtra* which teaches a modified reading (*ūhitapāṭha*) contrary to that: "O Agni, come hither, O red-horsed one, O great-luminous one, O smoke-bannered one, O Jātavedas, O all-seeing one! Or again, just as in the third section (*adhikaraṇa*) regarding the rule "likewise for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) as for the altar (*vedī*)," by the statement "he fixes it half within the altar (*antarvedi*)."

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is reached by arguing that since the half of the sacrificial post (yūpārdha) is prescribed as a subordinate element of the inner altar area (antarvedideśa) with reference to the half-post itself, it follows that the half-post would naturally occur outside the altar; thus, the phrase "outside the altar" (bahirvedi) is merely a restatement (anuvāda). Having established this, the final conclusion (siddhānta) is reached: what is being enjoined is a specific location that has not yet been consecrated, which is indicated indirectly (lakṣayitvā) by the two terms "inside the altar" and "outside the altar."

In that regard, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) holds that because the altar is an auxiliary to the sacrificial post (yūpa), when there is an increase in posts—as is necessary in the case of the *ekādaśinī* sacrifice involving eleven animals—an increase in the altar must necessarily occur for each individual post. This is the basis for the following statement by Āpastamba, which sets aside the original context and elevates the matter: "They dig out the altar as far as the sacrificial post.
This statement from the Kalpasūtra author contradicts the logic of the final conclusion (siddhānta).

Or, for example, as in the twelfth section (*adhikaraṇa*), regarding the scriptural statement concerning the animal sacrifice (*daikṣa*): "The wives perform the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings with the tail (*jāghanī*). Because the tail produced as a byproduct of the animal sacrifice requires a disposal (*pratipatti*), the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings are enjoined for the purpose of that disposal.

Consequently, since they are obtained through extension (*atideśa*) to the set of eleven animals (*paśvaikādaśinī*), all the tails must be treated as objects of refinement (*saṃskārya*) in accordance with that requirement.

Having established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings should be performed with all [the various parts of the sacrificial animal], and noting that since the *jāghanī* (tail) is obtained as an option alongside the clarified butter (*ājya*),

its prescription is justified as being for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), one need not assume that the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings and so forth serve a function other than their original (*prākṛta*) one.

Consequently, since the tail (*jāghanī*) is an accessory (*upādeya*) to the purposeful action (*arthakarma*), its singularity and other such qualities are intended; thus it is established that the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings are performed with "whichever one" [tail] there may be.

Therefore, the statement of the authors of the *Kalpasūtras*—which contains the word *jāghanībhiḥ* (in the plural) in the phrase "they perform the *patnīsaṃyāja* with tails"—is contrary to the principles of Mīmāṃsā.

As for the point made in the *Śāstradīpikā* that such statements, even when devoid of formal logical argumentation, are entirely lacking in authority whenever they contradict the principles of Mīmāṃsā—this is the sense.

Since there is no contradiction with that principle and because it cannot be determined that they lack a basis in Śruti, it is possible for the Smṛti regarding plurality and so forth to have a Śruti foundation; therefore, [the objection] is to be disregarded, as is clear in the Kaustubha.
In this regard, the text has already been explained.
Thus ends the sixth section concerning the Kalpasūtras.
(An undertaking of the investigation into specific details found in the Vedas, which serve as the source [of authority]: Thus,

having first established the authoritative status of the Smṛtis, customary practices, and personal satisfaction on the basis of their being rooted in the Veda, we shall now— since the occasion has arisen— inquire into specific details within certain Smṛtis and customs that result from an analysis of the eligibility or non-eligibility of various students and practitioners for those respective rites.
Thus, indicating the connection of the context through the word "atha" (now), he shows the subject matter: "Now, where..."
(An examination of the indicative nature of the terms *smṛti* and so forth:
The term "in the *smṛtis*" is indicative of the *Dharmaśāstras*, *Gṛhyasūtras*, and other works distinct from the Purāṇas, the Laws of Manu (*Mānava*), and the Itihāsas.
Likewise, the terms "Gautamīya" and "Chāndogya" are also indicative.
Just as the Gautama-smṛti is recited by the Chandogas alone, so too is the Gobhila-smṛti;
likewise, the Vasiṣṭha-smṛti is recited by the Bahvṛcas alone, and the Śaṅkha-Likhita-smṛti by the Vājasaneyins alone.
The *Āpastamba* and *Baudhāyana* [Kalpasūtras] are for the Taittirīyas alone,
since even they are subjects of inquiry according to the specific arrangement of their recensions; thus,
[the term refers to] the *Holākā* and so forth.
(The meaning of the phrase beginning with "holākādi":
by the two words beginning with "ādi," it is shown that just as the practice of the *holākā* is observed only by those in the East,
so too is the spring festival.)

Likewise, the practice of worshipping stationary objects such as the *karañja* and *arka* trees according to the traditions of one's own respective lineage, known as the *āhnīnaibuka*, is observed by the Southerners (*dākṣiṇātya*) alone;

similarly, the "bull-sacrifice" (*udvṛṣabhayajña*), described as "having worshipped the bulls on the full moon of the month of Jyeṣṭha, they cause them to run," is observed by the Northerners (*udīcya*) alone;
and likewise, this very festival on the new moon day of Bhādrapada is observed by the Southerners alone.
Likewise, because the practice of worshipping the group of Mothers (mātṛgaṇa) belongs specifically to those of the West according to established tradition, they too are subjects for investigation;
similarly, whatever is performed by certain individuals in a particular region is also included as an illustration.

(An indication of the refutation of the *Nyāyasudhā* regarding its determination that only those specific subjects not taught in the *Gṛhyasūtras* are the objects of inquiry here, and not even those prescribed in the *Gṛhyasūtras*, such as the *Pārvaṇa-sthālīpāka* or the initiation ceremony [*upanayana*]):

As for what was stated by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*—that only those particular subjects not taught in the *Gṛhyasūtras* are cited here as the objects of investigation, and not even those prescribed in the *Gṛhyasūtras* like the *Pārvaṇa-sthālīpāka* or the *upanayana* and so forth; [this is incorrect].
The refutation of that [position], preceded by its presentation, is to be seen in the Kaustubha itself.
