(Refutation of the nature of the inquiry as stated by some): As for what has been said by some regarding the nature of the inquiry— namely, whether or not practices such as the *holākā* and the *smṛtis* are authoritative for those other than Easterners and so forth according to the literal sense of the Bhāṣya—
that is improper and should be disregarded, because since their authority is non-exclusive to all persons, like light, the doubt regarding a restrictive rule (*vyavasthā*) is untenable.

In the passage beginning with "tatra," he demonstrates the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) regarding the specific points contained in the foundational scriptures that have become authoritative, together with the resulting deliberation (vicāra).
(B1) Inference.

Now, where there is a restriction of textual recitation (*pāṭha*) in the Smṛtis—as for instance, the Gautama-smṛti being for the Chandogas alone—and likewise a restriction of performers (*kartṛ*) in the customs (*ācāra*)—as for instance, the Holākā and other rites being for those who identify as Easterners and so forth—in such cases, the Vedic text inferred from them must also have a restricted scope of authority because the inferential means has a restricted object; thus, it follows that these are not to be performed by others. To this, [the reply is]: although the inferential means has a restricted object...
Nevertheless, it is not possible to provide qualifiers such as "being from the East" and so forth within the scripture that is to be inferred.
For "being from the East" cannot be defined by genus, individual, quality, configuration, and so on, in a way that encompasses all practitioners;
for even those residing in those various regions do not practice [the same things].
Furthermore, because this practice has been followed even by sons and grandsons who have long since passed away,
it possesses universal applicability due to the absence of any restrictive qualification.
However, in the *Smṛtis* such as those of Gautama, there is no mention of the *Chandogas* (Sāmavedins) as being the specifically authorized subjects.
By this, its existence even within the Śruti is rendered possible;

however, their mere recitation is also justified by the fact that the author of the Smṛti belonged to that particular Vedic branch (śākhā). For the author, being a Chandoga, taught his own work to his students who were also Chandogas, and they in turn taught others; thus, while the recitation remained established as limited to that alone, even there, the subject matter remains universal.

(B2) (The presentation of the opponent's position as conceived by [the author] himself: Just as, upon seeing that smoke exists on a mountain, fire is also inferred as existing specifically on that mountain, so too, because the mark (*liṅga*) consisting of *smṛti* and custom, which serves as the inferential indicator for the Veda, is established only in certain specific cases, that which is being inferred [must likewise be restricted].
It is more reasonable to assume that even the Vedic revelation (śruti) has a restricted scope.

If, however, that assumption is made on the basis of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), then even if one were to say that the assumption of a specific agent is not authoritative— since that [conflict] is resolved merely by assuming a corresponding Vedic text for that [limited] subject matter— [the following remains].

Nevertheless, the meaning is that since it would be impossible to avoid the logical inconsistency—namely, that if one were to assume a general Vedic revelation (śruti), then the Smṛti and custom (ācāra) prompted by it would also have to apply to all subjects—it is more appropriate to assume a restricted Vedic revelation.
(The determination of the means for knowing the specific agent in each case:
In every instance, knowledge of the specific agent is obtained through implication, by virtue of a prohibition, or from a qualifying word (upapada).

Just as, because only the twice-born possess the status of having maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), while Śūdras and others lack it, there arises from implication (*sāmarthya*) the knowledge of the specific agent for the *agnihotra* and other rites;

or just as, due to the prohibition of the fallen (*patita*) and eunuchs (*ṣaṇḍha*) and so forth, there arises by virtue of that prohibition the knowledge of the specific agents—the fallen and the eunuchs—only in relation to those acts not prohibited;
or just as, in the *rājasūya*, there arises the knowledge of the specific agent in the form of a king from the occurrence of the qualifying term "king" (*rāja*).
(How the absence of knowledge regarding a specific agent is established in the present case:
In the present context, however, there is neither a prohibition nor is there any capacity that serves as a restrictive factor;
for [the agent] is not perceived.
And because capacity (*sāmarthya*) is indistinguishable everywhere;
as for the fact that an unexpressed *upapada* must be supplied,
since that cannot possibly be provided in the revealed text (*śruti*), the author states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "even though" (*yadyapi*).
Although it is possible for specific designations such as "Taittirīya" and so forth— which denote particular lineages— to occur within the *śruti* passages that serve as the basis for the *smṛti*,
nevertheless, since there is no mention of such words in the *kalpaka-smṛti*, there is no evidence for postulating any such [specific lineage] that was not actually heard in the original text.
As for the reading [of those words], it is irrelevant, because a *smṛti* statement is capable of implying a corresponding *śruti* based merely on its being understood, even without such a reading.
Nor is it the case that the impossibility of the established order of recitation (*pāṭhavyavasthā*) necessitates its postulation [as being based on a specific author];

for since that order can be accounted for otherwise, it is impossible for it to serve as a basis for such a postulation. With this intention, he says: "gautamīyādi" (beginning with the works of Gautama).
Thus ends the seventh section concerning the Holākā.

— — — — — (The avoidance of redundancy with the section on grammar [Vyākaraṇādhikaraṇa] by means of the sections beginning with *Pīlu*) Here, in connection with the authority of custom (*ācāra-prāmāṇya*), the practice of employing correct words such as *go* is authoritative because it serves as the instrument for producing the cognition of the sentence-meaning— the effect— which is the object possessing a dewlap and so forth; likewise, the practice of employing incorrect words such as *gāvī* [is not authoritative].
The inquiry is whether such a thing possesses the status of being an instrument of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And although, in the *pīlu* and other examples within the *yavavarāha* section, it was established according to the view of the *Bhāṣya* that the practice of those situated in the scripture (*śāstrastha*) is stronger than the practice of those who are merely learned (*abhiyukta*), here too— because of the strength of the practice supported by grammar, whose authority has been established by the authority of Smṛti proven in the *Smṛti-adhikaraṇa*— [the former is stronger].

He demonstrates that even the previously established authority of the foundational grammar (*mūlabhūtavyākaraṇa*) for the purpose of [the claim] "it does not denote" is not possible, and thus this must necessarily be proven— this is indicated by the phrase "in the section on Smṛti" (*smṛtyadhikaraṇa*).
(An exposition of the commencement of this section by way of an objection to the section on *smṛti*:

If [the Vedic tradition] has its root [in the Veda], then because of its authority, only those words such as *go* that conform to it should be employed in rituals such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, and not even words such as *gāvī* which do not conform to it.

The meaning is as follows: since there is no basis [for the restriction], and because there is an absence of authority, all usage becomes established due to the lack of any restrictive factor that would distinguish one from another; therefore, having raised this objection, it is resolved.
"Thus one" means that there is a restriction on usage.
"Thus another" refers to the alternative view.
The meaning is that this is the rule regarding the true nature of the virtuous.

(An Examination of the Impossibility of Restricting the Use of Correct Words) In this regard, first of all, the initial restriction is not possible; for even in the absence of such a restriction, since the very form of usage and the expression of its function arise from incorrect words as well, there is no utility in [the restriction] regarding their form or their function.

Furthermore, because it is not prescribed, the usage lacks a transcendental purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), and thus it is illogical to assume that it serves toward the attainment of the unseen merit (*apūrva*), just as one might assume for the restriction on threshing and so forth.

Now, if it is argued that a rule for correct usage (sādhuniyama), which is established by the force of the context, is prescribed for the sake of merit (*dharma*)—just as the rule of facing east is established by the force of the context regarding eating based on desire—it is said in response:
"And not so" (*na ca*).
First of all, perception (*pratyakṣa*) and other means of knowledge cannot possibly serve as the basis for this.
Because for them, dharma and adharma do not function [as the source].

Even if one were to postulate the Vedic sentence as the source, such a postulation is impossible because it is impossible to study an infinite number of Vedic recensions while making a determination for every single word, such as "one should denote [the object] by the word 'go' and not by the word 'gāvī'.
Furthermore, it is not only those [words] that have been actually recited that can serve as the source.
Since the theory that [the Vedic injunction] has as its root an eternally inferable scripture (*nityānumeya-śruti*) has been refuted; and since,

given that for every single correct word (*sādhuśabda*) there are observed numerous incorrect words (*apaśabda*) such as *gāvī* and *goṇī*, it would follow that there is an absolute infinity in the postulation of prohibitions for each individual object— rendering a recitation impossible— and because it is impossible to define "correctness" and "incorrectness" by postulating them through such phrases as "one should speak with correct words, not with incorrect ones," the author says "perception" (*pratīti*), intending that such a possibility does not exist.

By the phrase "as before," the immediate connection [of this section] is indicated through the reliance on the reason—the impossibility of a derivative etymology (*upapada*)—established in the preceding section, from which the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises.
He demonstrates the impossibility of such an etymology with the words "beginningless" (*anādi*);
the meaning is that [a word] can only be expressive if its limit (i.e., its point of origin) is remembered.

Nor can the occurrence of usage and comprehension be explained by the recollection of a correct word (*sādhu-śabda*) or by a misconception regarding its expressive power (*śakti-bhrama*); for since it could be argued that the same applies to words such as *go*, there would be no decisive criterion (*vinigamanā-viraha*) [to distinguish between them].

One might object: "In the case of corrupt words (*apaśabda*), their status in relation to words like *go* is merely figurative (*gauṇa*), and they do not possess direct denotative power (*vācakatva*)."
Therefore, he says: "of corrupt words."
By this, even *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is refuted;

the sense is that those two [metaphorical and secondary usage] are preceded by the power (*śakti*) of a different meaning. Therefore, since it is impossible to invariably prevent the cognition of meaning arising from words such as "cow" (*go*), in the absence of the cognition of meaning—

And because the very application (*prayoga*) of that [grammar] is not established, the restriction that "only correct words" (*sādhūni eva*) are used is impossible in either case; with this intention, he concludes the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "therefore" (*ataḥ*).

Furthermore, how the purposes of grammar—namely, the protection of the Veda (*rakṣā*), the addition of missing elements (*āgama*), ease (*laghu*), and the removal of doubt (*asaṃdeha*)—are stated and established in the prima facie argument should be seen in the *Kaustubha* itself.
(B1) Because there is no scripture for the production of usage, there would be no fixed rule regarding words.
Although the authority of grammar is established by the principle of the *Smṛtyadhikaraṇa*, it is here challenged;
for that [principle] serves the purpose of two restrictive rules:
first, "one should employ only correct words (*sādhu*), not incorrect ones (*asādhu*)."

"Only *go* and the like are correct, not *gāvī* and the like"—this is the view of another [teacher]. Furthermore, a basis for these two restrictions is not possible; for it is impossible to recite each word such as *go* and so forth in numerous Vedic passages.

This is because, as in the previous case, it is impossible to provide a definition for "correctness" (*sādhutva*), and therefore it is untenable to postulate a single underlying commonality based on that term;
for correctness is neither the capacity to convey meaning nor the capacity to denote meaning while being beginningless.

Since [the capacity for denotation] exists even in corrupt words such as *gāvī* and the like, and since it is impossible for secondary usage (*gauṇatva*) to occur in words like *go* if corrupt words were entirely devoid of denotative power, it follows that because there is no distinction in their denotative capacity, no restriction can be established by grammar. This being the position reached—[we reply]: regarding usage and comprehension...

There is no need to postulate that words such as *gāvī* and others—which arise from the corruption (*apabhraṃśa*) of the word *sādhu*—possess denotative power (*vācakatva*), because their capacity for conveying meaning is established through the mediation of the presentation of that [original] word;

otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of postulating multiple expressive powers. Furthermore, for contemporary speakers, these [corrupted forms] function due to a misconception regarding the expressive power [of the original].
Nor is there a lack of a determining factor (vinigamanāviraha) as in the case of synonymous terms such as *ghaṭa* and *kalaśa*,
because the grammar composed by Pāṇini and others serves as the very regulator;
nor is it devoid of a foundation (*nirmūlatva*).
Regarding the restriction on usage, since its basis is a single scriptural injunction (śruti) of the form "one should employ only what is correct" (sādhūneva prayuñjīta),
correctness (sādhutva) consists either in being expressive from time immemorial or in being free from corruption (anapabhraṣṭatva).

Alternatively, it is the universal (*jāti*) manifested by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced through the practice of grammar, or else it is the capacity to convey meaning through a well-established usage; this has been thoroughly examined in the *Kaustubha* itself.
(This provides the scope for the injunction "one should not speak like a barbarian.")

And thus, since corrupt words such as *gāvī* and the like lack the status of being "corrupt" (*apaśabda*), prohibitions such as "one should not speak like a barbarian" (*na mlecchitavai*) and "one who has established the sacred fires should not employ a corrupt word" (*āhitāgnir apaśabdaṃ prayuñjīta*) must be understood as referring exclusively to Pārasīka (Persian) words, in accordance with the consistency of such Smṛti texts as "they should not learn the language of the barbarians" (*na mlecchabhāṣāṃ śikṣeta*).

Alternatively, they should be understood as forming a single syntactical unit with the phrase "a mantra deficient in accent" (*mantro hīnaḥ svarataḥ*); or rather, the sense is that they should be understood as referring to errors regarding the accents and phonemes within the subject matter of mantras.

(The justification for the rule of employing correct words, preceded by a description of how the usage and comprehension [of meaning] are possible even without the capacity to denote; the statement of the final position:
He states the established conclusion: "In usage... and so forth.
The presentation of that word.
The meaning is: "by way of presenting the word 'cow' which constitutes the basis.
[Regarding] "aneka" (many): //

The meaning is that this is because it would entail the conceptualization of multiple powers for numerous words. When, due to a speaker's lack of proficiency or other causes, a listener derives a cognition of the object from the word *gāvī* (a variant of *go*) uttered by the elder who employs it,

and that cognition occurs precisely through the presentation of the word *go*, at that very moment those standing beside the listener grasp the power (*śakti*) consisting of the relationship between the name and the named.

The meaning is that [the capacity to denote] arose from mere delusion for others in the present as well; therefore, there is no postulation of denotative power based on the "otherwise-unaccountability" (anyathānupapatti) of usage and cognition.

This is because it will be stated later that the prohibition against using incorrect words (asādhuśabda) is perceived through direct perception (pratyakṣa), and thus, by the very fact of the matter, there is no need for such a postulation in that case.

Or, having intended that [the Veda] is established, he demonstrates precisely the postulation of a scriptural source (*śruti*) which is the root of the usage of correct words, by saying "prayoga" and so forth.
(Definition of correctness as stated by Pārthasārathi, the commentary on that by the Prakāśakāras, and the purpose of the *dala*):
First, he states the definition of correctness (*sādhutva*) as propounded by Pārthasārathi: "anādi... [etc.].

On this point, the authors of the *Prakāśa* state the following regarding its definition in the *Harikārikā*: "Correctness (*sādhu-tā*) here is either non-corruption, or beginninglessness, or fitness for prosperity, or a certain universal (*jāti*) manifested through grammatical analysis (*vyākriyā*).
Thus, the etymological definition is set forth in three ways.

In this regard, Haradatta, setting aside the two positions concerning the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) as the means [of dharma], states: "Words that have not been produced for the first time are proclaimed to be correct (*sādhavaḥ*). Those very same words, when uttered otherwise by persons due to deficiency of capacity, negligence, laziness, and so forth, are cited as incorrect (*apaśabda*)."
Since the first position alone has been explained in detail, that very one was accepted by Pārthasārathi.

Although in that context it appears that the definition of correctness consists merely in being beginningless (*anāditva*), nevertheless, it should be understood as qualified by the term "uncorrupted" (*anapabhraṣṭa*).

This is because that very point is summarized at the end of that work with the statement, "Correctness (*sādhutva*) is beginninglessness and non-degeneration," and because even in Harikārikā the relationship between qualifier and qualified is shown by the phrase "of the other two, non-degeneration is beginningless," as well as by the use of the word "or" (*vā*) in the expression "non-degeneration is beginningless.
In that context, if only non-degeneration were stated, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to technical designations (*saṃjñā*) such as *ṭi*, *ghu*, and *bha*.
Therefore, there is an entry into beginninglessness.

As it was said by Haradatta: "As for these technical terms such as *ṭi*, *ghu*, and *bh* which are created by one's own will—how indeed can they possess correctness? They are not considered correct at all."
Because they possess a non-corrupt form, these [expressions] do not constitute ungrammatical words (*apaśabda*).
Just as hand gestures are used in the world, so too have these been established by convention. In their employment, there is neither spiritual merit (*abhyudaya*) nor transgression (*pratyavāya*).
Thus it is said.

If one were to state merely that [a word] is beginningless, it would over-extend to a collection of single phonemes that are meaningless; therefore, the term "uncorrupted" (*anapabhraṣṭa*) is included.
(The Ornament of Non-Corruption) Now,

an objection: if "non-corruption" here is defined as "that word which is beginningless and is expressive," then even in the case of words such as *Rudra*— which are established by conventional naming (*nāmakaraṇasaṃketa*)— there is the possibility of the definition applying, since they are beginningless words and they express meanings in the form of "offspring" (*apatya*).

Nevertheless, since the word *goṇī*—which denotes a "she-goat"—is beginningless and conveys the meaning of a cow, it would follow that it is correct (*sādhu*) when applied to a cow; therefore, to avoid this [consequence], if one were to say that a word is correct in a particular sense only if its capacity to convey that specific object is beginningless, then words such as *rudra* and so forth would result in being incorrect, because their capacity to convey meanings such as Śiva and so on lacks beginninglessness. If this is argued:

It is said: by means of the rite of naming (nāmakaraṇa), that which is indeed beginningless is designated through the limiting condition (upādhi) of "sonship" and is enjoined as something to be performed. Therefore, because of that general limiting condition, the capacity of words such as "Rudra" to convey [the meaning] "son" and so forth is indeed beginningless;
thus, there is no fault.
Consequently, it is logical that the definition [of a correct word] is: that which has been beginninglessly expressive of a certain meaning is correct (sādhū) with respect to that meaning.
(An explanation that in the phrase "the state of being a denoter from beginningless time," there is no relation of qualifier and qualified, but rather two distinct definitions):

Here, this should be noted— if the capacity to convey meaning is said to be denotation (*śakti*), then it would follow that the words *gaṅgā* and *agni* would be incorrect when referring to the bank and a young boy respectively.

Furthermore, in our view, it is not correct as stated by the author of the *Prakāśa* that because only the denoted meaning (*śakyārtha*) of words such as "Ganges" brings to mind the riverbank and so forth, these words possess grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) with respect to the bank only by virtue of denoting the current and so forth;
for if it were merely the capacity to convey the denoted meaning that were intended [by the opponent], even then the inclusion of the word "beginningless" (*anādi*) would be redundant.

Since there is an absolute absence of expressive power (*śakti*) in technical designations such as *ṭi*, *ghu*, and *bha*, it is logically consistent to reject them on the grounds that they merely indicate meanings that cannot be expressed by their own power;
furthermore, if one were to admit a primary expressive power (*sādi-śakti*) in them, it would follow that they would also possess grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*).

Otherwise, due to the absence of meaningfulness (*arthavattva*), they would lack the designation of *prātipadika*, and consequently, the genitive case ending in forms such as *ṭeḥ* would be impossible.

As for the argument that—by accepting the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of words such as *ṭeḥ* on the grounds that they are imitations of sounds (*śabdānukāra*), and by raising the objection that if these were intended as referring to the word-form itself rather than its meaning, the operations of elision (*lopa*) and so forth would apply to the word alone; and that therefore, through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), even a word-referring term must be taken as meaning-referential—it is [untenable] because you yourself previously did not accept their grammatical correctness, and thus it contradicts your own prior position. Furthermore, since there is no beginninglessness (*anāditva*) even for the status of being a word-referring term, this is inconsistent with what is stated in the Veda.

Because words such as "helaya" are accepted as correct by virtue of being admitted as mere imitations (*anukaraṇa*), and because they lack the capacity to convey any meaning other than their own form, the definition [of a word] is under-extended (*avyāpti*); thus, [the opponent's position] is incorrect.

In reality, however, since it is impossible for *ṭi*, *ghu*, *bha*, and so forth to convey meaning in the absence of the apprehension of their grammatical function (*vṛtti*), and this applies to the grammatical function itself as well—

Since metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and secondary usage (*gauṇī*) are impossible because they must be preceded by a primary denotation (*śakyārtha*), and since—as in the case of words such as *gāvī*—it is untenable for them to convey meaning either through the presentation of the word itself as a convention (*saṃketa*) or through an error regarding its expressive power (*śakti-bhrama*), one must necessarily postulate a primary denotative power (*śakti*). Given that this power is accepted as residing in the word itself, it is more logical that the word’s purpose lies solely in the object. Consequently, because there is an absence of the capacity to convey a beginningless meaning in that [word], correctness (*sādhutva*) is indeed difficult to establish; thus, the inclusion of the term "beginningless" (*anādi*) is entirely redundant.
Therefore, "being beginningless" is one distinct definition, and furthermore, "not being corrupted" is another definition; they do not stand in a relationship of qualifier and qualified.

Therefore, with the intention of showing that there is also no contradiction with the root text—since it is stated in the *Śāstradīpikā*: “Being existent at all times is precisely what constitutes beginninglessness (*anāditva*) and correctness (*sādhutva*); and this is easily established through the tradition of unbroken succession and the remembrance of those proficient [in the language]”—he accepts the literal meaning of the term *anapabhraṣṭatā* as it occurs in the verse of Hari.
He states the second characteristic: "or non-corruption."
The meaning is: being free from corrupt forms (apabhraṃśa) produced by such factors as lack of proficiency in the organs of articulation.
(Because of the lack of appropriateness in the second definition, he explains the third definition, and because of the lack of appropriateness in that as well, he states the third definition:
This [definition] too is over-extensive (*ativyāpta*) with respect to meaningless phonemes such as "hum" and so forth;
therefore, he states another definition: "grammar... and so on.

In this regard as well, it is not possible for there to be a genus called "correctness" (*sādhutva*) that resides only in words such as *go* and excludes words such as *agāvi*; for there is no evidence to accept such a thing, since in common worldly usage there is an absence of the employment of words as "correct" restricted solely to words like *go*.
Furthermore, if one were to accept it as residing in all words that conform to grammar, then even the form *vacanti* would result in being considered correct.

Considering that the definition provided—namely, "being grammatically derived while being currently in use"—is untenable because it fails to account for the universal of correctness (*sādhutvajāti*), [the author] offers an alternative definition stated by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*. For, since a word such as "cow" (*go*) consists of a collection of multiple sequential phonemes, simultaneity is impossible; thus, according to the maxim, "If the word 'cow' has not yet been produced, how could the property of being the word 'cow' (*gośabdatva*) exist?", universals such as "word-ness" (*padatva*) and even "correctness" (*sādhutva*) would likewise be impossible. Thinking this definition to be flawed, he states another definition as follows:
"By means of the *pramitavṛtti* commentary."
(Regarding the author’s refutation of the objection concerning the impossibility of defining "mode of operation" [vṛttitva] within the definition of a mode of operation):
As for the objection raised here by the authors of the *Prakāśa*, namely that "nothing called 'vṛttitva' can be defined as something common to *śakti* and the rest," that is incorrect;

for since the term *vṛtti* has been conventionally established by the authors of the treatises specifically for *śakti*, *lakṣaṇā*, and *gauṇī*, there is no need for a formal definition, as it is included in the definition by means of a simple expedient. Thus, the objection is untenable due to the lack of necessity for such a definition.

As for the objection that the definition is under-extended (*avyāpti*) because it lacks application to names based on modern conventions—since those names do not exist [prior to the convention]—that is incorrect, because the capacity [of such names to denote] is established by the general injunction, "On the twelfth day, the father shall give a name," which establishes the convention for all names such as *Devadatta* through the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of being a son.
And as Harivṛṣabha has said: "In the case of the naming of sons and others, a restrictive rule is heard in the Gṛhya-sūtras..."
"Even in the case of designations, its state of being beginningless is not at all contradicted.
Thus [it is said].
Regarding them, there is also the reading "anāditā-saṃjñāsu api" (even in their notions of beginninglessness).

Therefore, since their beginninglessness is also accepted, the admission of *śakti* (potency) is indeed necessary in accordance with the effect consisting of the communication of meaning; thus, there is no fault.

The meaning is that even in the case of technical designations such as *ṭi*, *ghu*, and *bha*, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*), because—as explained by the aforementioned method—one accepts a primary denotative power (*sādi-śakti*) directed toward the meaning.

Furthermore, since corrupt words (*apaśabda*) convey meaning by presenting their corresponding correct forms (*tattacchabda*) and do not possess a [direct] function (*vṛtti*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*); thus, this is a valid definition.
(The means for avoiding the incorrectness of words such as *vacanī* and so forth:

Here, even if the term "cognized" (*pramita*) is included to prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to corrupt words (*apaśabda*) that convey meaning through a misconception of their expressive power (*śakti*), it must also be stipulated that only that specific word which is employed in a given context possesses the capacity to convey that particular meaning.

Otherwise, the word *ghaṭa* would incur the status of being grammatically correct (*sādhutā*) when applied to a cloth. Consequently, it is precisely this conformity with grammar that serves as the manifestor for determining the expressive power (*śakti*), by means of the determination of such correctness. This is because, regarding forms such as *vacanti*, Kātyāyana stated: "The root *vac* is never used in the sense of the root *ant*."

The sense is that since there is no correctness (*sādhutva*) due to the absence [of usage] resulting from the act of prohibition, and since a single [prohibition] determines the expressive power (*śakti*) by characterizing both correctness and incorrectness (*asādhutva*), there is no lack of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*), unlike the case of *ghaṭa* and *kalaśa*.
(An examination of the nature of the rule that one should speak only with correct words, preceded by the removal of doubts, and of the aspects excluded by it:
Now, what kind of restriction is intended here? Is it a restriction concerning the action, such that one must necessarily speak with correct words?
Or is it that only what is spoken by the virtuous is [authoritative], referring to the subject of the means of proof (*sādhana*)?
Not the first, because the fault of silence would follow.
Nor the second; for speech is not merely the communication of meaning.
Because [the meaning] is not conveyed through the winking of an eye or similar gestures, but rather the communication of meaning is to be accomplished through the operation of words;

and since in that context only a correct word (*sādhuśabda*) which is expressive is obtained, there is no possibility of employing an incorrect word (*asādhu*) that is absolutely non-expressive. Therefore, if a restriction is made regarding the use of the incorrect word because it might somehow be obtained, then since the winking of an eye and so forth might also somehow be obtained, [the restriction would be over-extensive].
If it is argued that this results in a logical fallacy (*nivṛttyāpatti*), this has already been refuted by the Teachers (*ācārya*).
By the expression "one should speak here," it is indicated through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) that one should merely illuminate the meaning by means of revealing one's own intended purpose.
If speech were defined as the communication of meaning by means of the operation of sound, then,

since there would be no possibility of any means other than correct words (*sādhu*), the restriction to correct words would be purposeless; however, in this context, with respect to the injunction for the restriction to correct words directed toward speech that communicates meaning by way of manifesting one's own intention, there is no fault in remaining silent.

In this regard, since there is no injunction (*vidhi*) operative precisely because there is no object to be enjoined (*uddeśya*), silence is excluded. Even in cases such as eating where silence is prescribed by rule, it is through the operation of this very injunction that the winking of eyes and so forth are excluded; thus, one must not perform actions such as signaling with the hands to indicate vegetables and the like.

Alternatively, by the principle of the general and the particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-nyāya*), the injunction for speaking properly sublates the injunction for silence; consequently, since even the exclusion of winking and other such acts—which are the results of that [general] silence—is sublated, there is no contradiction with the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*).
For there is no possibility of the wicked engaging in such speech;
therefore, the restriction is appropriate as an exclusion of them.
Another interpretation has also been established in the Vārttika and should be consulted therein.
Therefore, it is indeed logical to postulate a Vedic revelation that serves as the foundation for the rule regarding the correct usage of words.
(B1) And its absence constitutes ungrammaticality (*asādhutva*).
The direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*) itself—“One should not speak barbarously; for he who uses an incorrect word (*apaśabda*) is indeed a barbarian (*mleccha*)”—is the source [of this rule].
Furthermore, this prohibition is a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice due to the context (*prakaraṇa*).

Furthermore, there is a prohibition even regarding sacrifice itself, according to the *Mahābhāṣya* and other sources, which state: "There is a restrictive rule regarding sacrificial acts, but none elsewhere.
Moreover, the arising of the fruit occurs subsequent to the restriction of using correct forms, because of the scriptural statement:
"A single word, correctly understood and well-employed, becomes a cow of plenty in the heavenly world."

(B2) (The demonstration that the word *mleccha* in the injunction *na mlecchitavai* refers to corrupt words (*apaśabda*), followed by the demonstration that this [injunction] is rooted in the very same perceptible [usage], which is the rule for employing correct words.
In reality, however, there is not even an inference of a Vedic revelation (*śruti*) here;
rather, he says "only perceptible" because that [usage] is observed as a direct reading.
For in the Vājasaneyi-śākhā, where the Śruti is recited as: "Those Asuras, saying 'helayo helaya,' were defeated;

therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should not speak barbarously (mlecchitavai), for he who uses an incorrect word (apaśabda) is indeed a barbarian (mleccha)," it is understood through the suffix *tavya* prescribed in the sense of an injunction that one should not speak barbarously, and because there is an explicit prohibition against speaking corruptly.
The rule regarding the practice of speaking correctly is understood [here].

Furthermore, the term *mleccha* does not refer specifically to Persian words; for, upon considering the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) situated at the beginning and the conclusion, it is understood that its scope extends to corrupt words (*apaśabda*) in general.

And at the beginning, by employing "he araya" instead of "he araya," by using the letter *la* (*lakāra*) in place of the letter *ra*, by not employing the protracted vowel (*pluta*) as prescribed by the rule "haihe prayoge haihayoḥ," and by the absence of the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) as prescribed by the rule "plutapragṛhyā aci nityam," one understands that the utterance of the improper word (*apaśabda*) "hetalaḥ"— which was composed by an Asura— is a cause of undesirable results in the form of defeat. Therefore...
The sense is that, since the conclusion is understood precisely as being due to the status of being a corrupt word (*apaśabda*), it does not refer to the language of the Mlecchas.
(An exposition on the fact that the prohibition against speaking incorrect words serves the purpose of the sacrifice;
and an exposition on how the prohibition against incorrect words applies even by way of substitution in the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Now, one might ask: how can the prohibition against speaking incorrect words serve the purpose of the sacrifice?
Since speaking incorrect words (apaśabda) is for the sake of human purpose, it is logical that the prohibition concerning them should have the same referent as the thing prohibited;
therefore, he says: "And this... (ayaṃ ca).

The meaning is that there is no fault, because of the general rule that "the prohibition has the same purpose as the action for which it exists," according to the method stated in the Vārttika: "Even though [acts such as] approaching women, eating meat, and so forth are for the sake of the person, the prohibition is held to be a subsidiary of the sacrifice due to its dependence on the context (*prakaraṇa*)," just as the injunction "one should not speak untruth" is a subsidiary of the Jyotiṣṭoma by virtue of the context. Thus, the prohibition pertains to the same purpose as the act itself.
He states that this prohibition applies not only to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, but to all sacrifices in general: "And even in every sacrifice."

Nor does this contradict the following: [the objection that] based on the Smṛti statement, "One who knows the application of speech (*vāgyoga*) is not defiled by corrupt words (*apaśabda*)," and the indicative mark (*liṅga*) showing that sacrifice proceeds through both speech and mind, one concludes that the term *vāgyoga* refers specifically to sacrifice; thus, for one who knows that [sacrifice], there is a fault in uttering corrupt words during any sacrifice whatsoever. Consequently, even the statement from the Mahābhāṣya, "In sacrificial ritual (*yājñe karmaṇi*)," which appears to enjoin a prohibition regarding all sacrifices, would be contradicted.

It should not be argued that, since [the prohibition] is understood as pertaining only to sacrifice in general, both the injunction and the prohibition apply equally to the Jyotiṣṭoma as they do to other sacrifices, and therefore the specific mention of the prohibition is redundant. This is because its purposefulness is established either for the sake of ensuring that the expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*) prescribed for errors in the Yajurveda occurs upon transgressing the prohibition, or for the sake of ensuring that the prohibition applies equally to both the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).

Alternatively, its purposefulness may be established according to the method shown in the Kaustubha: even though incorrect words (*asādhu*) have ceased to be used by virtue of the rule for correct words (*sādhu*), since the employment of correct words is impossible, there arises the contingency—similar to the impossibility of threshing—that one might resort to substitutes such as scratching with the fingernails; it is therefore for the sake of prohibiting that [substitution] that the prohibition [of incorrect words] is stated. Thus, its meaningfulness is justified.

And on this view, it should also be understood that in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, when the use of correct forms is impossible, only things such as secret gestures or signs can serve as substitutes, and not an incorrect word.

In reality, however, this [sūtra], "one who knows the application of speech" (*vāgyogavit*), is not an independent prohibition; rather, since the use of correct forms is restricted by rule, the avoidance of speaking incorrectly follows as a matter of course. Thus, it is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*)—like the expression "O mountain! (*nagire*)—for the purpose of praising the restriction to correct usage prescribed in the three preceding quarters (of the *Puruṣasūkta*): "But he who, being skilled in the distinctions [of words], employs them correctly at the time of communication, attains infinite fruit in the hereafter. This is to be understood from the *Kaustubha*.

And this [statement] is also an indication of the prohibition of *apaśabda*s (corrupt words), which is inferred from the necessity of accounting for the expiatory injunction: “Having used an *apaśabda*, one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) should perform the *Sārasvata* sacrifice.

Since the term *āhitāgni* is employed there as well, and because the prescription of expiation applies to the use of an *apaśabda* occurring only in the context of sacrifices performed by such a person, it is determined that the prohibition pertains to sacrifice in general.

As for the view of the author of the *Prakāśa*— namely, that this [sūtra] is intended to prohibit the use of corrupt words (*apaśabda*) in ordinary discourse outside of sacrifice as a matter of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*)— the refutation of that position is to be found in the *Kaustubha*.

Therefore, the statement of the Bhāṣyakāra, "there is no restriction elsewhere," supports the practice of even those who maintain the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) of uttering the name of Hari and speaking ungrammatical words (*apaśabda*) during the time of worldly interaction; enough with this prolixity.

[This concludes the refutation of the final position in the *Śāstradīpikā* and its commentary, which holds that the injunctions "one should speak the truth" and "one should not speak falsehood" are based on rules regarding formal usage.]

As for the point that— because of the employment of the words *satya* (truth) and *anṛta* (falsehood), which denote correctness and incorrectness— it is not logical to reject the postulation of a source [for the Smṛti] by means of a single indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*), since the basis for the restrictive application of the very injunctions and prohibitions heard in Śruti and Smṛti as "one should speak the truth" and "one should not speak falsehood" is thereby established— the Vārtika states another position, which has been followed in the *Śāstradīpikā*.

Just as [the word] *iti* has the purpose of denoting the meaning of that [preceding statement], so too the word *anṛta* (untruth) must either intend truth with respect to the object or intend corruption with respect to the word; for it is impossible for a single word heard once to have multiple referents, and thus it is impossible for it to negate both simultaneously. On the contrary, [the scripture says]: "He who speaks the truth offers into the truth when he offers after sunset, and in the morning when the sun has risen; [but] in the morning, [he offers] untruth (*anṛta*)."

They argue that, upon examining such scriptural passages as "Those who offer the Agnihotra before sunrise," one concludes that the intent is the meaning (*artha*) and not the literal word (*śabda*), because the latter is untenable; furthermore, since words such as *gāvī* are not censured by the learned (*śiṣṭa*), [the claim that they are incorrect] is merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*). This is made explicit in the *Rāṇaka*. As for what Somanātha says—that "truth" (*satyatva*) consists in being a communicator of a meaning that is not sublated by its own function (*vṛtti*)—[that too is addressed].

And in the case of the expression "this is a cow" (*gaur iyam*), because the object "cow" is not sublated, there is truth regarding the object; and because the word "cow" conveys [the meaning] through its primary power (*śakti*), there is truth regarding the word. Thus, both are the meaning of the single term "truth" (*satya*) in the form described above. However, in the case of "gāvī exists," although the object is not sublated, because there is an absence of primary usage (*vṛtti*), there is verbal untruth (*śabdānṛtatva*).

However, in a case where there is a contradiction regarding the meaning (*arthabādha*), even though the capacity to convey a sense (*pratipādakatva*) exists, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) because the meaning lacks the quality of being uncontradicted (*abādhitatva*).

Thus, since both [the words *satya* and *anṛta*] lack the aforementioned capacity to convey [a true or false sense], they constitute the meaning of the single word *anṛta* alone; therefore, it has been stated that the words *satya* and *anṛta* do not incur the fault of having multiple meanings.

Since it is impossible for two expressed meanings to be simultaneously connected with the act of speaking even by means of a single form, and since the fault of repetition (āvṛtti) resulting from the postulation of multiple meanings in the verbal expression cannot be avoided, this [interpretation] must be disregarded.
(Conclusion on the prohibition against speaking corrupt words as being for the sake of the sacrifice:

And thus, although prohibitions such as "one should not learn the Mleccha language" establish that the Mleccha language is prohibited everywhere because it serves human purposes, the prohibition against other languages in the form of *apaśabda* (corrupt words) is understood to apply exclusively and in every respect for the sake of the sacrifice.
It is established that there is no transgression at the time of formal usage because of the utterance of those [words].
(Through the refinement of the sacrificer, or directly, there is the utility of the *apūrva* resulting from the restriction of correct performance for the *kratvapūrva*.

Thus, although it might initially appear that a prohibition occurring within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma serves the purpose of the sacrifice itself due to that context, it is understood—by the logic of the *jañjabhyamāna-anuvacana*—that it is a refinement of the sacrificer, who is designated by the word "Brāhmaṇa" as a means to the *apūrva* of the Jyotiṣṭoma; and in that case, it pertains to the sacrificer alone.

By the logic of the third [instance], since it is to be refined by way of being the agent, the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restriction to correct forms—prescribed by a restrictive injunction postulated through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) for that purpose—is for the sake of the sacrifice.
Because it serves the *apūrva* of the sacrifice by means of producing the capacity to be the locus for the fruit generated thereby, there is no futility.
Likewise, because of the statement of the author of the Mahābhāṣya, "in a sacrificial rite" (*yājñe karmaṇi*), it serves even the *apūrva* of every sacrifice; thus, there is no futility.

However, this much is the distinction: since the statement of the author of the Mahābhāṣya contains no word denoting a person engaged in a sacrifice, there is no evidence for its being a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of such a person; rather, because the avoidance of speaking untruth is a duty of the pure sacrifice itself, it serves—along with the officiating priests and the sacrificer alike—to prevent defects caused by that [untruth] and to facilitate the use of words like *vrīhi* (rice) as constituent parts of the ritual within common parlance.

Since there is a restriction on words governed by grammar when [the act] is to be performed, that *apūrva* which is produced— just like the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by the restriction of threshing and so forth— is understood to be purely for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), and it is postulated as residing specifically in the rice and other materials that constitute its constituent parts.

(The demonstration that [the rule] serves both the purpose of the sacrifice and the purpose of the person, by means of the principle of the separateness of connection, just as it serves the purpose of the sacrifice):

Having thus dispelled the objection regarding the futility of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) of the restriction on the grounds that it serves the purpose of the sacrifice, the author—indicating by the use of the word "also" (*api*) that the status of serving the person's purpose is accepted through the principle of the separateness of connection (*saṃyogapṛthaktvanyāya*)—states the following to dispel that [objection of futility]: "Because of the restriction to the use of correct forms. (*sādhuprayoganiyamāt*).

The meaning is as follows: because the sentence "A single word, well-employed [yields merit]"—which is studied as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*)—also teaches a connection with a fruit, and because such a fruit cannot be accomplished without an *apūrva*, and because that *apūrva* is useful for the performance of the effect characterized by the enjoyment of the fruit produced by the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is no futility; for just as by shaving and so forth, a refinement (*saṃskāra*) consisting in fitness for receiving the fruit is produced through the rule of using correct words, it serves a purpose.
(The manner of accomplishing the sentence-meaning "one word" in accordance with the context.
And here, some read "conformity with the treatise" (*śāstrānvaya*) after the word "well-employed" (*suprayukta*).

By that word *śāstra*, which by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) denotes a branch of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), only grammar is designated; thus, one understands that the rule of speaking correct words in conformity with the grammatical treatise is a means for attaining heaven.
The status of being for the sake of human purpose (*puruṣārthatā*) is thus determined.

And so, just as the rule of facing east while eating—which depends on a practice already prompted by desire—is enjoined for the sake of the fruit of longevity, the restriction to correct forms (*sādhuniyama*) is enjoined for the sake of the fruit of heaven, depending on a usage already prompted by passion (*rāga*).

Furthermore, since it is impossible for that word, which has not yet been known, to depend upon usage, the phrase "well-known" (*samyagjñāta*) is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of its being the object of the knowledge arising from grammar, which is obtained through the meaning [of the word].

And thus, since the statement of the result here is based precisely on the performance [of the ritual], the position that "dharma arises from knowledge alone," although mentioned in the Bhāṣya and other texts, must be understood as a mere concessive argument (*abhyupetyavāda*).

(An argumentative demonstration that the status of being a means to a fruit belongs only to the employment of correct words (*sādhu-śabda*) and not to mere knowledge): For this very reason, since knowledge has a purpose for others (*parārthatva*) by virtue of its function as a rule governing the use of correct words, those statements which set forth the fruits of knowledge must be merely explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), according to the principle of the *parṇamayī* [wooden ladle], just like the statement: "He who sacrifices with the horse-sacrifice, and he who knows it thus. By this, the claim of the author of the *Vārttika* on Grammar—that only an employment preceded by knowledge arising from the scripture is the cause of merit (*dharma*)—is refuted.
Since the performance [of speaking] is obtained through natural inclination (*rāga*) and is not something to be enjoined, it is impossible for it to have a connection with a fruit.

Nor should it be suspected that because speaking also serves the purpose of conveying meaning and is thus for the sake of another (*parārtha*), the phrase "in the heavenly world" (*svarge loke*) is merely an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*), like the hearing of blameless verses;

for there is no evidence that speaking—which is prescribed independently (*anārabhya*)—is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), since its function is to serve as a cause for worldly discourse based on perceptible purposes.

The sense is that, since it is understood that [the rite] has the human goal as its sole purpose, when there is a desire for a result, it is appropriate for it to convey a result according to the principle: "The result [is established] by the mention, as Ātreya [holds]."
(An investigation into the means of cognition that presents [the act] as a fit substratum for connection with a well-performed practice obtained through desire):

Now, one might object that while it is possible for eating—which has a visible purpose and is obtained through desire—to serve as a substratum by means of the *prakaraṇa* known as "qualification" (*adhikāra*), here, in the absence of such [a qualification], if it were to serve as a substratum merely by way of being presented, then other actions would also result in being substrata; thus, [the term] "well-performed" (*suprayukta*)...
Thus, he dispels the doubt that a restatement as if it were an eternal rule (nityavad-anuvāda) would be untenable by stating: "even of that which is obtained through passion" (rāgaprāptasyāpi).
Therefore, it is said: "This [is so]."

The meaning is that because grammar—which consists of the application of roots, suffixes, and bases—establishes the relationship between the act of speaking and its substratum (the *dhātvartha*), it is not difficult to establish that speaking has a substratum.
For here, the rule regarding correct usage (*sādhu-niyama*), which is dependent upon actual linguistic practice (*prayoga*), is enjoined for the sake of a specific result.

Furthermore, even though the use of correct forms is prompted by natural inclination (*rāga-prāpta*), their status as a substratum is established by the scriptural statement, "Therefore, this speech was uttered as refined" (*tasmādeṣā vyākṛtā vāgudyata*); this is made clear in the Kaustubha.
Regarding the restriction on the nature of correct words—that only *go* and so forth are correct, and not *gāvī* and so forth—the very root is the beginningless tradition of usage.
Therefore, grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is authoritative.
As for that which is based on logic, such as the theory of *sphoṭa*, it is stated [by us] that it contradicts the revealed scripture (*śruti*).
If that contradicts reason and scripture, let it indeed be invalid.
Thus ends the eighth section, concerning the authority of the scriptural expositions.
(B2) (In this section, the refutation of the view of the author of the *Prakāśa*:

Here, the author of the *Prakāśa*, having accepted that this [sūtra] is a prescriptive injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*) for the rule of speaking correctly—which constitutes a human goal—stated that the phrase "one word" (*ekaḥ śabdaḥ*) serves to indicate its connection with a result.

To indicate that this is incorrect—because both [the rule and the result] could be established by the phrase "one word" alone, making [the present sūtra] redundant, and because it must be understood as enjoining a relationship with a substratum that cannot be obtained otherwise—he stated "from the statement" (*vacanāt*).
By the statement "not even one [word]," it is not understood that the rule of speaking correctly (*sādhubhāṣaṇaniyama*) has heaven as its fruit; rather,

because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the phrase "well-employed [speech] is a cow of plenty" (*suprayuktaḥ kāmadhuk*), it is logical that this [text] merely indicates the connection with the required substratum for the very rule of correct words based on usage, since there is no need for a separate injunction to speak correctly.
Therefore, the intention is that in the *Śāstradīpikā* it was stated precisely as "the restriction to correct forms is based upon that."

As for the claim made by the author of the Nyāyasudhā that this [text] is an injunction because it serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), that has been refuted in the Kaustubha; it should be consulted therein.
(Regarding the determination that only words such as *go* are correct, this establishes that the very root is the beginningless succession of usage:
"It is precisely the beginningless succession of usage."

Since words that serve as the substrata for correctness are established through auditory perception, it is only the determination of their authoritative status that depends upon grammar. Even in that regard, because [grammar] itself is rooted in another grammar, the knowledge of the rules governing the nature of beginningless correct words is indeed justified;

for it is appropriate to accept that grammar, like the *Kalpa* and other [Vedic auxiliary sciences], possesses a continuous eternity (*pravāha-nityatā*) by virtue of being included among the fourteen great branches of knowledge (*mahā-vidyā-sthāna*).
Otherwise, it would be impossible for grammar to be the object of the injunction for the eternal *brahmayajña*.

For this very reason, the prescription for the use of specific case-endings found in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa—“one should employ the case-endings in the *prayāja* and *anūyāja* offerings”—is logically consistent.
Nor does this lead to a "blind tradition" (*andhaparaṃparā*) on the grounds that it is based on another Smṛti;

for although the fact that the Aṣṭakā and other rites are means to an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) is not an object of perception, and thus such a tradition might otherwise be considered blind, [this is not the case here] because [the rule applies to] a Brāhmaṇa woman...

Just as the perception of a *brāhmaṇa* is possible through the ear aided by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by repeated practice of the manifesting factors— such as roots and suffixes— as understood from successive grammatical analyses, and aided by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the knowledge of meaning, so too here [in the case of grammar], there is no possibility of that [objection] arising; for the perception of correct words from the beginning until now is established by the ear, which is assisted by the knowledge that manifests them as stated in the Smṛti— "one born of a Brāhmaṇa is a Brāhmaṇa"— and by the requirement that the knowledge of meaning cannot be explained otherwise.
Therefore, the sense is that regarding the restriction of form—namely, that "only words such as *go* and the like are correct"—the very succession of beginningless usage is the root.

Consequently, it is established that the process of grammar (*vyākaraṇaprakriyā*) is useful as a procedural requirement (*kartavyatā*) because it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to Dharma, which consists in the correct usage of words as understood from the Veda; thus he concludes the authority of grammar with the word "ataḥ" (therefore).
This should be examined in the Kaustubha, where it is demonstrated as being contrary to logic after having been established through supporting arguments;
and it is also contrary to Śruti.

(An examination of the lack of authority—characterized by non-implementation—of the two grammatical explanations *kaler ḍhak* and *vāmadevād ḍyaḍḍyau*, which contradict scriptural injunctions, like the rule regarding covering everything with cloth.

Under the governing heading *dṛṣṭaṃ sāma*, the grammatical correctness of the words *kāleya* and *vāmadevya* is established by the two rules *kaler ḍhak* and *vāmadevād ḍyaḍḍyau* in the sense of "a Sāman seen by Kali" or "seen by the seer Vāmadeva. However, this grammatical explanation is in contradiction with the Śruti.

“Because he brought [the world] at the proper time (*kāla*), that is the reason for his name *Kāleya*”—thus, in this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the word *kāleya* is stated to have as its cause the attainment of the time characterized by the acceptance of pleasure.
Likewise: “The waters, indeed, reached their season; on their surface Vāyu moved about. From that, the desirable wealth (*vāmaṃ vasu*) was produced.
Mitra and Varuṇa perceived it. They both said: ‘This desirable thing has been born for mortals from the gods; therefore, it is called *Vāmadevya*’.”

Thus, in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), because the quality of being caused by the act of uttering the two words co-occurring as "Vāmadevya" is predicated of the word *vāmadevya*, let that [word] be subject to non-authoritativeness characterized by the non-performance [of the rite] due to the non-perception of its foundational Vedic source—just like the Smṛti rule regarding the "entirety of covering"—but it does not follow from this that everything [in the Smṛti] is non-authoritative; such is the meaning.
The practical utility arising from the prima facie and final positions has already been shown previously.
Thus ends the eighth section, concerning the authority of the scriptural expositions.
(B1) (Section 9:
The injunction regarding the performance [of ritual action].
In connection with the word that denotes, there arises the inquiry whether the denoted object is the universal (jāti), such as "pot-ness," or the individual (vyakti).
For that purpose, it must be considered whether words in common usage and in the Veda are different or not.

For if they were different, the first inquiry would not be worth undertaking, because the apprehension of the power of Vedic words would be impossible due to the lack of a means [for such apprehension].

However, since in common worldly usage the capacity [of words] is apprehended in accordance with the linguistic conventions of the elders, it is logical to consider how that same capacity will bear fruit in the Veda.

In this regard, although there is no difference in the phonemes (*varṇa*), because of differences in properties such as accent, Vedic phonetic substitutions (*chāndasa-varṇāgama*), elision (*lopa*), modification (*vikāra*), and rules regarding non-recitation (*anadhyāya*), the words in the world and in the Veda are distinct from one another—just as in the case of the two words *saraḥ* and *rasaḥ*. This being the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*), [the author states]: "In cases where [a word] is conducive to the comprehension of a different meaning..."
In that very case, a difference in meaning entails a difference in the word;
for example, "sara" and "rasa" according to their sequence,
or "brahma" and "brāhmaṇa" due to being deficient or excessive [in syllables].

In the case of *sthūlapṛṣatī*, [the meaning is determined] by accent—specifically, by the fact that the compound is either a *karmadhāraya* or a *bahuvrīhi*, resulting in an oxytone or an ādyudātta accent respectively; in the case of "Give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the one who cooks," [it is determined] by the sentence consisting of the proximity of words in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*);

and in the case of "He who has gone returns; Devadatta and Yajñadatta have both gone," [it is determined] by the direct statement (*śruti*) consisting of the proximity of words in the same grammatical relation (*samānādhikaraṇa*).
According to the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*), the word *aśva* signifies "goer" (*agama*).
This is because one who is familiar with that [tradition] experiences a distinction between the words.

However, where there is no perception of a difference in meaning, even though there is a difference in phonetic form (*dharmabheda*), the identity of the word is determined by the force of a more robust recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). Therefore, since there is no difference in the words between the worldly and Vedic contexts, the first inquiry (regarding the identity of words) is appropriate.
(B2) [The determination of the cause for the commencement of the *ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*, which serves as an introduction to the *lokavedādhikaraṇa*:

With the aim of investigating whether words in common usage (*loka*) and in the Veda (*veda*) are different or not, one might consider that the *lokavedādhikaraṇa* lacks connection with the previously established *vyākaraṇaprāmāṇyādhikaraṇa*.
However, out of a desire for logical connection (*saṅgati*), it is the *ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* itself that should be undertaken first.
And because this follows logically as a relevant consequence (*prasaṅga*), there is no lack of coherence.

However, the section concerning the world and the Veda (*lokavedādhikaraṇa*) is connected in the middle as an introductory supplement (*upoddhāta*) to that [following discussion]. Thus, in order to indicate this connection, he first presents the inquiry of the *ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* with the words "vācaka" (the expressive).
The phrase "as an incidental consequence" (*prasaṅgāt*) is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the connection with the exception (*apavāda*).

This is because it is appropriate here to provide an exception even regarding the portion concerning the denotation of individual instances (*vyakti*), which was previously raised by Kātyāyana against the authority of grammar that had already been established.

For this very reason, no such introductory section (*upodghāta*)—in the form of the *pratipadādhikaraṇa* and so forth—is undertaken here, as it was not done previously without first proceeding to the main subject.
Because there would otherwise follow the consequence of a lack of connection (*asaṅgati*).
The distinction here is that, since it begins with the section on *adhyāya* and so forth, it does not depend on an immediate connection (*anantarasamgati*).

Alternatively, it is to indicate that in that context, the sūtra from the *Bhāvārtha-adhikaraṇa*, "Words denoting action have the meaning of being" (*bhāvārthāḥ karmaśabdāḥ*), cannot in any way be applied even to the *Pratipadā-adhikaraṇa*.
The distinction is that this is an undertaking without having first proceeded with what was previously begun.
(An exposition of how all [words] denoting substance, quality, and action serve as examples:
"The universal such as potness (*ghaṭatva-jāti*)," and so forth.
One should not, however, fall into the error of thinking that only words denoting substances (dravya) are cited as examples here.

For there is no obstacle to accepting that universals such as "whiteness" (śuklatva), which are subsumed under the universal of quality (guṇatva), exist just as universals such as "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva), which are subsumed under the universal of substance (dravyatva), do. Furthermore, since universals subsumed under the universal of action (karmatva)—such as "Jyotiṣṭoma-ness" and others—are established by means of other authorities like "distinct terminology" (śabdāntara) in the section on repetition (abhyāsādhikaraṇa), it is logical that these words for qualities and actions are also appropriate as examples.

Even though it has been thus explained and established that both the base (prakṛti) and the suffix (pratyaya) denote the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) and the productive operation (bhāvanā), one should regard this as an illustrative example because there remains the possibility of investigation as to whether they denote a property (dharma) consisting of either a genus (jāti) or an adjunct (upādhi) residing therein, or else whether they denote the individual (vyakti) characterized by those.

(An exposition on the necessity of the *Lokavedādhikaraṇa* through the doubt and resolution regarding the necessity of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*, even though the words of common usage (*loka*) and the Veda (*veda*) are distinct.
He shows the introductory context for the inquiry into the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*: "And for that purpose... and so forth.
The phrase "of words" is also an elliptical expression that includes "of meanings" as well.
"I know that it will bear fruit."

If it were another [type of] word, then, since worldly usage has the purpose of conveying meaning, it would be possible to understand either of the two meanings through some kind of intentionality (*tātparya*) alone; thus, there would be no purpose for investigating whether that specific [meaning] is denotable.
Although such a purpose is indeed possible in the case of the Veda, [the situation differs].

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), regarding the statement "one offers in the *āhavanīya* fire," since the connection of the *āhavanīya* with the specific instance of offering other than the [foot-]offering would be obtained by direct audition (*śruti*) itself—just as it is for the word "foot"—there would be no possibility of sublation (*bādha*) of the general rule; thus, there would be an option (*vikalpa*). However, when, according to the reasoning established in this section, the term "offers" (*juhoti*) denotes the universal class (*jāti*) of "offering" and the manifestation of the individual instances occurs through implication (*ākṣepa*), then—even though the manifestation of the instances occurs through the general rule’s common implication—the sublation of the general rule does not apply only to the foot-offering instance located at a distance, because in the statement "one offers on the foot," the term "offers" implies its co-occurrence [with that specific instance]. Thus, there is sublation of the general rule.
[Objection: "It is a conceptual construction (vikalpa).

[Response: Even so, although the word-potency (*śakti*) of the word *yūpa* (sacrificial post) may be grasped in instances such as "He cuts the sacrificial post" through its co-occurrence with words like "cutting," which are well-known in common worldly usage, this purpose is not possible because there is no means for grasping potency elsewhere in the Veda. Thus, the sense is that once the oneness of words has been established, this is the fruit of that inquiry.

(An exposition of another purpose for the aforementioned inquiry, by demonstrating that the *āhavanīya* word and sentence fall under the principle of the "conflicting" (*sāvakāśa*) and "unconflicting" (*niravakāśa*), and by establishing the validity [of the argument] even if the word denotes an individual.

Although this purpose—consisting of the sublation or non-sublation of the *āhavanīya*—has been stated in the authoritative treatise (*ākara*), nevertheless, in another context, even under the view that the word denotes an individual, there is the passage: “Whatever is prior to the *agnīṣomīya*, with that they proceed in a low voice.”

It should be observed in the *Kaustubha* that it is incorrect [to argue] that, although the low-voicedness (*upāṃśutva*) is prescribed for that specific individual entity presented by the pronoun through the sentence, it would be sublated here as well— just as it is sublated by the low-pitched tone (*mandra-svara*) prescribed for the *prāyaṇīyā* sacrifice because it has no scope— by means of the principle of the "conflict between the general and the specific" (*sāvakāśa-niravakāśa-nyāya*). This is because [the low-voicedness] is indeed sublated by the low-pitched tone due to its lack of scope.
Therefore, another purpose will be stated by [the author] himself.
(The purpose of the word *ititu* regarding unity:

Now, one might object that even if there is unity [between the means and the fruit], because they have different domains—being respectively the domain of the Veda and the world—the deficiency of a single constituent part cannot be avoided. To this, [the author] replies: even in the Veda, just as there are differences in the utterances belonging to various individuals in the world, although there is a difference in the mere act of utterance, [the essence remains the same].
The word "but" (tu) indicates that [the objection] is incorrect because there is no difference in the nature of the sound itself.
He states the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa): "In that case... (tatra).
(An examination of the difference between words despite the non-difference of phonemes, due to differences in accent and so forth):

Now, one might object—since in the *Tarkapāda* [of the *Śābarabhāṣya*], in the sūtra beginning with “*saṃkhyābhāvāt*,” the difference between words such as *ga* and others was established precisely through powerful recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), the non-difference of the words composed of those [phonemes] is likewise established by that very same [recognition]. To refute this objection by means of a concessive argument (*abhyupetyavāda*), [the author] demonstrates that even though the non-difference of phonemes exists in cases such as *jarā* and *rājā*, such non-difference is not the determining factor for the non-difference of the words.
It has been stated that "even when there is no difference in phonemes.
Therefore, the meaning is that just as in that case the difference in properties alone is the cause for the difference in words, so it is here as well.
He demonstrates precisely the distinction between the dharmas: "the tone," and so forth.
In Vedic texts, the accentuation is fixed.
In instances such as "devāsaḥ," there is a Vedic addition of a phoneme;
in instances such as "tmanā deveṣu," there is the elision of the vowel *ā* in *ātmanā*.
In passages such as "udgrābhaṃ ca nigrābhaṃ ca," there is a modification of the letter *ha* into the form of *bha*.

Since there is an absence of vowels in the Chāndogya and Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇas, and an absence of augmentations (*āgama*) in words such as *go*, he states a pervasive distinction of properties: "anadhyāyādi" (beginning with [days of] non-study).

The term *anadhyāya* (non-study) is also an indicator for *svādhyāya* (Vedic study). *Svādhyāya* refers to the study performed by the three *varṇas* who have been initiated (*upanīta*) at the prescribed time.

Furthermore, *anadhyayana* (cessation of study) refers to the non-study by those such as *śūdras* who have not been initiated, and by those [of the three *varṇas*] during prohibited times; the meaning is that there is a distinction in *dharma* regarding Vedic [texts], but not regarding worldly ones.

Although Pāṇini provided instruction on accents (svara) in the world just as he did for the Veda, nevertheless, because the learned (śiṣṭas) in the world disregard the rules of accent and because [the correct accent] is not even used in speech, it should be understood that the rule of accent is not mandatory.
By the word "etc. (ādi), service to the teacher, worship, salutation, and so forth are included.

Intending that a difference in meaning follows as a general rule from a difference in words—according to the principle of the section on names (*saṃjñādhikaraṇa*)—he concludes by stating merely the difference in words: "the difference of the words."

(An exposition of the commencement of the final conclusion by reflecting on the meaning of the Vārttika: "The means for determining words"): And here, in this final conclusion (*siddhānta*), although the non-difference and difference of the meanings are not intended as the causes for the non-difference and difference of the words—since there is a difference [of words] even when there is no difference of meaning between the sentences of different recensions (*śākhā*)—

Since there is no difference in the word itself even when there is a difference in the meaning of words such as "akṣa" and so on, it is of no use to say that "where there is a difference in properties conducive to the cognition of a difference in meaning, there is a difference in the word.
Nevertheless, in the final system (siddhānta), recognition and non-recognition alone are the primary causes of identity and difference.

Intending to show that the distinction and non-distinction of meaning are employed as indicators based on their predominance, while the comprehension of that [meaning] arises from the distinction of properties (*dharma*), he states the meaning of the verse found in the *Vākyādhikaraṇa*—which sets forth the means for determining the word—in order to demonstrate what causes the distinction between words: "The wise desire many means for the determination of the word:
sequence, deficiency, excess, accent, sentence, *śruti*, and *smṛti*. This refers to the verse beginning with "where" (*yatra*).
(The sequential indication of examples:
He shows the examples in sequence with the word "yathā" (for example).
The meaning is: "due to a sequence of forms with distinct characteristics," as in the case of the expression *sthūlapṛṣatīm*.

In this case, when there is doubt regarding two meanings due to a difference in compound formation, the distinction between words is established because the difference in meaning is determined by the difference in the properties of accent and form.
(The determination of a difference in meaning resulting from a difference in accentuation in the term *sthūlapṛṣatī*, and the subsequent demonstration of the resulting difference in word-formation.

For instance: in the injunction *“one should sacrifice a *sthūlapṛṣatī* ox”* (*sthūlapṛṣatīmanaḍvāhīmālabheta*), if it is taken as a *karmadhāraya* compound, then—while the rule *ataḥ* is still in force—the rule *“samāsasya”* prescribes the default final acute accent (*antodātta*). Subsequently, by the rule *“anudāttaṃ padamekavarjam”*...
By the [application of the] sūtra, the first four [words] would be unaccented;

at that time, through the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) by the word *pṛṣatī*, just as the quality of having spots (*bindumattva*) is connected to that very [cow], so too the quality of being large (*sthūlatva*) is connected to that same [cow]. Thus, the meaning is established: "A cow that is both large and spotted is the means for the sacrifice."

In the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, however, by another specific rule— namely, the sūtra *“In a *bahuvrīhi*, the first member retains its original accent”* (*bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā pūrvapadam*)— the general rule prescribing that the final syllable is acute (*antodātta*) is set aside, and the original accent of the first member is ordained.
