Consequently, since the acute accent would apply to the vowel *ya* following the letter *la* in the word *sthūla*, and because the quality of stoutness (*sthaulya*) can only be construed with the speckles (*pṛṣat*), it follows that a cow possessing large speckles, or one that is naturally large itself, is the means for the sacrifice.

The meaning is that when there is doubt as to whether the word means "the purpose is accomplished" (*arthasya sidhyati*) or something else, the distinction between the words is established by the determination of the specific meaning through the accent following the *bahuvrīhi* compound, based on the recitation of the vowel *ā* as udātta after the letter *l*.

(Refutation of the author of the *Prakāśa* regarding the determination of the purpose for subverting the natural goat-species under the *karmadhāraya* interpretation) As for what was stated here by the authors of the *Prakāśa*: that under the *karmadhāraya* interpretation there is a subversion of the natural goat-species (*prākṛtachāgajāti*), whereas under the *bahuvrīhi* interpretation there is no such subversion because it merely prescribes the quality of possessing drops on the body (*sthalabindumattā*), and thus there is a difference in purpose; [this is now refuted].

Since the sentence containing the word *anaḍvāhīm*— namely, "sa sthūlapṛṣatīmanaḍvāhīm"— is indeed what is cited in both the Mahābhāṣya and the Nyāyasudhā, it is evident in the Kaustubha that [the opponent's view] is incorrect; for since the prescription of a female ox (*anaḍvāhī*) is necessary in both positions, the sublation of the generic class "goat" (*chāga-jāti*) is logically established.
(An example of the distinction between words based on a sentence: "Based on a sentence" means as follows.
From the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the word "dehi" (give), the first sentence is determined to be a noun ending in the dative case;

subsequently, from the co-occurrence with the phrase "for the purpose of eating" (*bhojanārtham*), it is determined to be a verbal form (*tiṅanta*). Thus, the meaning is that there is a distinction between words due to a distinction in their referents (*arthabheda*), which arises from the difference in the property of co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra-rūpa-dharmabheda*).
(This is the presentation of examples following the definition of the meaning of the term *śruti*.)
He states the meaning of the word "śruti" as shown by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*: "samānādhikaraṇa... (co-referential).

The meaning is as follows: there is a distinction between words due to a difference in meaning, determined by the fact that [the word *yāti*] is a noun (*nāman*) because it ends in the nominative case denoting the agent (*kartṛ*), which is established through its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the verbal form [of the other word]. Similarly, there is a distinction between words due to a difference in meaning, determined by the fact that the verbal form [in *yātaḥ*] ends in the third person dual, which is established through its grammatical coreferentiality with the words *Devadatta* and *Yajñadatta* ending in the dual case. Thus, because of the difference in properties consisting of coreferentiality with the words *yāti* and *yātaḥ*, there is a distinction between the two words.
(An example of a distinction in words based on recollection: "A horse."

In the expression "aśvastvaṃ devadatta" (You are a horse, Devadatta), from the root *śvi* (meaning "to go" or "to increase")—as in the rule *ṭu o śvi gativṛddhyoḥ*—the suffix *cli* is applied by the rule *cliluṅi*.

By the rule *jṝstambhvityādinā*, *cli* is replaced by *aṅ*; then, by the rule *śvayateraḥ*, the vowel *i* is replaced by *a*. Once the augment *aṭ* has been added, the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) determines the second person singular ending. Thus, [the word] denotes one possessing the genus (*jāti*) of being a horse.

The meaning is that there is a distinction [between words] based on memory (*smṛti*), because a different object is cognized in relation to the meaning of the word "horse" as determined by worldly convention.

Even though in the sentence "O Devadatta, you are a horse," the distinction from the word "horse"—which denotes the class *aśva*—is established by direct audition (*śruti*) in the form of the co-occurrence of words in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), nevertheless, since that [apposition] can also be accounted for through figurative usage (*gauṇī vṛtti*), the determination of the difference between the two words based on the second person singular ending depends precisely upon memory. This is the intended sense.
(An examination of the absence of means for discerning word-differences in cases like *loka* and *vada*):

Having thus demonstrated the means for understanding the distinction between words, he now shows their absence in the present case— the meaning is that in instances such as *devā devāsaḥ*, since the previously mentioned sublaters of firm recognition are absent, there is no difference in the words by virtue of the force of recognition.
He concludes the introduction with the words: "Thus it is logical."

(An investigation into the grounds for [the application of words] by setting aside only the two positions of *jāti* and *vyakti*, while abandoning the infinite alternatives stated in the *Vārttika* and other texts—such as "necessarily," "optionally," and so forth—and also abandoning the three positions accepted in the *Śāstradīpikā*.

In that regard, although it has been said: “The relation is either necessarily, or optionally, or both together in combination; or it is a collection, or a qualified [entity], or one [of these] is the other.”
"When the word 'cow' (gauh) is uttered, seven things appear to us:

the universal (jāti), the individual (vyakti), the relation (saṃbandha), the collection (samūha), gender (liṅga), the grammatical case-role (kāraka), and number (saṃkhyā) as the seventh. Of these, there are two groups of eight positions," and so forth; thus, many alternative views are stated in the Vārttika.

All of that has been established in the *Nyāyasudhā* by such passages as: "In this [work], twenty-seven thousand, six hundred and sixty-four [arguments] have been combined; and there are another seven points regarding the object.

Nevertheless, since those [arguments] are easily refuted simply by rejecting the position that words denote individuals qualified by form (*ākṛti*), and because of the impossibility of adopting [that position], the *Śāstradīpikā* states: "Is it the form, or the individual, or the individual qualified by the form?"
Three positions have been presented primarily;

among them, since the possibility of the position that words denote individuals qualified by form (*ākṛti*) must be established by oneself within the very position that words denote individuals, one considers even the third position to be redundant. Thus, with the intention that only two positions are primary according to the Bhāṣya:

Showing that the introduction (upodghāta) has the same purpose as the [main] subject, he begins the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) without explicitly stating the doubt, since it has already been presented; thus [he says]: "In that regard" (tatra).

(B1) In this regard, since actions such as threshing, as well as gender, grammatical case, number, and so forth, are incompatible with the universal (*jāti*), and because of the use of coreferential expressions such as "the cow is white," words must indeed denote the individual (*vyakti*). Nor does this result in the failure to cognize the universal; for the cognition of the universal is established through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Alternatively, the delimitor of the effect for the apprehension of the word-meaning as a particular (vyakti) is simply the state of being a verbal cognition qualified by a universal (jāti).
Therefore, there is no fault.
Nor is there a lack of a deciding factor (vinigamanāviraha); [for the latter alternative would entail the postulation of an infinite number of causal capacities].
Because parsimony (*lāghava*) alone is the determining factor. To explain: the apprehension of semantic power (*śaktigraha*) is not a cause in its own right;
rather, it is the cognition of the possession of the word "jar" through a relation such as "being capable of being denoted" (*śakyatva*), which is the cause, on account of parsimony.

Therefore, in our view, taking "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) as the delimiting factor of the subject (*dharmitāvacchedaka*), the cognition that "the word 'pot' possesses [the pot] through the relation of denotability" (in the form "the pot possesses the word 'pot'") is the cause for a qualified verbal cognition delimited by the nature of being a qualified verbal cognition (*viśiṣṭaśābdabodhatva*), [the effect] being related to it by way of the relation of qualificandumness (*viśeṣyatā*).
In your view, however, this must be stated taking "pot-ness-ness" (*ghaṭatvatva*) as the delimiting factor of the subject.

And for this reason, because the property of "pot-ness" (ghaṭatvatva)—which consists of its not occurring in things other than pots and so forth—is composed of multiple entities, your causal relation involves complexity (gaurava), whereas mine does not.
Nor is there the fault of an infinite number of [required] capacities (śakti) and so on; for that [complexity] is a matter of the result (phalamukha).

And therefore, on account of parsimony (*lāghava*), it is established that the expressive power (*śakti*) resides only in the individual (*vyakti*), or in the individual qualified by the universal (*jāti*), but not in the universal alone; this being the position reached, [the author] states: "(B2) [The demonstration of the universal's unsuitability for connection with gender, number, case-role, etc.
because of its unsuitability (*ayogyatvāt*)."
In injunctive statements, actions such as threshing that are being enjoined are unsuitable for application to a genus (*jāti*), because a genus, being formless, is incapable [of such action].
Likewise, in prohibitions such as "A Brāhmaṇa woman must not be killed," the genus is unsuitable because, being eternal, the possibility of its being killed does not arise.
Similarly, because a genus is a single entity, it is unfit for connection with numbers such as duality and so forth, which exceed oneness.
The meaning is that because a genus (jāti) is feminine, it is unfit for connection with masculinity;
and precisely because it is incorporeal, it is unfit for connection with kārakas such as the object (karman), which consists in being the locus of an effect produced by an action, and so forth.

In reality, however, since the impossibility of the gender-sign (*liṅga*)—defined as "one who has breasts and hair is a woman; one who is hairy is remembered as a man"—is equal in both the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*), its unfitness for connection with gender should be regarded as a further supporting argument.
The grammatical coreferentiality in the expression "the cow is white" is only possible if [the words] denote individuals.
"The cow is white."

Since words such as *śukla* (white) refer to the possessor of a quality (*guṇin*), and since it is impossible for a genus (*jāti*) to be the locus of a quality, the word *go* (cow) cannot have grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—defined as the conveying of a single object—in relation to it. Nor can it be argued that, even in accordance with that [objection], coreferentiality is established by taking the individual qualified by both as one, because although the word *go* denotes the cow as qualified by the genus *gotva* and the word *śukla* denotes that which is qualified by the quality of whiteness, there is a difference between the qualifiers and thus a difference between the qualified entities; for, despite the difference in qualifiers, since there is no cognition such as "the cow is not white," coreferentiality is established by accepting the identity of the individual qualified by both.

"By means of indication (*lakṣaṇā*): [this explains] how the appearance of the universal (*jāti*) is possible even when the expressive power (*śakti*) resides in the individual, and why one must resort to an alternative position due to the contradiction of two simultaneous functions."

Nor should it be argued that there is a lack of a decisive reason (vinigamanāviraha); on the contrary, because one postulates the expressive power (śakti) in a single universal (jāti) due to parsimony (lāghava), the opposite is the decisive factor—that the secondary indicative function (lakṣaṇā) applies only to the individual (vyakti). This is because the universal, since it exists in other particular individuals even without a specific individual [being intended], is inconstant (vyabhicārin) and thus incapable of determining a specific [referent].
Because the individual instance, by not deviating [from its own nature], determines the specific universal, it alone possesses the causal efficacy (niyāmaka) for the definition of a universal.

Dissatisfied with this position because it entails the contradiction of two simultaneous functions [of a word], he states another alternative: "only of the apprehension of the power residing in the individual" (vyaktiśaktigrahasyaiva).

(An exposition on the justification for the simplicity of the causal relationship in verbal cognition according to those who maintain that the expressive power resides in the individual word-forms): [The view] that the causality [of the word-meaning] exists independently.

It cannot be argued that, since in the causal relation defined by the apprehension of the pot’s capacity (*ghaṭa-śakti*), the capacity— whether in the Naiyāyika view it consists of God’s will (*īśvarecchā*) or in the Mīmāṃsaka view it is a distinct category (*padārthāntara*)— is a constituent of the cause, and therefore the specific verbal cognition arises solely from the knowledge of that [capacity];
for this is not established by experience.
The meaning is that even in the absence of knowledge in its true nature (*tattva*), such a cognition is established by experience;
therefore, it does not function as a cause independently.
[This refers to] "of knowledge alone."
The meaning is that it is precisely the ascertainment of the possession of the word "pot" [that is required].
And in that case, even if the power (śakti) is not manifested in the form of "power-ness" when it appears as a relation, there is no deficiency whatsoever;
for the power resides in the individual object itself.
(On the theory that the word’s power resides in the individual, the cognition of another individual is established through the apprehension of the power residing in a specific individual.
Now, an objection: if the convention is grasped with respect to a specific pot-individual belonging to Devadatta, how can there be usage of the word for another individual?
If that were the case, it would follow that the word "pot" could be used even for an individual cloth.

If this is argued, [we reply that] just as when it is said, "That which has such a form and is qualified by the universal *gotva* (cowness) is a cow, specifically Devadatta’s cow," the property of wearing white clothes— which is not denoted by the word "Devadatta"— serves as an *upalakṣaṇa* (a secondary indicator) for grasping the word-potency (*śakti*) of the term "Devadatta," so too here, having made the universal *ghaṭatva* (potness) an *upalakṣaṇa*, [the same applies].
For it is possible for even that which is inexpressible, such as "cowness" (gotva) and so forth, to function as a secondary indicator (upalakṣaṇa).
(Shifting to another position according to the maxim of "pleasing the wicked woman")—

when there is a rule that the property-qualifier (*dharmitāvacchedaka*) belongs to the subject itself (*abhidheya*), then he states another alternative (*pakṣāntara*), even though it was not presented among the options for the doubt, because it has been mentioned in the *Vārttika*: "qualified by the genus" (*jāti-viśiṣṭa*).
(Refutation of the theory that the word denotes the individual, due to defects such as the infinity of denotative powers:
It cannot denote the individual, because that would entail the postulation of an infinite number of denotative powers for individuals.

Even though there is identity in the generic form (*jāti-rūpa*) that characterizes each individual instance, just as there is a difference in denotative power (*śakti-bheda*) in words such as *saindhava* due to [the difference between] salt and horse-ness, so too here,

because pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*) lacks the status of being the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*), it is the particularity of each respective instance (*tattadvyaktitva*) alone that serves as that delimitor; therefore, their difference is unavoidable.

Now, even if it is held that [the word] denotes a single individual, since "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) is over-pervasive (*atiprasakta*), it cannot logically serve as the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). Consequently, only the "individuality of that specific instance" (*tadvyaktitva*) could be the delimitor of denotability; thus, in the absence of a recollection having that specific instance as its object, there would be the undesirable consequence (*anāpatti*) that no cognition of any other individual arises from the word "pot. However, if—according to the method previously stated—it is postulated that the cause is a certainty (*niścaya*) regarding the possession of the word "pot" through the relation of denotability, taking that "individuality of that specific instance" as the delimitor of the subject (*dharmitāvacchedaka*), [then the desired result follows].
And although there is an infinity of capacities (*śakti*), nevertheless, because it pertains to the result (*phalamukha*), there is no fault;

for since the capacity of that particular individual is accepted as the delimiting factor of the capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), even when the capacity is grasped with respect to a single individual, the capacity appears as a relation (*saṃbandha*). Thus, even if there is no recollection of it in its specific form, there is no deficiency.

If it were argued that even though "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) is over-pervasive, its status as a delimiting property of the subject (dharmitāvacchedakatva) with respect to that specific individual alone is not untenable, he replies to that: "Pot-ness," etc.

(B1) In your view, there would be an infinite regress of causal relations—and thus excessive complexity—due to the lack of a decisive reason (*vinigamanāviraha*) for choosing between two possibilities: either that the cause is the certainty that "the pot possesses the word 'pot' (*ghaṭapada')" by way of the relation of denotability (*śakyatva*), with "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) as the delimiting property of the subject (*dharmitāvacchedaka*), in the form "the pot possesses the word 'pot'" (*ghaṭo ghaṭapadavān*); or that the cause is the certainty that "the word 'pot' possesses the pot" by way of the relation of denotative power (*śaktatva*), with "word-ness" (*padatva*) as the delimiting property of the subject, in the form "the word 'pot' possesses the pot" (*ghaṭapadaṃ ghaṭavat*).

In our view, however, there is parsimony (*lāghava*), because we postulate that the cause of the cognition "the word *ghaṭa* possesses potness" (*ghaṭatvavat*)—which takes the state of being the word *ghaṭa* (*ghaṭapadatva*) as the delimiting property of the subject (*dharmitāvacchedaka*) and consists in the certainty that it possesses potness through the relation of denotative power (*śaktatva*)—is simply that very certainty.
Nor can you charge me with the opposite error;

for if that were the case, since potness cannot be the subject in its own form (*svarūpeṇa*), the property of "potness-ness" (*ghaṭatvatva*) would have to enter as the delimiting property of the subjecthood, and you yourself have already stated that this results in complexity (*gaurava*).

Therefore, the cognition "the word 'ghaṭa' possesses the property of being denotable (śakyatva) by means of the relation of denotation, [and this property] is delimited by 'pot-ness-ness' (ghaṭatvatva)" is not the cause;
rather, it is only the cognition "the word 'ghaṭa' possesses the property of pot-ness by means of the relation of denotative power (śaktatva).
This is because, since it is possible for a universal (jāti) to function as a qualifier in its own right, there is no need to include 'pot-ness-ness' (ghaṭatvatva).

Furthermore, there is no evidence that the universal (*jāti*) is a qualifier (*prakāratā*) by its own nature only through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), and not through any other relation; for even our opponents do not accept it in such a way.
Consequently, even in the case of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), the capacity (*śakti*) resides in "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) alone, on account of parsimony (*lāghava*).
Furthermore, [the objection regarding] the infinity of capacities and so forth does not apply to our view;
therefore, because it is the first to be presented to the mind, the expressive power (śakti) resides in the genus (jāti) alone.
The same applies to words such as *aruṇā* ("red"), where the power resides either in the quality (*guṇa*) itself or in the state of being a quality (*guṇatva*).
But it does not [denote] the substance qualified by that [universal].

How, then, is there a cognition of the individual (*vyakti*)? It is because of their non-difference (*abheda*), or because it is logically consistent to accept that the delimitor of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) belongs precisely to the verbal cognition of the individual as qualified by the universal and the quality, given the aforementioned cause.
In reality, however, the state of being a word denoting a genus (*jāti*) or a quality (*guṇa*) alone is the delimitor of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) due to parsimony (*lāghava*).

As for the individual (*vyakti*), it does not appear from the word at all in instances involving the instrumental case, such as "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*) or "one buys with a red [cow]" (*aruṇayā krīṇāti*);
for it is the genus and the quality themselves that are logically established as the instruments (*karaṇa*) by means of delimiting the substance (*dravya*).

Even in the case of gender and number, by the principle of the *pāśādhikaraṇa*, there is a secondary (pārṣṭhika) connection with the genus (*jāti*) or quality (*guṇa*) through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Therefore, in that context, the cognition of the substance occurs precisely through the mode of a relation. However, in instances such as those ending in the accusative case, since it is impossible for the genus or quality to be construed as the object (*karman*) and so forth, the individual (*vyakti*) is understood through indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

The connection of that [universal] itself with [grammatical] functions such as being the object (*karman*) and so forth, as well as its connection with gender, number, and so on, occurs precisely through direct relation;
and its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is mediated by the individual (*vyakti*). Thus, everything is well-established.

The purpose [of this discussion] is as follows: according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), since words such as *rathantara* denote the *ṛc* verses, in injunctions such as "he sings the *rathantara* on the two *uttara* verses," there would be an application of the original (*yoni*) verse to the function indicated by the word *uttara*.
However, according to the established conclusion (siddhānta), it will be stated that there is an extension of the mode of singing (*gīti*) to the *uttara* verses.
Thus ends the third quarter of the first chapter in the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā* composed by the venerable Khaṇḍadeva.
(B2) (The establishment of two alternative positions: that it is a quality, or that it is the nature of being a quality. It is indeed a quality.

The meaning is this: when even the quality of redness existing on the surface of the earth is one and the same, then it is simply the quality [itself]; but when there is a distinction among the various instances of the quality of redness, then, because a genus residing in multiple individuals is possible, the denotative power resides in the quality-ness (guṇatva).
(The justification for the cognition of the individual through the non-difference of the universal and the individual, etc.
"Because of non-difference" (abhedāt).

For just as there is a distinction between the cloth and its "cloth-ness" or here the "whiteness," based on the cognition "this is a cloth" or "this is white"—a distinction established between two things that are inseparable (ayutasiddha)—likewise, their non-difference is also established by cognitions such as "this is a cow" or "this is white.
Nor does this imply that the universal (jāti) would be non-eternal if it were non-different from the individual (vyakti);
for although it is eternal in its nature as a universal, its non-eternality in its nature as an individual is something we also accept.

Therefore, even though words such as "jar" denote a genus (*jāti*), because there is no difference from the individual (*vyakti*), the cognition of the individual is established through the genus itself.
Nor does this lead to the redundancy of the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) on the grounds that the individual would also become a denotation due to such non-difference;
for even if the individual is a denotation, it is not so in its aspect as an individual, since we accept both difference and non-difference.

Moreover, this is stated by relying on the position established as primary in the *Nyāyasudhā*, for the purpose of demonstrating that [the self] consists of birth (*jāti*) and so forth, thereby ensuring the meaningfulness of the section (*adhikaraṇa*).

(Another alternative view: that the delimitor of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) is precisely the status of being a verbal cognition qualified by a genus (*jāti*), etc., which possesses the knowledge of the word’s power (*śaktijñāna*).

However, even if non-difference [between the genus and the individual] is accepted, if one were to maintain that the status of being a verbal cognition of the individual (*vyaktiśābdabodhatva*)—just like the status of being a verbal cognition of the genus (*jātiśābdabodhatva*)—is a separate delimitor of the effect for the cause consisting in the knowledge of the power, then one would have to accept that the cognitions of the genus and the individual occur sequentially; yet such sequential occurrence is not experienced.)

Since [otherwise] there would be no cognition of the specific qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) and it would consequently result in being of the nature of indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*), they maintain that by accepting the status of "verbal cognition qualified by potness" as the effect-determinant (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) for the previously mentioned cause—the cognition of the possession of potness—one can thus have the cognition of both through the single power of the genus (*jāti*).
According to their view, he states another position: "in the manner described."
(An introduction to one's own view, preceded by a critique of the second position:

In this view, since the individual entity (*vyakti*) which serves as the substantive (*viśeṣya*) would alone be connected to the action through the medium of being the instrument (*karaṇatva*) and so forth, the genus (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*) which serve as its qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) would not be so connected.

Consequently, in the case of the *caru* offering of seventeen jars, when the handfuls are poured out (*nirvāpa*), the preservation of the number four by means of omitting the subordinate handfuls (*jaghanyamuṣṭi*) would not be established.

Because it is more logical that the favoring of the fist itself should take precedence over even the subordinate [member], he states another position as his own view due to this underlying dissatisfaction: "In reality, however... (vastutastu).

(The manner in which the cognition of individuals is established according to our own view; [this applies] to words ending in the singular as well as those ending in the plural, etc.,) by way of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
This [phrase] is to be applied by connecting it with the words "because the status of being an instrument is established.

Thus, gender and number also, through the proximity of being expressed by the same word, are construed with the status of being an instrument itself via the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
The meaning is that the connection with the genus (*jāti*) and the quality (*guṇa*) occurs subsequently (*pārṣṭhika*).

Now, one might object: "Since gender and number are perceived as qualifiers of the individual, let it be that the nominal stem (prātipadika) indicates the individual itself in accordance with them. To refute this doubt, it was stated, "by the principle of the *pāśādhikaraṇa*";
the meaning of this is as follows:

Just as in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*), the elevation of the primary noun-base *pāśa* (rope) was not accepted in the *pāśa*-mantra in accordance with the requirement for the connection with the plurality of the subordinate elements,

so too here figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not appropriate. However, where even the subsequent connection with duality or plurality is sublated in the case of a genus (*jāti*), [the application of the mantra is barred].
In that case, let it be accepted as referring to the very individual (vyakti) characterized by its arrival;
however, in the present context, the sense is that "it" (saḥ) is properly connected with the genus (jāti) and the quality (guṇa) through the singular ending.

(An explanation of how the cognition of an individual is established through secondary indication in cases such as those ending in the accusative case): "In the case of [words] ending in the accusative case, etc. means: In instances where a word ends in the accusative case, the cognition of an individual is established by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). This is because the primary denotation (*śakya-artha*) of a word—such as a universal (*jāti*)—cannot logically serve as the direct object (*karman*) of an action like "bringing" (*ānayanādi*), since a universal is devoid of spatial location and cannot be moved. Therefore, the word indicates its own substrate (*vyakti*), which is the actual substratum of the universal; it is this indicated individual that is understood as the object of the action. Thus, in such cases, the cognition of the individual is justified through secondary indication.
By the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), other kārakas such as the recipient (saṃpradāna) are included.

Nor is there a contradiction regarding the simultaneous occurrence of two functions [primary and secondary]; for, just as in the case of the word *gaṅgā*, where after the primary meaning (the current) has been presented, the secondary function (lakṣaṇā) is accepted before the cognition of the connection with the meaning of another word occurs, so too here, by accepting that [simultaneity], such a contradiction does not arise.

Therefore, it should be understood that this [repetition] occurs only when that very same word conveys its meaning through another function (*vṛtti*) subsequent to the cognition of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

Nor does the acceptance of two successive cognitions lead to the undesirable consequence of the [second cognition] being indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*) due to the absence of a cognition of qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*);
for the point is that such a result is actually desired.
And there is grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya).

The meaning is that when gender and number are construed with [the action of] "object-ness" (karmatva) and so forth through the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) by virtue of being heard in the same word (*samānābhidhānaśruti*), their coreferentiality is to be understood as residing in a single locus (*ekavṛttitva*).
(Refutation of the view that the individual qualified by the genus is the denotation):

Thus, it should be understood that the impossibility of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in expressions such as "the cow is white" must be resolved solely through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). As for the position that the individual qualified by the configuration (*ākṛti*) is the denotation, that too must be rejected; for once the denotability of the genus is established as necessary, to further postulate the denotability of the individual would result in the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).
The purpose is as follows.

In the view that the term *ṛk* denotes the verse-text itself, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) holds that because it is impossible to enjoin a verse within another verse, the word *uttarā* (the subsequent verse) must be taken as indicating its function through secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), thereby enjoining [the chant] by way of occupying its place. However, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), since chanting is possible even within another verse, there is no figurative indication; rather, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of that [quality]. This is the purpose of this section, which will be examined in the seventh book (*adhyāya*). This is the meaning.
(Refutation of the prima facie view and established conclusion as formulated by the *Prakāśakāra*, followed by the presentation of his own intended purpose.

As for what the *Prakāśakāra*s have stated—namely, that in cases such as "He sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*) and "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), since the prima facie view holds that all individual instances of rice and oblations are denoted, the sprinkling, curd, and so forth are applied there by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*); thus, by subverting the context (*prakaraṇa*) and proximity (*sannidhi*), [the injunction applies] even to worldly rice-grains...
In the case of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other oblations (*homa*), there would be curd in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*);

however, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), since the universals of "rice-ness" (*vrīhitva*) and "oblation-ness" (*homatva*), which constitute the literal meaning of the words, are fully present even in the original rice-oblations, there is no violation of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) even while favoring the context (*prakaraṇa*) and proximity (*sannidhi*).
Thus, [the rule applies] only to the original [rites].

Since, even according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), that [universal] is present as pervading the individuals other than the rice used in the primary oblation (*prakṛta-vrīhi-homa*)— and thus cannot be excluded— and since all [individuals] would otherwise be incapable of being employed in linguistic practice, it is necessary to examine the context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth in order to avoid such futility; therefore,

just as the exclusion of those other than the primary ones occurs by virtue of that [examination], the same possibility exists under the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) as well, and thus there is no distinction between the two cases, such as in the instance of the second [oblation] and others.

Since it must be established that all individuals are manifested through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), the fault remains as it was; therefore, this [position] is incorrect and was disregarded by the Venerable Master.
Thus ends the ninth section, the Discussion on Form (Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa).
Thus ends the third quarter of the first chapter in the *Bhāṭṭadīpikāprabhāvalī*, composed by Śambhubhaṭṭa, the ornament of the scholarly circle and disciple of the venerable Khaṇḍadeva.
